parts.label: a
parts.text:
A solution of an unknown salt is tested. Aqueous sodium hydroxide gives a white precipitate that dissolves in excess to give a colourless solution. Aqueous ammonia gives a white precipitate that does not dissolve in excess. Which cation is present?
A Al³⁺
B Ca²⁺
C Zn²⁺
D Cr³⁺
parts.working: Al³⁺: white ppt soluble in excess NaOH(aq), insoluble in excess NH₃(aq). Zn²⁺ is wrong because its white ppt also dissolves in excess ammonia; Ca²⁺ ppt does not dissolve in excess NaOH; Cr³⁺ gives a green ppt.

practice.stem: Four gases, A to D, are collected in test-tubes during practical work.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Gas A relights a glowing splint. Identify gas A.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Gas B turns damp red litmus paper blue. Identify gas B.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Gas C bleaches damp litmus paper. Identify gas C.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Gas D turns acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII) from purple to colourless. Identify gas D.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Describe the test for carbon dioxide and its positive result.
parts.answer: Bubble the gas through limewater; limewater turns milky.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Four colourless solutions are each acidified with dilute nitric acid and then aqueous silver nitrate is added. Which solution gives a cream precipitate?
A sodium chloride
B sodium bromide
C sodium iodide
D sodium nitrate
parts.working: Silver bromide is a cream precipitate. Silver chloride is white and silver iodide is yellow. Sodium nitrate gives no precipitate, because all nitrates are soluble. The dilute nitric acid removes carbonate or hydroxide ions that would form a different precipitate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a test for sulfate ions in a solution. Give the reagents you add, in the order you add them, and the result of a positive test.
parts.answer: Add dilute hydrochloric acid (dilute nitric acid is also acceptable), then add aqueous barium chloride (or barium nitrate). A white precipitate shows that sulfate ions are present.
parts.working: 1 mark: dilute hydrochloric acid added first. 1 mark: aqueous barium chloride (or barium nitrate). 1 mark: white precipitate for a positive result.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solid X is calcium carbonate. A student adds dilute hydrochloric acid to solid X in a test tube and a gas is given off. Describe the test for this gas and state the result of a positive test.
parts.answer: Pass the gas into (or shake it with) limewater. Limewater turns milky (cloudy) if the gas is carbon dioxide.
parts.working: 1 mark: limewater used. 1 mark: milky or cloudy result.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the word equation for the reaction of calcium carbonate with dilute hydrochloric acid.
parts.answer: calcium carbonate + hydrochloric acid → calcium chloride + water + carbon dioxide
parts.working: 1 mark: correct reactants. 1 mark: all three products, correct.

practice.stem:
A student in a Lahore school laboratory tests a blue-green solid X dissolved in water.
Test 1: flame test — blue-green flame.
Test 2: aqueous sodium hydroxide added dropwise then in excess — light blue precipitate, insoluble in excess.
Test 3: aqueous ammonia added dropwise then in excess — light blue precipitate, which dissolves in excess to give a dark blue solution.
Test 4: dilute nitric acid added, then aqueous silver nitrate — white precipitate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the cation in X. Give one observation from the table that supports your answer.
parts.answer: Copper(II) ion, Cu²⁺; e.g. light blue precipitate that dissolves in excess ammonia to give a dark blue solution (or blue-green flame).
parts.working: B1 Cu²⁺/copper(II); B1 one correct supporting observation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the anion in X.
parts.working: B1 white precipitate with acidified silver nitrate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why dilute nitric acid, and not dilute hydrochloric acid, is used to acidify the solution in test 4.
parts.answer: Hydrochloric acid contains chloride ions, which would themselves give a white precipitate with silver nitrate, so a false positive result.
parts.working: M1 HCl adds Cl⁻ ions; A1 these would give a white ppt whatever X contained.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest the formula of X.

practice.stem: A student collects a colourless liquid from a well near Mithi in the Thar desert and wants to know whether it is water and whether it is pure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a chemical test that shows the liquid contains water. Give the result.
parts.answer: Add anhydrous copper(II) sulfate: it turns from white to blue (or anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride: blue to pink).
parts.working: B1 reagent; B1 colour change both colours.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The chemical test does not show that the water is pure. Describe a physical test that would show whether the water is pure.
parts.answer: Measure its boiling point (or melting point): pure water boils at exactly 100 °C (melts at 0 °C) at normal pressure.
parts.working: B1 boiling/melting point; B1 correct value 100 °C / 0 °C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The well water boils at 101.5 °C. What does this tell you about it?
parts.answer: It is impure; it contains dissolved substances.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A gas is collected in a test tube and a lighted splint is held at the mouth of the tube. The gas burns with a squeaky pop. Which gas is it?
A carbon dioxide
B hydrogen
C oxygen
D nitrogen
parts.working: Hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop. Oxygen relights a glowing splint but does not pop with a lighted one. Carbon dioxide and nitrogen both put out a lighted splint.

practice.stem: A student has four solutions: lithium chloride, sodium chloride, potassium chloride and copper(II) chloride. The student carries out flame tests with a clean nichrome wire.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the nichrome wire is cleaned before each flame test.
parts.answer: Dip the wire in concentrated hydrochloric acid, then hold it in the blue flame until no colour is seen. Repeat if needed.
parts.working: 1 mark: dipped in concentrated hydrochloric acid. 1 mark: heated in the flame until the flame shows no colour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the flame colour expected for copper(II) chloride.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two reasons why the wire must be cleaned between tests.
parts.answer: Any two: a colour left on the wire from the previous solution would mix with the new colour; so the flame colour shows only the metal ion in the sample being tested; so the results are not wrong.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of the points above.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solid Y is suspected to be ammonium chloride. State the reagent you add to solid Y and describe what you do to make a gas.
parts.answer: Add aqueous sodium hydroxide, then warm the mixture gently.
parts.working: 1 mark: aqueous sodium hydroxide. 1 mark: warm the mixture.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the test for the gas and the result of a positive test.
parts.answer: Hold a piece of damp red litmus paper at the mouth of the tube. It turns blue, showing ammonia is given off.
parts.working: 1 mark: damp red litmus paper held at the mouth of the tube (or a glass rod with concentrated hydrochloric acid to give white smoke). 1 mark: turns blue.

practice.stem:
Solution Y contains one cation and one anion.
Test 1: aqueous sodium hydroxide added — green precipitate, insoluble in excess.
Test 2: the mixture from test 1 is warmed — no gas that affects damp red litmus paper.
Test 3: aluminium foil is added to the warm mixture — a gas is produced that turns damp red litmus paper blue.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the cation in Y. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Iron(II), Fe²⁺: green precipitate with NaOH(aq) that does not dissolve in excess.
parts.working: B1 Fe²⁺; B1 green ppt insoluble in excess.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the anion in Y.
parts.working: B1 ammonia produced only when aluminium is present.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why test 2 was needed before the result of test 3 could be used.
parts.answer: Ammonium ions also give ammonia when warmed with NaOH(aq); test 2 shows no ammonium ions are present, so the ammonia in test 3 must come from reduction of nitrate by aluminium.
parts.working: M1 NH₄⁺ gives ammonia with warm NaOH; A1 test 2 rules out NH₄⁺ so ammonia comes from nitrate.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest what the student would see if the green precipitate in test 1 was left to stand in air for some time.
parts.answer: It turns orange-brown / red-brown at the surface (iron(II) is oxidised to iron(III)).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which reagent can be used to tell aqueous sodium sulfite apart from aqueous sodium sulfate?
A dilute nitric acid followed by aqueous barium nitrate
B acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII)
C aqueous sodium hydroxide
D a flame test
parts.working: Sulfite ions decolourise acidified potassium manganate(VII) (purple to colourless); sulfate ions do not. A is wrong because nitric acid oxidises sulfite to sulfate, so both would give a white precipitate; C and D give the same result for both (both contain Na⁺).

practice.stem: A technician in Peshawar has four unlabelled bottles of colourless solution. She knows they are zinc chloride, aluminium chloride, potassium bromide and potassium iodide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using aqueous ammonia only, describe how the technician could tell the zinc chloride solution from the aluminium chloride solution. Give the result for each.
parts.answer: Add aqueous ammonia dropwise then in excess to each. Both give a white precipitate. With zinc chloride the precipitate dissolves in excess to give a colourless solution; with aluminium chloride the precipitate does not dissolve.
parts.working: M1 dropwise then excess; A1 Zn²⁺ white ppt soluble in excess; A1 Al³⁺ white ppt insoluble in excess.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the technician could tell the potassium bromide solution from the potassium iodide solution. Give the result for each.
parts.answer: Acidify with dilute nitric acid and add aqueous silver nitrate. Bromide gives a cream precipitate; iodide gives a yellow precipitate.
parts.working: B1 acidify with dilute nitric acid + silver nitrate; B1 cream for bromide; B1 yellow for iodide.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest a test that would show that the potassium solutions both contain potassium ions. Give the result.

practice.stem: Solution R gives a white precipitate with aqueous sodium hydroxide. The precipitate does not dissolve when more sodium hydroxide is added. Solution R also gives a white precipitate with aqueous ammonia that does not dissolve in excess ammonia.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the cation in solution R.
parts.working: 1 mark. Aluminium ions would give a precipitate that dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide, but magnesium does not.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the ionic equation, with state symbols, for the reaction of the cation with aqueous sodium hydroxide.
parts.working: 1 mark: Mg(OH)₂ is the solid product. 1 mark: correct ions on the left and balanced with state symbols.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the result with excess sodium hydroxide tells magnesium ions apart from aluminium ions.
parts.answer: Aluminium hydroxide dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide (forming a soluble complex). Magnesium hydroxide does not dissolve, so a white precipitate that stays in excess shows Mg²⁺.
parts.working: 1 mark: aluminium hydroxide dissolves in excess. 1 mark: magnesium hydroxide does not, so the precipitate remains.

practice.stem: Gas Z is a pale yellow-green gas with a choking smell. It is made in the laboratory and tested as follows.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name gas Z.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A piece of damp blue litmus paper is held in the gas. Describe what is seen.
parts.answer: The paper turns red first, then the colour is bleached so the paper becomes white.
parts.working: 1 mark: turns red. 1 mark: then bleached (white).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why dry litmus paper held in the same gas does not show the same result.
parts.answer: Dry chlorine does not form the acid and bleaching species that need water, so the litmus paper does not change colour.
parts.working: 1 mark: needs water to form acid and bleaching products.

practice.stem: A student investigates how the concentration of hydrochloric acid affects the rate of its reaction with marble chips. She collects the carbon dioxide over water in an upturned measuring cylinder and records the volume every 30 seconds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the measuring cylinder is not a good way to measure the volume of gas.
parts.answer: Some carbon dioxide dissolves in the water / gas escapes before the bung is replaced / the readings are hard to read accurately while the cylinder is in the water.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name a piece of apparatus that would give more accurate measurements of the gas volume.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the student should use the same mass of marble chips each time.
parts.answer: Only one variable (the concentration of acid) should be changed so that the test is fair; more marble would change the volume of gas / rate.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the student should repeat each experiment.
parts.answer: To check the results are reliable / to identify anomalous results and calculate an average.

practice.stem: A student investigates how temperature affects the time taken for a cross drawn on paper under a flask to disappear when dilute hydrochloric acid is added to aqueous sodium thiosulfate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the independent variable.
parts.answer: Temperature of the sodium thiosulfate solution

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the dependent variable.
parts.answer: Time for the cross to disappear

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two variables that should be controlled.
parts.answer: Any two of: volume of thiosulfate; concentration of thiosulfate; volume of acid; concentration of acid; same flask/cross; same observer.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest how the student could keep the solution at a steady temperature.

practice.stem: A student compares the energy released by three fuels: ethanol, paraffin and butane. Each fuel is burned under a metal can containing water, and the temperature rise of the water is measured.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the independent variable.
parts.answer: The type of fuel (ethanol, paraffin or butane).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two variables that should be kept the same.
parts.answer: Any two: volume of water; starting temperature of the water; distance from the flame to the can; time for which each fuel burns.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of the variables above.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one way to reduce heat lost from the can to the surroundings.
parts.answer: Put a lid on the can, use a draught shield, or insulate the can.

practice.stem: A student prepares dilute sulfuric acid from concentrated sulfuric acid in a school laboratory.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one safety precaution the student should take.
parts.answer: Wear eye protection (safety goggles), a lab coat and gloves.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the correct order of mixing and explain why.
parts.answer: Add the concentrated acid slowly to the water, not the water to the acid. Mixing releases a large amount of heat; adding the acid to a large volume of water spreads the heat out and reduces the risk of boiling and spitting.
parts.working: 1 mark: acid added to water (not water to acid). 1 mark: heat released is spread out, so the mixture does not boil or spit.

practice.stem: A student investigates the effect of temperature on the time taken for a cross to disappear when sodium thiosulfate solution reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one variable that must be kept the same in each run.
parts.answer: Any one: the volume and concentration of the sodium thiosulfate; the volume and concentration of the hydrochloric acid; the same flask and cross.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the temperature of the reaction mixture is controlled.
parts.answer: Warm the sodium thiosulfate solution in a water bath to the chosen temperature. Measure the temperature just before adding the acid and use a thermometer in the mixture.
parts.working: 1 mark: water bath used to warm the thiosulfate. 1 mark: temperature checked just before adding the acid.

practice.stem: Rock salt from a mine in the Salt Range contains sodium chloride mixed with insoluble rock.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an experiment to find the percentage by mass of insoluble impurities in a sample of crushed rock salt. You may use common laboratory apparatus, including an electronic balance and an oven.
parts.answer: Weigh, dissolve, filter, wash and dry the residue, weigh, calculate.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: weigh a known mass of rock salt (e.g. 10.0 g) on a balance; add to a beaker of water and stir (warm) until all the salt has dissolved; weigh a filter paper; filter the mixture; wash the residue with a little distilled water to remove salt solution; dry the residue and paper in an oven (or warm place) and weigh; repeat drying and weighing until mass is constant; mass of impurity = mass of dried paper + residue − mass of paper; % = mass of impurity ÷ mass of rock salt × 100.

practice.stem: A student measures the temperature change when 25 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid is mixed with 25 cm³ of aqueous sodium hydroxide in a glass beaker.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a polystyrene cup is better than a glass beaker for this experiment.
parts.answer: Polystyrene is a poor conductor of heat (insulator), so less heat is lost to the surroundings and the temperature rise measured is larger / more accurate.
parts.working: M1 insulator / less heat loss; A1 temperature change nearer the true value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one further improvement to reduce heat loss. Explain why it is an improvement.
parts.answer: Put a lid on the cup — this reduces heat lost by convection/evaporation from the surface.
parts.working: B1 lid (or stand cup in a beaker / lag it); B1 reason.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The student uses a measuring cylinder to measure 25 cm³ of acid. Suggest a more accurate piece of apparatus and explain why it is an improvement.
parts.answer: A volumetric pipette (or burette); it measures a fixed volume more accurately / smaller uncertainty.

practice.stem: A student in a Karachi college compares the energy released by burning two liquid fuels, ethanol and propan-1-ol. Each fuel is burned in a spirit burner under a copper can containing water, and the temperature rise of the water is measured.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two variables that must be kept the same to make this a fair comparison.
parts.answer: Any two of: volume (mass) of water; distance from flame to can; starting temperature of water; temperature rise / time of heating; same can; same burner design.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The temperature rise measured is much smaller than expected from data books. Suggest two reasons.
parts.answer: Heat lost to the surroundings/air; heat used to warm the can; incomplete combustion (soot); evaporation of fuel from the wick.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how the student finds the mass of fuel burned.
parts.answer: Weigh the spirit burner (with cap) before and after heating; subtract.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation into how the surface area of marble chips affects the rate of reaction with dilute hydrochloric acid. Your answer should include: the apparatus; the method in numbered steps; the variables (independent, dependent and controlled); and how the results will be made reliable.
parts.answer: Apparatus: conical flask with bung and delivery tube, gas syringe or measuring cylinder over water, stopwatch, balance. Independent variable: surface area (lumps compared with powder). Controlled: same mass of marble, same volume and concentration of acid, same temperature. Method: add the acid, record the volume of gas at regular times. Reliability: repeat each experiment and calculate averages; plot volume against time and use the gradient as the rate.
parts.working: 1 mark for apparatus. 1 mark for the independent variable (surface area). 1 mark for at least two controlled variables. 1 mark for a clear measuring method (gas volume at set times). 1 mark for repeats or averages. 1 mark for plotting and using the gradient as the rate.

practice.stem: A student measures the temperature change when a metal powder reacts with 50 cm³ of dilute acid in a polystyrene cup. The temperature rises by 4.0 °C. The student concludes that the reaction released 4.0 °C of energy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the error in the student's conclusion.
parts.answer: The temperature rise (4.0 °C) is not an energy value. The energy released depends on the mass and specific heat capacity of the water (and mixture) as well as the temperature change.
parts.working: 1 mark: the student confused a temperature change with an energy value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two sources of heat loss in this experiment.
parts.answer: Any two: heat escapes to the air from the open top of the cup; heat is absorbed by the cup and the thermometer; heat is lost through the walls of the cup.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two sources.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one improvement to reduce heat loss.
parts.answer: Put a lid on the cup, with a hole for the thermometer.

practice.stem: A student investigates how the voltage across an electrolysis cell affects the mass of copper deposited on a copper cathode from copper(II) sulfate solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student should prepare the copper cathode and measure its mass.
parts.answer: Dry the cathode and weigh it before the electrolysis; after the electrolysis, dry it again and weigh it. Record both masses.
parts.working: 1 mark: weighed before. 1 mark: dried and weighed again after.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two variables that should be kept the same in each experiment.
parts.answer: Any two: the time for electrolysis; the electrode area; the concentration of the copper(II) sulfate solution; the distance between the electrodes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the mass of copper deposited may increase when the voltage is increased.
parts.answer: A higher voltage gives a larger current, so more electrons pass and more copper is deposited.

practice.stem: Antacid tablets are sold in many pharmacies in Pakistan. Three brands, P, Q and R, each claim to relieve indigestion by neutralising stomach acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an experiment to find which brand of antacid tablet neutralises the most hydrochloric acid per tablet. You are provided with dilute hydrochloric acid of known concentration, methyl orange indicator and common laboratory apparatus. Each tablet is an insoluble base.
parts.answer: Direct titration: titrate one crushed tablet of each brand (in water with methyl orange) with the hydrochloric acid from a burette; the brand needing the largest volume of acid neutralises the most.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: crush one tablet of brand 1 and place in a conical flask with water / measured volume of distilled water; add a few drops of methyl orange; fill a burette with the hydrochloric acid and record the initial reading; add acid from the burette while swirling until the indicator changes from yellow to orange/red and stays; record the final reading and work out the volume of acid used; repeat with one tablet of each other brand (same mass or same number of tablets, same indicator amount); repeat each to get concordant results; brand needing the largest volume of acid neutralises the most.

practice.stem: A metal higher in the reactivity series than copper displaces copper from aqueous copper(II) sulfate, and the reaction releases heat.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an experiment to put three metals, magnesium, zinc and iron, in order of reactivity using the temperature change when each metal powder is added to aqueous copper(II) sulfate. Say how you will use your results.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: measure a fixed volume (e.g. 25 cm³) of copper(II) sulfate solution into a polystyrene cup; record the starting temperature with a thermometer; add a fixed mass (e.g. 1.0 g, an excess) of one metal powder; stir and record the highest temperature reached; repeat with each metal using fresh solution of the same concentration and same mass of powder; calculate the temperature rise; larger temperature rise = more reactive metal; repeat for reliable averages.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an experiment to find the mass of water in a sample of hydrated copper(II) sulfate. Include: the apparatus; the steps; the measurements; how you are sure all the water has been removed; and how the mass of water is found.
parts.answer: Apparatus: crucible or evaporating basin, balance, tripod and gauze or heat source, clamp. Steps: weigh the empty crucible, add the crystals and weigh again, heat gently until the blue colour turns white, allow to cool, weigh. Repeat heating and weighing until the mass is constant. Mass of water = mass before heating minus mass after heating.
parts.working: 1 mark: suitable apparatus. 1 mark: weighing of empty container and of the crystals. 1 mark: gentle heating until blue turns white. 1 mark: cooling before weighing. 1 mark: heating and weighing repeated until a constant mass. 1 mark: mass of water = loss in mass.

practice.stem: A student collects hydrogen over water in a measuring cylinder by reacting zinc with dilute hydrochloric acid. The student expects 40.0 cm³ of gas but measures 35.0 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two reasons why the measured volume could be less than expected.
parts.answer: Any two: some gas escapes before the cylinder is full; a leak at the delivery tube connection; some hydrogen dissolves in the water; misreading of the scale.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid reasons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the student could make the volume measurement more accurate.
parts.answer: Use a gas syringe (or a measuring cylinder with finer scale); make sure the apparatus is airtight; read the scale at eye level.
parts.working: 1 mark for a suitable change of apparatus or method. 1 mark for a correct explanation (less gas lost or misread).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one way to make the results more reliable.
parts.answer: Repeat the experiment and calculate a mean volume.

practice.stem:
A student adds a piece of magnesium ribbon to excess dilute sulfuric acid and collects the hydrogen in a gas syringe.
Time / s: 0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180
Volume of gas / cm³: 0, 46, 66, 75, 79, 80, 80

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the rate of reaction changes during the experiment.
parts.answer: The rate is fastest at the start and decreases over time; it becomes zero by 150 s when the reaction stops.
parts.working: B1 fast then slower; B1 stops / zero by 150 s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average rate of reaction in the first 30 s, in cm³/s. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the total volume of hydrogen produced.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the reaction stops.
parts.answer: One of the reactants (the magnesium) has all been used up.
parts.working: B1 accept the limiting reactant is used up.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Different masses of magnesium are reacted with excess dilute hydrochloric acid at room temperature and pressure. 1 mol of gas occupies 24 dm³.
Mass of Mg / g: 0.024, 0.048, 0.072, 0.096
Volume of H₂ / cm³: 24, 48, 60, 96
Which mass gave an anomalous result?
A 0.024 g
B 0.048 g
C 0.072 g
D 0.096 g
parts.working: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂; each 0.024 g (0.001 mol) gives 24 cm³, so 0.072 g should give 72 cm³, not 60 cm³. The other results fit the 1 g : 1000 cm³ pattern.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The four titres are 24.10 cm³, 24.05 cm³, 24.00 cm³ and 24.45 cm³. What is the mean of the concordant titres?
A 24.05 cm³
B 24.15 cm³
C 24.25 cm³
D 24.45 cm³
parts.working: 24.45 cm³ is anomalous (more than 0.1 cm³ away from the others) and is discarded. Mean of 24.10, 24.05 and 24.00 = 24.05 cm³. B is the mean of all four titres, which wrongly includes the anomalous value.

practice.stem: A student reacts different masses of magnesium with 50 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid in a polystyrene cup and records the temperature rise. Mass of magnesium (g): 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.40. Temperature rise (°C): 6.0, 12.1, 17.9, 24.2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the dependent variable.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the temperature rise per gram of magnesium for the 0.20 g result. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the acid should be in excess in this experiment.
parts.answer: So that all the magnesium reacts; the temperature rise then depends on the mass of magnesium used.
parts.working: 1 mark: the magnesium is the limiting reagent and all of it reacts.

practice.stem: Calcium carbonate reacts with excess dilute hydrochloric acid. The mass lost (carbon dioxide escaping) is measured every minute. Time (min): 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Mass lost (g): 0.00, 0.45, 0.80, 1.05, 1.10, 1.10.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the rate of mass loss changes over the 5 minutes.
parts.answer: The rate is fastest at the start and slows down. The mass stops changing after about 4 minutes, so the reaction has finished (one reactant used up).
parts.working: 1 mark: rate decreases over time (steepest at the start). 1 mark: mass becomes constant at about 4 minutes, showing the reaction is complete.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of mass loss between 0 and 2 minutes, in g/min.

practice.stem: A student measures the volume of hydrogen made by four different metals reacting with the same acid. The results are to be shown on a graph.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the type of graph that should be drawn.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a line graph is not suitable.
parts.answer: The metals are separate categories rather than a continuous variable, so the points should not be joined by a line.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the variable that goes on the x-axis (horizontal axis).

parts.label: d
parts.text: State how the y-axis should be labelled.
parts.answer: Volume of hydrogen / cm³ (name and unit).

practice.stem:
25.0 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid is placed in a polystyrene cup. Aqueous sodium hydroxide of concentration 1.00 mol/dm³ is added from a burette in portions, and the highest temperature is recorded after each addition.
Volume of NaOH / cm³: 0.0, 4.0, 8.0, 12.0, 16.0, 24.0, 28.0, 32.0, 36.0
Temperature / °C: 21.5, 24.0, 26.5, 27.6, 31.4, 33.0, 32.4, 31.8, 31.2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which temperature reading is anomalous?
parts.working: B1 it lies below the straight line through the other early points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: When the two straight lines of best fit are drawn, the first line has the equation T = 21.5 + 0.62V and the second line has the equation T = 36.6 − 0.15V, where V is the volume of NaOH added in cm³. Calculate the volume of sodium hydroxide at which the lines meet. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of the hydrochloric acid in mol/dm³. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the temperature falls after the point where the two lines meet.
parts.answer: Neutralisation is complete; the cooler alkali added no longer reacts and heat is lost to the surroundings.

practice.stem:
A student titrates 25.0 cm³ of aqueous sodium carbonate with dilute hydrochloric acid using methyl orange.
Titration 1: initial burette reading 3.40 cm³, final 28.35 cm³
Titration 2: initial 1.90 cm³, final 26.30 cm³
Titration 3: initial 0.10 cm³, final 24.55 cm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of acid used in each titration.
parts.answer: Titration 1: 24.95 cm³; titration 2: 24.40 cm³; titration 3: 24.45 cm³
parts.working: B1 for two correct; B1 for all three, to 2 d.p.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which titrations are concordant and calculate the mean titre.
parts.working: B1 2 and 3 (within 0.10 cm³); B1 mean 24.43 (accept 24.43 or 24.42).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why titration 1 gave a larger volume.
parts.answer: It was the rough (trial) titration and the end-point was overshot.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A graph of volume of gas (cm³) against time (s) is a straight line through the origin. The volume is 60 cm³ at 120 s. What is the mean rate of reaction?
A 0.5 cm³/s
B 2.0 cm³/s
C 60 cm³/s
D 120 cm³/s
parts.working: Rate = volume ÷ time = 60 ÷ 120 = 0.5 cm³/s. B divides the time by the volume (120 ÷ 60 = 2.0), which gives the time per cm³, not the rate.

practice.stem: The solubility of potassium nitrate in 100 g of water was measured at four temperatures: 20 °C: 32 g; 40 °C: 64 g; 60 °C: 110 g; 80 °C: 169 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the trend in solubility as the temperature increases.
parts.answer: The solubility increases as the temperature increases. The increase is larger at the higher temperatures (the curve gets steeper).
parts.working: 1 mark: solubility increases with temperature. 1 mark: the increase per 20 °C is greater at higher temperatures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Estimate the solubility at 50 °C, assuming the graph between 40 °C and 60 °C is a straight line. Show your working.
parts.answer: 87 g of potassium nitrate per 100 g of water
parts.working: 1 mark: 64 + (110 − 64) × 10 ÷ 20. 1 mark: 87 g per 100 g of water.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the estimate in (b) may not be exact.
parts.answer: The graph is curved, not straight, so a straight-line estimate is only approximate. The estimate is also based on only four data points; more readings would improve it.
parts.working: 1 mark: the curve is not a straight line. 1 mark: only a few readings, so the estimate is an approximation.

practice.stem: A student titrates 25.0 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid with aqueous sodium hydroxide. The titres (cm³) are: 24.30, 24.25, 25.90, 24.35.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous titre and explain why it is not used in the mean.
parts.answer: 25.90 cm³. It differs by about 1.6 cm³ from the other titres (more than 0.1 cm³), so it is discarded; it was probably caused by a mistake such as overshooting the end point.
parts.working: 1 mark: 25.90 identified. 1 mark: reason (too far from the other results, so a mistake).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean of the concordant titres. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one way to improve the accuracy of the titration results.
parts.answer: Add the alkali drop by drop near the end point, or repeat until titres agree within 0.10 cm³.

practice.stem:
The solubility of a salt Z in water was measured at different temperatures.
Temperature / °C: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70
Solubility / g per 100 g water: 21, 32, 46, 64, 85, 110, 138

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the data to estimate the solubility of Z at 45 °C.
parts.answer: About 74 g per 100 g water (accept 72–76 from a smooth curve).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A saturated solution of Z in 50 g of water is cooled from 70 °C to 20 °C. Calculate the mass of Z that crystallises.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the trend shown by the data.
parts.answer: Solubility increases with temperature, and increases more steeply at higher temperatures.
parts.working: B1 both points for the mark: increases, and by larger amounts at high T.

practice.stem:
A student electrolyses aqueous copper(II) sulfate with a constant current and weighs the cathode at intervals.
Time / min: 5, 10, 15, 20, 30
Mass of copper deposited / g: 0.06, 0.12, 0.17, 0.24, 0.36

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result and suggest what its value should have been.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the relationship between mass of copper deposited and time.
parts.answer: Mass is directly proportional to time.
parts.working: B1 accept straight line through the origin.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict the mass of copper deposited after 25 minutes.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the 15-minute result was lower than expected.
parts.answer: Some copper fell off the cathode / cathode not dried properly before weighing / was weighed wet the other times / current changed.

practice.stem: Magnesium reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid at 25 °C. The volume of hydrogen is measured at intervals. Time (s): 0, 20, 40, 60, 80. Volume of hydrogen (cm³): 0, 18, 34, 46, 54.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average rate of reaction between 20 s and 40 s. Give the unit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the data, estimate the time when 30 cm³ of hydrogen has been collected. Show your working.
parts.working: 1 mark: straight-line estimate between 20 s (18 cm³) and 40 s (34 cm³): 20 + (30 − 18) ÷ (34 − 18) × 20. 1 mark: 35 s.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the rate decreases as time goes on.
parts.answer: The concentration of the acid falls as it is used up, so there are fewer particles per cm³ and fewer collisions per second.
parts.working: 1 mark: acid concentration falls as it is used. 1 mark: fewer collisions per second so the rate slows.

practice.stem: A student heats 2.50 g of hydrated copper(II) sulfate in a crucible until the blue colour has gone. The crucible and solid are weighed after each heating. The masses after successive heatings are 1.61 g, then 1.60 g, then 1.60 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage mass of water lost. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the crucible is heated, cooled and weighed again until the mass is constant.
parts.answer: Repeated heating shows that all the water has been driven off. When the mass no longer changes, no more water is being lost, so the heating is complete.
parts.working: 1 mark: to show all the water has been removed. 1 mark: a constant mass shows the reaction is complete.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify the reading that is not yet a constant mass and suggest why.
parts.answer: 1.61 g; some water was still present because heating was not complete.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student needs exactly 25.0 cm³ of aqueous sodium hydroxide to put into a conical flask for a titration. Which apparatus should be used?
A beaker
B measuring cylinder
C volumetric pipette
D gas syringe
parts.working: A volumetric pipette delivers a fixed volume accurately (25.0 cm³). A measuring cylinder is less accurate; a beaker only gives a rough volume; a gas syringe is for gases.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The burette reading is 12.60 cm³ before the titration and 36.15 cm³ after. Calculate the volume added.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A stop-watch shows 1:23 (minutes:seconds). Give this time in seconds.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the units used for the volume of a gas collected in a gas syringe.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name the piece of apparatus used to measure the mass of a solid.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student reads the level of water in a measuring cylinder. Which method gives the correct reading?
A look down on the surface from above the cylinder
B read the bottom of the curved surface with the eye level with it
C read the top edge of the curved surface
D read from the side of the cylinder at the top of the liquid
parts.answer: B read the bottom of the curved surface with the eye level with it
parts.working: For water the meniscus curves up at the edges, so the bottom of the curve is read with the eye level with it. Reading from above or from the side causes parallax error.

practice.stem: A student weighs an empty evaporating basin, then the basin with dry salt in it. The balance reads to 0.01 g and each reading is taken to have an uncertainty of ±0.01 g. Mass of basin = 48.27 g; mass of basin and salt = 52.91 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of salt.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the uncertainty in the mass of salt.
parts.working: 1 mark: each reading has an uncertainty of ±0.01 g. 1 mark: the two uncertainties are added, giving ±0.02 g.

practice.stem: A thermometer has 1 °C divisions. The temperature of a liquid rises from 21 °C to 37 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the temperature rise.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the uncertainty in each reading if each is read to the nearest 1 °C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the uncertainty in the temperature rise.
parts.working: 1 mark: the two uncertainties (±0.5 °C each) are added.

practice.stem: A student makes up 250 cm³ of a standard solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the advantage of using a volumetric flask rather than a beaker to make up a standard solution.
parts.answer: A volumetric flask has a single calibration mark, so it holds a fixed volume accurately (250 cm³); a beaker is only approximate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the solution is made up to the correct volume.
parts.answer: The solid is dissolved, the solution is transferred and then distilled water is added until the bottom of the meniscus reaches the mark.

practice.stem: A thermometer has 1 °C divisions. At the start the liquid level is halfway between the 19 °C and 20 °C marks. At the end it is level with the 27 °C mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Record the starting and final temperatures to the nearest 0.5 °C.
parts.working: B1 each; both must show one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the temperature rise.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why recording the final temperature as '27' is not acceptable.
parts.answer: Readings must be recorded to the same resolution/precision as the thermometer allows, i.e. 27.0 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which apparatus is best for measuring the volume of carbon dioxide given off every 20 seconds during a reaction?
A a burette
B a gas syringe
C a volumetric pipette
D a balance
parts.working: A gas syringe collects the gas and shows its volume directly at any time. A burette and pipette measure liquid volumes; a balance can follow the mass lost, not the volume.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A 50 cm³ measuring cylinder is marked in 1 cm³ divisions. A reading of 20 cm³ has an uncertainty of ±0.5 cm³. What is the percentage uncertainty of the reading?
A 0.25 %
B 1.0 %
C 2.5 %
D 50 %
parts.working: 0.5 ÷ 20 × 100 = 2.5 %. A divides by 200 instead of 20 (or halves the wrong value). D divides the uncertainty by the 1 cm³ division size instead of by the reading.

practice.stem: A student times a reaction with a stopwatch. The reaction takes 40.0 s. The total uncertainty from reaction time is ±0.5 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why there is an uncertainty in the timing.
parts.answer: The student's reaction time when starting and stopping the stopwatch is not zero.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the time. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one way to improve the timing.
parts.answer: Use a light gate or data logger, or video recording with a timer, which removes the reaction-time error.

practice.stem: A pipette is labelled 25.00 cm³ ± 0.03 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the volume delivered. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one reason why the pipette is preferred to a measuring cylinder for measuring this volume.
parts.answer: A pipette delivers a fixed volume with a smaller uncertainty than a measuring cylinder.

practice.stem: A student has to heat 50 cm³ of ethanol to 60 °C in the laboratory.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a safer way to heat the flammable liquid.
parts.answer: Use a water bath (no naked flame).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a naked flame is unsafe for this liquid.
parts.answer: The vapour of the flammable liquid can catch fire from the naked flame; the liquid could then ignite.
parts.working: 1 mark: flammable vapour. 1 mark: can ignite from the flame.

practice.stem: A student weighs an empty crucible as 13.21 g and then the crucible with the solid as 15.87 g. Each balance reading is ±0.01 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of solid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the uncertainty in the mass of solid.
parts.working: 1 mark: ±0.01 g from each reading, added.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the mass of solid. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest and explain how the percentage uncertainty could be reduced.
parts.answer: Use a larger mass of solid. The same ±0.02 g uncertainty is then a smaller fraction of the mass.
parts.working: 1 mark: use a larger mass of solid. 1 mark: the uncertainty is then a smaller percentage of the mass.

practice.stem: A student uses a gas syringe to collect carbon dioxide from the reaction of a carbonate with an acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one problem with the gas syringe that would give a wrong reading.
parts.answer: The plunger sticks, so it does not move freely and the volume is not read correctly.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two other ways the reading could be wrong because of leakage.
parts.answer: Any two: a joint or bung is not airtight; the delivery tube is not sealed; gas escapes before the syringe is connected.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the reaction flask must be sealed except for the syringe connection.
parts.answer: So that all the gas made goes into the syringe and none escapes.

practice.stem: A thermometer reads to 0.1 °C, with an uncertainty of ±0.05 °C in each reading. The temperature rise measured is 2.4 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the uncertainty in the temperature rise.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the temperature rise. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a thermometer reading to the nearest 1 °C would give a much larger percentage uncertainty for this rise.
parts.answer: The uncertainty (±1 °C) is then a much larger fraction of a small temperature rise of 2.4 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A mixture of two liquids with different boiling points is separated by heating. Which method is used?
A filtration
B fractional distillation
C chromatography
D sublimation
parts.working: Fractional distillation separates liquids by boiling point: the liquid with the lower boiling point vaporises and condenses first. Filtration separates insoluble solids from liquids, chromatography separates by how strongly substances stick to the paper, and sublimation applies to solids.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to separate sand from a mixture of sand and water. Give the name of the method, what stays on the filter paper and what passes through.
parts.answer: Filtration: pour the mixture through filter paper in a funnel. The sand is the residue left on the filter paper. The water passes through as the filtrate.
parts.working: 1 mark: filtration. 1 mark: sand is the residue. 1 mark: water passes through as the filtrate.

practice.stem: A student has a solution of copper(II) sulfate and wants to obtain dry blue crystals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to obtain dry blue crystals of copper(II) sulfate from the solution. Give three steps.
parts.answer: Heat the solution to evaporate some water until it is saturated (hot and nearly full of crystals). Leave it to cool slowly so crystals form. Filter off the crystals and dry them between sheets of filter paper.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three correct steps: saturate the solution by evaporating some water; cool slowly to form crystals; filter and dry the crystals.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the solution is not heated until it is completely dry.
parts.answer: Heating to dryness would drive off the water of crystallisation and could decompose the crystals, so the crystals would not be the correct hydrated salt.
parts.working: 1 mark: water of crystallisation lost or crystals decomposed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to separate a mixture of iron filings and sulfur powder.
parts.answer: Bring a magnet close to the mixture. The iron filings are attracted to the magnet and removed, and the sulfur is left behind.
parts.working: 1 mark: use a magnet. 1 mark: iron attracted, sulfur left behind.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why filtration cannot separate salt from a solution of salt in water.
parts.answer: The salt is dissolved, so its particles are very small and pass through the filter paper with the water.
parts.working: 1 mark: dissolved particles pass through the filter paper. 1 mark: the filtrate is still a solution (would need evaporation or distillation).

practice.stem: Separating mixtures is an important skill in a chemistry laboratory.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how pure, dry crystals of salt can be obtained from a mixture of sand and salt.
parts.answer: Add water and stir to dissolve the salt; filter to remove sand (residue); heat the filtrate to evaporate some water until crystals start to form / to the point of crystallisation; leave to cool and crystallise, then filter and dry the crystals (on filter paper).
parts.working: 1 mark each for dissolve, filter, evaporate to crystallisation point, cool/dry crystals.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the method used to separate ethanol (boiling point 78 °C) from water.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why this method works.
parts.answer: Ethanol has a lower boiling point so it evaporates first and is condensed and collected first.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Pure water boils at 100 °C at normal pressure. A sample of salty water boils at 101.2 °C. What does this show?
A the sample is pure water
B the sample contains dissolved solid, which raises the boiling point
C the thermometer is wrong
D the sample has a lower boiling point than pure water
parts.answer: B the sample contains dissolved solid, which raises the boiling point
parts.working: A dissolved solid (solute) raises the boiling point of a solvent, so a salty sample boils above 100 °C. A is wrong because pure water boils at 100 °C. C is unlikely as a reason for the boiling point to be higher for a dissolved solid. D is the opposite of what the data show.

practice.stem: A mixture of ethanol (boiling point 78 °C) and water (boiling point 100 °C) is separated by fractional distillation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the thermometer reading changes as the mixture is distilled.
parts.answer: The reading rises to about 78 °C and stays steady while the ethanol distils. Then it rises to 100 °C when the water starts to boil.
parts.working: 1 mark: steady at about 78 °C while ethanol distils. 1 mark: rises to 100 °C after the ethanol has been collected.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the ethanol is collected first.
parts.answer: Ethanol has the lower boiling point, so it turns to vapour first, and the vapour condenses first.
parts.working: 1 mark: lower boiling point. 1 mark: vaporises and condenses first.

practice.stem: Pure water is obtained from sea water in the laboratory.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the separation method.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the water collected is pure.
parts.answer: The water is heated and turns into vapour, which condenses to pure liquid water. The dissolved salts are not volatile, so they stay in the flask.
parts.working: 1 mark: water vapour condenses to pure liquid. 1 mark: the dissolved salts do not boil off and stay behind.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the crystals are dried between filter papers rather than heated strongly.
parts.answer: Filter paper absorbs the surface water, so the crystals dry faster. Strong heating could drive off water of crystallisation or decompose the crystals. Gentle drying keeps the crystals intact and pure.
parts.working: 1 mark: filter paper absorbs surface water. 1 mark: strong heating could remove water of crystallisation or decompose. 1 mark: gentle drying keeps the crystals intact.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A pure substance melts at 136 °C. A student's sample of the same substance melts over the range 128 °C to 133 °C. Which conclusion is correct?
A The sample is pure, because it melts below 136 °C.
B The sample is impure, because it melts over a range below 136 °C.
C The sample is impure, because impurities raise the melting point.
D The sample is a different substance, because pure substances have no melting point.
parts.answer: B The sample is impure, because it melts over a range below 136 °C.
parts.working: Impurities lower the melting point and make the substance melt over a range of temperatures. C is wrong because impurities lower, not raise, the melting point.

practice.stem: Crude sodium chloride (25.0 g) contains insoluble sand. The salt is dissolved in water, the mixture is filtered and the filtrate is evaporated to dryness. The dry pure salt has a mass of 21.5 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the substance that remains on the filter paper.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of sand in the crude salt.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by mass of sand in the crude salt. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the calculated mass of sand (25.0 g − 21.5 g) might be too high.
parts.answer: Some salt was lost during transfer or by spitting during evaporation, so less pure salt was recovered than the crude salt contained, and the lost salt is wrongly counted as sand.
parts.working: 1 mark: salt is lost (transfer, spitting or incomplete drying), so the mass of salt recovered is less than it should be and the sand mass is overestimated.

practice.stem: Potassium nitrate that is contaminated with a small amount of sand and a soluble impurity is purified by crystallisation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the impure solid is dissolved in the minimum amount of hot water.
parts.answer: So the solution is saturated, and most of the salt crystallises when it cools.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the hot solution is filtered.
parts.answer: To remove insoluble impurities while the solution is hot, so the salt does not crystallise in the funnel.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the solution is cooled slowly.
parts.answer: Slow cooling gives larger, purer crystals.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the crystals are washed with a little cold water.
parts.answer: To remove soluble impurities from the surfaces of the crystals. Cold water is used so that little of the salt dissolves and is lost.
parts.working: 1 mark: removes soluble impurities. 1 mark: cold water minimises loss of product.

practice.stem: A mixture of propanone (boiling point 56 °C) and water (boiling point 100 °C) is to be separated.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the separation method.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the bulb of the thermometer is placed level with the side arm of the distillation flask.
parts.answer: So that the thermometer measures the temperature of the vapour that is passing into the condenser. This gives the boiling point of the liquid being distilled (about 56 °C for propanone).
parts.working: 1 mark: the bulb sits in the vapour at the side arm. 1 mark: so the reading shows the boiling point of the fraction being collected.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the vapour is passed through a condenser.
parts.answer: To cool the vapour and turn it back into a liquid, so it can be collected.

practice.stem: A mixture contains sand, iron filings and sodium chloride.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a full method to obtain separate dry samples of the sand, the iron filings and the sodium chloride. Give the order of the steps and the reason for each step.
parts.answer: 1. Use a magnet to remove the iron filings (the magnet attracts only iron). 2. Add water to dissolve the sodium chloride; the sand does not dissolve. 3. Filter to separate the sand as the residue. 4. Evaporate the filtrate to crystallise the sodium chloride, then dry the crystals.
parts.working: 1 mark: magnet removes iron first. 1 mark: water dissolves salt. 1 mark: filtration removes sand. 1 mark: evaporation or crystallisation gives salt. 1 mark: sand and salt are dried. 1 mark: reason for the order given.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the conical flask is rinsed with distilled water but not with the alkali solution before the titration.
parts.answer: Any water left in the flask does not change the number of moles of alkali present, so the titre is not affected. Rinsing with alkali would add extra alkali and change the amount present.
parts.working: 1 mark: water does not change the moles of alkali. 1 mark: rinsing with the alkali would add extra alkali.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to find the end point of a titration in which sodium hydroxide solution is titrated with hydrochloric acid, using phenolphthalein indicator.
parts.answer: Pipette 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide into a conical flask and add a few drops of phenolphthalein (the solution turns pink). Add the acid from a burette, swirling the flask. Near the end point add the acid drop by drop. Stop when the last drop makes the solution colourless.
parts.working: 1 mark: 25.0 cm³ alkali and phenolphthalein (pink). 1 mark: acid from the burette, with swirling. 1 mark: drop by drop near the end point. 1 mark: stop at the first permanent colourless point.

practice.stem: Ammonia solution is a weak base. It is titrated with hydrochloric acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name a suitable indicator for the titration of ammonia solution with hydrochloric acid, and state its colour change.
parts.answer: Methyl orange; it changes from yellow (alkaline) to red (acidic).
parts.working: 1 mark: methyl orange. 1 mark: yellow to red. Phenolphthalein changes too far from the end point of this weak base and strong acid titration.

practice.stem: A burette is filled with hydrochloric acid before a titration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State why the funnel is removed from the top of the burette after it is filled.
parts.answer: So that no liquid from the funnel drips into the burette and changes the reading.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why the burette reading is taken from the bottom of the meniscus.
parts.answer: The meniscus of a colourless liquid curves, and the bottom of the curve is the standard place to read.

practice.stem: A student in Islamabad titrates 25.0 cm³ of aqueous potassium hydroxide with dilute nitric acid from a burette.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the burette is rinsed with the acid, not water, before it is filled.
parts.answer: Water would dilute the acid and change its concentration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the conical flask is placed on a white tile.
parts.answer: To see the colour change of the indicator more clearly.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Thymolphthalein is used as the indicator. State the colour change at the end-point when acid is added to the alkali.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the acid is added drop by drop near the end-point and the flask swirled.
parts.answer: So the end-point is not overshot; swirling mixes the reactants so the indicator change is permanent/accurate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a rough titration is done before the accurate titrations.
parts.answer: It gives the approximate end point, so the accurate titrations can add most of the acid quickly and then add the last few cm³ drop by drop.
parts.working: 1 mark: finds the approximate volume at the end point. 1 mark: accurate titrations are then done more carefully near the end point.

practice.stem: Hydrochloric acid of concentration 0.100 mol/dm³ is used to titrate 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide. The mean titre is 24.50 cm³. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the moles of HCl in the mean titre.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the mole ratio of HCl to NaOH in the reaction, and the moles of NaOH in 25.0 cm³.
parts.working: 1 mark: 1:1 ratio, so the moles of NaOH are the same.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of the sodium hydroxide in mol/dm³. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

practice.stem: A student titrates 25.0 cm³ of alkali with an acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State why a white tile is placed under the conical flask.
parts.answer: It makes the colour change easier to see.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the piece of apparatus used to measure the 25.0 cm³ of alkali.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why the flask is swirled during the titration.
parts.answer: To mix the reactants so that the acid is evenly mixed with the alkali as it is added.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the ionic equation for neutralisation.
parts.working: 1 mark: correct equation, balanced with state symbols.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the moles of H⁺ ions in 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid.

practice.stem: Three students carry out the same titration of 25.0 cm³ of aqueous sodium hydroxide with dilute hydrochloric acid, but each makes a different change to the method.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Student 1 left an air bubble in the burette tip, which came out during the titration. State and explain the effect on the measured titre.
parts.answer: The titre is too large: the bubble's volume is counted as acid added though no acid was delivered.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Student 2 rinsed the pipette with water and did not dry it before measuring the alkali. State and explain the effect on the measured titre.
parts.answer: The titre is too small: the alkali is diluted, so the 25.0 cm³ contains fewer moles of alkali and needs less acid.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Student 3 added water to the conical flask during the titration to wash the sides. State the effect on the titre.
parts.answer: No effect: the number of moles of alkali in the flask is unchanged.

practice.stem: 25.0 cm³ of 0.0500 mol/dm³ sodium carbonate solution is titrated with hydrochloric acid. The mean titre is 22.40 cm³. Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the moles of sodium carbonate in 25.0 cm³ of the solution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the moles of HCl that reacted with this amount of sodium carbonate.
parts.working: 1 mark: the ratio Na₂CO₃ : HCl is 1 : 2. 1 mark: 2 × 0.00125 = 0.00250 mol.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of the hydrochloric acid in mol/dm³. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

practice.stem: 25.0 cm³ of ethanoic acid is titrated with 0.100 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide. The mean titre is 20.00 cm³. CH₃COOH + NaOH → CH₃COONa + H₂O

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of the ethanoic acid in mol/dm³.
parts.working: 1 mark: moles NaOH = 0.100 × 20.00 ÷ 1000 = 0.00200. 1 mark: 1:1 ratio, so moles of acid = 0.00200. 1 mark: 0.00200 ÷ 0.0250 dm³. 1 mark: 0.0800 mol/dm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the moles of sodium hydroxide in 0.25 g of pure solid sodium hydroxide (Mr = 40).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the moles of sodium hydroxide in 25.0 cm³ of the solution made by dissolving the solid in 250 cm³ of water.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the volume of 0.100 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid needed to neutralise this 25.0 cm³. Give your answer in cm³.

practice.stem: A student's three concordant titres are 23.40 cm³, 23.35 cm³ and 23.30 cm³. In one of these titrations the burette readings were: start 0.50 cm³, end 23.85 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean titre from the three concordant titres.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The burette is read to 0.05 cm³ at each reading. Calculate the uncertainty in the titre.
parts.working: 1 mark: ±0.05 cm³ from each reading, added.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the titre. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State how the titre could be made more accurate.
parts.answer: Repeat the titration and use concordant results.

practice.stem: A student reads the burette at the top of the meniscus, instead of the bottom, for both the initial and final readings of a titration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the titre is still accurate.
parts.answer: The same error (reading the top of the meniscus) occurs in both readings. Subtracting the two readings cancels the constant error, so the volume added is still correct, but only if both readings are taken the same way.
parts.working: 1 mark: the same error affects both readings. 1 mark: subtraction cancels it. 1 mark: only if read consistently.

practice.stem: A student sets up paper chromatography to separate the dyes in a food colouring.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what the baseline (pencil line) is drawn with, and explain why ink is not used.
parts.answer: Pencil. Ink contains dyes that would move up the paper and mix with the spots being tested.
parts.working: 1 mark: pencil. 1 mark: ink dyes would move and confuse the results.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where the solvent level must be.
parts.answer: Below the baseline, so the spots do not dissolve into the solvent in the beaker.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the formula for the Rf value.
parts.answer: Rf = distance moved by the spot ÷ distance moved by the solvent front

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Rf value has no unit.
parts.answer: Both distances are measured in the same unit, so the unit cancels in the division and the Rf is a ratio.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the solvent level must be kept below the baseline.
parts.answer: If the baseline is under the solvent, the spots dissolve into the solvent in the beaker and are lost from the paper.
parts.working: 1 mark: spots dissolve into the solvent. 1 mark: the mixture is lost, so no separation can be seen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the stationary phase and the mobile phase in paper chromatography.
parts.answer: Stationary phase: the water held in the paper (cellulose). Mobile phase: the solvent.
parts.working: 1 mark: water in the paper. 1 mark: the solvent moving up the paper.

practice.stem: A food colouring used in mithai (sweets) is tested by paper chromatography. The solvent front moves 8.0 cm from the starting line. The colouring gives two spots, at 2.4 cm and 5.6 cm from the starting line.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the Rf values of the two spots.
parts.working: B1 each: Rf = distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent front.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the starting line is drawn in pencil, not ink.
parts.answer: Pencil (graphite) does not dissolve in the solvent / move up the paper; ink would separate and interfere.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the starting line must be above the level of the solvent.
parts.answer: Otherwise the dyes dissolve into the solvent in the beaker instead of moving up the paper.

parts.label: d
parts.text: How many dyes are in the food colouring?

practice.stem: A chromatogram is run with a solvent front that moves 9.0 cm from the baseline. Spot X moves 6.3 cm and spot Y moves 3.6 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the Rf value for spot X. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the Rf value for spot Y. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which spot is more soluble in the solvent? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Spot X. It moves further up the paper, so it is more soluble in the solvent (or less strongly attracted to the paper).
parts.working: 1 mark: spot X. 1 mark: moves further, so more soluble in the solvent.

practice.stem: Known dyes are run on the same paper in the same solvent. Dye P: Rf 0.32; Dye Q: Rf 0.55; Dye R: Rf 0.78. A colour from a sweet gives a spot with Rf 0.55.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the dye in the sweet.
parts.answer: Dye Q (its Rf value of 0.55 matches).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two conditions that must be kept the same so that the Rf values can be compared.
parts.answer: Any two: the same solvent; the same type of paper; the same temperature.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why one matching Rf value is not enough to be sure of the dye.
parts.answer: A different dye could have the same Rf value, so the test should be repeated with a second solvent.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the Rf value of a dye would change if a different solvent is used.
parts.answer: The solubility of the dye in the new solvent is different. The dye's attraction to the paper compared with the solvent also changes. So the spot moves a different distance.
parts.working: 1 mark: solubility in the solvent changes. 1 mark: attraction to the paper relative to the solvent changes. 1 mark: so the distance moved changes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to show that a dye is pure using chromatography.
parts.answer: Run the dye, and the mixture for comparison, on a pencil baseline. Run the dye in at least two different solvents. A pure dye gives a single spot in each solvent; more than one spot in any solvent shows that the dye is a mixture.
parts.working: 1 mark: spot the dye on the baseline (with a sample of the mixture for comparison). 1 mark: run it in one solvent and see a single spot. 1 mark: run it in a second, different solvent. 1 mark: a single spot in each solvent shows purity (the Rf values may differ between solvents).

practice.stem: A student removes the paper from the solvent before the solvent reaches the top of the paper.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the paper is removed from the solvent before the solvent reaches the top.
parts.answer: So that the position of the solvent front can be marked clearly before it dries out.
parts.working: 1 mark: the solvent front is marked before it evaporates. 1 mark: the distance moved by the solvent is needed for the Rf calculation.

practice.stem:
A sample containing one amino acid is analysed by chromatography. The solvent front travels 12.5 cm and the spot travels 4.0 cm.
Rf values of amino acids in this solvent: glycine 0.26; alanine 0.32; valine 0.51; leucine 0.70

parts.label: a
parts.text: Amino acids are colourless. State what must be done to the chromatogram so that the spots can be seen.
parts.answer: Spray it with a locating agent (and dry/heat).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the Rf value of the spot. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the table to identify the amino acid.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the Rf values in the table are only useful if the same solvent is used.
parts.answer: Rf depends on the solvent: how soluble the substance is in it and how strongly it is attracted to the paper change with the solvent.

practice.stem: A food colouring is run in a solvent on paper. The baseline is 1.5 cm above the bottom edge of the paper and the solvent front reaches 10.5 cm from the bottom edge. Spot A is 6.0 cm and spot B is 4.1 cm from the bottom edge.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the distance moved by the solvent front from the baseline.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the Rf value of spot A. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the Rf value of spot B. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name the spot that is more soluble in the solvent.

practice.stem: A student wants to find out which dyes are in a green food colouring.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the method the student should follow to find which dyes are in a green food colouring.
parts.answer: Draw a pencil baseline and put a small spot of the colouring on it. Place the paper in a solvent below the baseline and let the solvent rise. Remove it, mark the solvent front and let it dry. Locate the spots and calculate the Rf value for each.
parts.working: 1 mark: spot on pencil baseline, solvent below. 1 mark: run and mark solvent front. 1 mark: calculate Rf for each spot.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the dyes are identified.
parts.answer: The Rf values are compared with those of known dyes run on the same paper, in the same solvent and at the same temperature.
parts.working: 1 mark: compare with known dyes. 1 mark: same conditions.

practice.stem: A student measures distances from the bottom edge of the paper, not from the baseline. Baseline: 1.8 cm. Solvent front: 14.2 cm. Spot centre: 9.3 cm (all from the bottom edge).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the distance moved by the spot from the baseline.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the distance moved by the solvent front from the baseline.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the Rf value. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the Rf value the student would wrongly get by measuring from the bottom edge of the paper. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark: 9.3 ÷ 14.2 = 0.65 (wrong, because the baseline was not used as the start).

practice.stem: A student puts a large drop of sample on the baseline. When the chromatogram is run, the spots run into each other and form a streak.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the spots run into one another and form a streak.
parts.answer: Too much sample was applied, which overloads the paper. The spots spread out and merge as the solvent carries them.
parts.working: 1 mark: too much sample. 1 mark: spots spread and merge.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the student can correct the chromatogram.
parts.answer: Apply a small, concentrated spot, let each spot dry before adding more, and keep the spots small and well spaced.
parts.working: 1 mark: small concentrated spot. 1 mark: spots allowed to dry between applications.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which compound is an alkane?
A C₅H₁₀
B C₅H₁₂
C C₅H₈
D C₅H₁₁OH
parts.working: Alkanes have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂: n = 5 gives C₅H₁₂. A fits CₙH₂ₙ, the alkenes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three characteristics of a homologous series.
parts.answer: Any three of: same general formula; same functional group; similar chemical properties; trend in physical properties; each member differs from the next by CH₂.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the name of the homologous series with the functional group –OH.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the molecular formula of ethene.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the empirical formula of ethene.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the structural formula of ethene.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State what is shown by a displayed formula that is not shown by a molecular formula.
parts.answer: Every atom and every bond in the molecule (how the atoms are joined).

practice.stem: Name the homologous series to which each compound belongs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: C₃H₈

parts.label: b
parts.text: C₂H₅OH

parts.label: c
parts.text: C₄H₈ (decolourises bromine water)

parts.label: d
parts.text: HCOOH

parts.label: e
parts.text: CH₃COOC₂H₅

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the general formula of the alkanes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the relative molecular masses of methane, ethane and propane. [Ar: C = 12, H = 1]
parts.working: B1 two correct; B1 all three.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the difference in Mr between neighbouring members and name the group of atoms responsible.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by structural isomers.
parts.answer: Compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural formulae.
parts.working: B1 same molecular formula; B1 different structural formula.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the structural formulae of the two structural isomers with molecular formula C₄H₁₀.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the unbranched isomer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the functional group present in each compound: (i) propanoic acid, (ii) but-1-ene, (iii) propan-1-ol.
parts.answer: (i) carboxylic acid, –COOH; (ii) C=C double bond (alkene); (iii) hydroxyl, –OH (alcohol)

parts.label: b
parts.text: But-1-ene and but-2-ene have the formula C₄H₈. Give the structural formula of each and state how they are related.
parts.answer: but-1-ene CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃; but-2-ene CH₃CH=CHCH₃; they are structural isomers

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which pair of compounds are structural isomers?
A butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol
B ethane and ethene
C propan-1-ol and propanoic acid
D methane and ethane
parts.working: Butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol are both C₄H₁₀O with the –OH on different carbons: same molecular formula, different structure. B, C and D have different molecular formulae (D are members of one homologous series, not isomers).

practice.stem:
Three structural formulae are written by a student:
P: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃
Q: CH₃(CH₂)₂CH₃
R: CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₃

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which two formulae represent the same compound? Explain.
parts.answer: P and Q; both show a straight chain of four carbon atoms (butane) – Q is just a shortened way of writing P.
parts.working: B1 P and Q; B1 same unbranched chain.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the molecular formula of all three compounds.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why R is a structural isomer of P.
parts.answer: Same molecular formula (C₄H₁₀) but a different structure – R has a branched chain.
parts.working: B1 same molecular formula; B1 different arrangement / branched.

practice.stem: Name each compound and give its molecular formula.

parts.label: a
parts.text: CH₃CH₂CH₂OH

parts.label: b
parts.text: CH₃CH₂COOH

parts.label: c
parts.text: CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃

parts.label: d
parts.text: CH₃COOCH₂CH₃

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH, and methyl methanoate, HCOOCH₃, have the same molecular formula, and calculate their Mr. [Ar: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why they are structural isomers but are NOT members of the same homologous series.
parts.answer: Same molecular formula, different structural formula; they have different functional groups (–COOH and –COO– ester), so they belong to different series.
parts.working: B1 same molecular formula, different structure; B1 different functional groups.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe a simple test to tell them apart.
parts.answer: Add sodium carbonate (or magnesium): ethanoic acid fizzes; the ester does not.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the compounds: (i) CH₃CH₂OH, (ii) CH₃COOH, (iii) CH₃CH=CH₂, (iv) CH₃COOCH₃.
parts.answer: (i) ethanol; (ii) ethanoic acid; (iii) propene; (iv) methyl ethanoate

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the molecular formula of the alkene with six carbon atoms and calculate its relative molecular mass. [Ar: C = 12, H = 1]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name one carboxylic acid and two esters that have the molecular formula C₃H₆O₂.
parts.answer: Propanoic acid; methyl ethanoate; ethyl methanoate

parts.label: b
parts.text: Compound X has this formula. It fizzes with aqueous sodium carbonate. Identify X and name the gas formed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Compound Y also has this formula. Y is an ester made from methanol and a carboxylic acid. Identify Y.
parts.working: B1 (methanol + ethanoic acid → methyl ethanoate; C₃H₆O₂).

practice.stem: An unbranched alcohol contains 64.9% carbon by mass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that this percentage fits an alcohol with four carbon atoms. [Ar: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the general formula of the alcohols.

parts.label: c
