parts.text: Calculate the percentage of carbon in the alcohol with two carbon atoms, to 3 significant figures, and explain why the percentage increases along the series.
parts.answer: 52.2%; each extra CH₂ adds more carbon relative to the single O atom.
parts.working: B1 24 ÷ 46 × 100 = 52.2%; B1 oxygen becomes a smaller fraction of the mass as the chain grows.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hydrocarbon contains 85.7% carbon by mass. Find its empirical formula. [Ar: C = 12, H = 1]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Its Mr is 42. Find the molecular formula and name the compound.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the molecular formula of the product when this compound reacts with steam.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the type of polymerisation used to make poly(ethene) from ethene.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the repeat unit of poly(ethene) as a structural formula.
parts.working: Accept a written description: two carbon atoms joined by a single bond, each with two H atoms, with continuation bonds at both ends.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two problems caused by the disposal of poly(ethene) shopping bags.
parts.answer: Any two of: non-biodegradable, so they stay in landfill for a long time; litter and harm to animals (e.g. in rivers and seas); burning releases toxic gases / greenhouse gases.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why plastic bottles found on a beach in Karachi can stay there for hundreds of years.
parts.answer: Plastics are non-biodegradable (not broken down by microorganisms).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one disadvantage of burning waste plastics.
parts.answer: It releases toxic gases / carbon dioxide (greenhouse gas).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way of reducing the amount of plastic waste.
parts.answer: Recycling (e.g. PET bottles) / reusing / using less plastic packaging.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which substance is a natural polymer?
A protein
B nylon
C PET
D poly(ethene)
parts.working: Proteins are natural polyamides made from amino acids. Nylon, PET and poly(ethene) are synthetic polymers (plastics/fibres).

practice.stem: Used PET drinks bottles are collected in Lahore for recycling.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give one reason why recycling PET is better than putting it in landfill.
parts.answer: PET is non-biodegradable and would stay in landfill for a very long time / saves raw materials (petroleum).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what happens to PET in chemical recycling.
parts.answer: It is broken down (converted) back into its monomers, which are then polymerised again to make new PET.
parts.working: B1 back to monomers; B1 re-polymerised.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one problem caused by burning waste plastics.

practice.stem: State whether each polymer is made by addition or by condensation polymerisation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: poly(chloroethene)

parts.label: b
parts.text: nylon

parts.label: c
parts.text: PET

parts.label: d
parts.text: poly(propene)

parts.label: e
parts.text: State one difference between addition and condensation polymerisation.
parts.answer: Condensation polymerisation also forms a small molecule (e.g. water); addition forms only the polymer.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Poly(chloroethene) is used to make water pipes. What is its monomer?
A CH₃CH₂Cl
B CH₂=CHCl
C CH₂Cl–CH₂Cl
D CCl₂=CCl₂
parts.working: An addition polymer is made from an alkene; chloroethene is CH₂=CHCl. A has no C=C double bond, so it cannot undergo addition polymerisation.

practice.stem: Poly(propene) is used to make ropes for fishing boats in Gwadar. It is made from propene, CH₃CH=CH₂.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the structural formula of the repeat unit of poly(propene).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the relative formula mass of one repeat unit. [Ar: C = 12, H = 1]

parts.label: c
parts.text: A molecule of poly(propene) has a relative molecular mass of 84 000. Calculate the number of repeat units in the molecule.

practice.stem: Lentils (daal) are a good source of protein.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the monomers from which proteins are made.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Proteins are natural polyamides. Name the type of polymerisation that forms them.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the name of the small molecule released each time two monomers join.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the name of the synthetic polymer that has the same linkage as proteins.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A section of an addition polymer is –CH₂–CH(CN)–CH₂–CH(CN)–CH₂–CH(CN)–. What is the monomer?
A CH₂=CHCN
B CH₃CH₂CN
C CH₂=C(CN)₂
D CH≡CCN
parts.working: The repeat unit is –CH₂–CH(CN)–; the monomer has a C=C between these two carbons: CH₂=CHCN. B is saturated so cannot polymerise by addition; C would put two CN groups on one carbon.

practice.stem: Silk is a protein fibre; nylon is a synthetic fibre often used as a substitute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the linkage that joins the monomers in both proteins and nylon and give its formula.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe one difference between the monomers used to make a protein and those used to make nylon.
parts.answer: Proteins are made from amino acids (each monomer has both –NH₂ and –COOH, and many different amino acids are used); nylon is made from two different monomers, a dicarboxylic acid and a diamine.
parts.working: B1 protein: amino acids; B1 nylon: diamine + dicarboxylic acid.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the small molecule formed each time a linkage is made.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Nylon is made from a dicarboxylic acid and a diamine. Name the type of polymerisation and the small molecule formed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the linkage in nylon and give its structure.

parts.label: c
parts.text: PET is made from a dicarboxylic acid and a diol. Name the type of linkage in PET.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two differences between addition polymerisation and condensation polymerisation.
parts.answer: Addition: only one product (the polymer) and monomers have C=C bonds; condensation: a small molecule (e.g. water) is also formed and monomers have two functional groups.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
PET is used to make drinks bottles. Which linkage joins the monomer units in PET?
A –CONH–
B –COO–
C –C=C–
D –O–H
parts.working: PET is a polyester; its linkage is the ester group –COO–. A is the amide linkage found in nylon and proteins.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A nylon chain is made from 200 molecules of a dicarboxylic acid and 200 molecules of a diamine joined alternately in one unbranched chain. Calculate the number of water molecules released.
parts.working: M1 400 monomers in a chain form 399 linkages; A1 one water per linkage.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the reaction is a condensation polymerisation.
parts.answer: Monomers join and a small molecule (water) is eliminated at each linkage.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a monomer with only ONE –COOH group could stop the chain growing.
parts.answer: It has only one reactive group, so once it joins the chain end there is no group left to react further.

practice.stem: PVC, poly(chloroethene), is used for water pipes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the Mr of the repeat unit, –CH₂–CHCl–. [Ar: C = 12, H = 1, Cl = 35.5]

parts.label: b
parts.text: A molecule of PVC has Mr = 125 000. Calculate the number of repeat units.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by mass of chlorine in PVC to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why burning PVC waste is particularly harmful.
parts.answer: It releases hydrogen chloride (acidic, toxic gas) as well as other toxic products.

practice.stem: A nylon is made from hexanedioic acid, HOOC(CH₂)₄COOH, and 1,6-diaminohexane, H₂N(CH₂)₆NH₂.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the structural formula of the repeat unit of the nylon formed.
parts.working: B1 amide linkages; B1 correct chains (4 CH₂ and 6 CH₂).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the molecular formula of the repeat unit and calculate its Mr. [Ar: C = 12, H = 1, N = 14, O = 16]

parts.label: c
parts.text: PET is also a condensation polymer. Name the linkage in PET.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the process used to separate petroleum into fractions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one use of each fraction: (i) refinery gas, (ii) kerosene, (iii) bitumen, (iv) naphtha.
parts.answer: (i) heating and cooking; (ii) jet fuel; (iii) surfacing roads (and roofs); (iv) feedstock for making chemicals

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how chain length changes from the top to the bottom of the fractionating column.
parts.answer: Chain length increases (molecules get larger) towards the bottom.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name three fossil fuels.
parts.answer: Coal, natural gas and petroleum (crude oil)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the main constituent of natural gas.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why fossil fuels are described as non-renewable.
parts.answer: They took millions of years to form and are used much faster than they form, so they will run out.

practice.stem:
Five fractions from the fractional distillation of petroleum:
A: below 25 °C
B: 40–100 °C
C: 160–250 °C
D: 250–350 °C
E: above 400 °C (residue)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which fraction is a gas at room temperature?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which fraction is the most viscous?
parts.working: B1 highest boiling range, longest chains.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which fraction contains molecules with the shortest chains apart from A?

parts.label: d
parts.text: Fraction C is used as jet fuel. Name fraction C.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Fraction E is used to surface roads. Name fraction E.

practice.stem:
A teacher heats a sample of a synthetic crude-oil mixture and collects four fractions.
Fraction 1: collected up to 70 °C, colourless, runny, lights easily with a clean flame
Fraction 2: 70–120 °C, pale yellow, runny, lights fairly easily
Fraction 3: 120–170 °C, yellow, slightly thick, lights with difficulty, some smoke
Fraction 4: 170–220 °C, dark yellow-brown, thick, very hard to light, smoky flame

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the colour and viscosity change from fraction 1 to fraction 4.
parts.answer: Colour gets darker (colourless/pale yellow to dark brown); viscosity increases (thicker).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the ease of lighting and the flame change from fraction 1 to fraction 4.
parts.answer: Harder to ignite; flame becomes smokier/sootier.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the fractions boil over a range of temperatures rather than at one temperature.
parts.answer: Each fraction is a mixture of hydrocarbons with similar but different boiling points.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one safety precaution in this experiment.
parts.answer: Use a heat-proof mat / safety glasses / mineral wool in the tube / keep flammable liquids away from flame.

practice.stem: A refinery near Karachi separates petroleum into fractions. Give one use of each fraction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Gasoline (petrol)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Diesel oil (gas oil)
parts.answer: Fuel for diesel engines, e.g. lorries, buses, tractors

parts.label: c
parts.text: Fuel oil
parts.answer: Fuel for ships / home heating systems

parts.label: d
parts.text: Lubricating oil

parts.label: e
parts.text: Refinery gas
parts.answer: Gas for heating and cooking (bottled gas)

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two conditions used to crack long-chain alkanes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Complete the equation: C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + ______

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two reasons why cracking is carried out.
parts.answer: To meet the demand for shorter-chain alkanes such as petrol; to produce alkenes for making polymers (and hydrogen).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how petroleum is separated into fractions in a fractionating column.
parts.answer: Petroleum is heated so it vaporises; vapour enters near the bottom of the column; column is hotter at the bottom and cooler at the top; vapours rise and condense at different heights where the temperature is below their boiling point; fractions with lower boiling points (smaller molecules) collect higher up; residue (bitumen) at the bottom.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: heated/vaporised; temperature gradient (hot bottom, cool top); vapours rise; condense at the level matching their boiling point; small molecules / low boiling point at top; large molecules at the bottom.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the physical property used to separate the fractions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete the equation: C₁₂H₂₆ → C₂H₄ + C₃H₆ + ______

parts.label: b
parts.text: Complete the equation: C₁₄H₃₀ → C₈H₁₈ + 2 ______

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the homologous series of C₃H₆ and of C₇H₁₆.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the conditions used in catalytic cracking.
parts.answer: High temperature; a catalyst (e.g. aluminium oxide / silica / zeolite).

practice.stem:
A refinery's data (percentage by mass):
Fraction: supply %, demand %
Refinery gas: 4, 6
Gasoline: 18, 30
Kerosene: 12, 12
Diesel oil: 20, 24
Fuel oil and bitumen: 46, 28

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the fraction with the largest shortfall of supply compared with demand and calculate the shortfall.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the fraction that is in greatest surplus and calculate the surplus.
parts.answer: Fuel oil and bitumen; 18 percentage points (46 − 28)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the refinery can use cracking to match supply and demand.
parts.answer: Crack the surplus long-chain fractions (fuel oil) into shorter alkanes for gasoline, plus alkenes (and hydrogen).
parts.working: B1 long-chain → short-chain; B1 gives more gasoline/alkenes.

practice.stem: A student cracks liquid paraffin in the laboratory. Mineral wool soaked in paraffin is at the closed end of a boiling tube, and porcelain chips are heated strongly in the middle of the tube. Gas is collected over water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the purpose of the heated porcelain chips.
parts.answer: They act as a catalyst for cracking.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The gas collected decolourises bromine water. What does this show?
parts.answer: The gas contains an alkene (unsaturated hydrocarbon).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the delivery tube must be removed from the water before heating stops.
parts.answer: Otherwise, as the tube cools, the gas contracts and cold water is sucked back into the hot tube (suck-back), which could crack it.
parts.working: B1 suck-back; B1 hot glass cracks.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the first tube of gas collected is thrown away.
parts.answer: It is mainly air displaced from the apparatus.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hexadecane, C₁₆H₃₄, is cracked to form octane, C₈H₁₈, two molecules of propene and one molecule of compound Z. Deduce the molecular formula of Z.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name compound Z and state the homologous series to which it belongs.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the supply of long-chain fractions from fractional distillation is greater than the demand for them.
parts.answer: Petroleum naturally contains a large proportion of long-chain hydrocarbons, but they have few uses (e.g. fuel oil, bitumen), so less is needed than is produced.
parts.working: Accept: more long chains in crude oil than are needed / demand is mainly for short chains such as petrol.

practice.stem:
Energy released on complete combustion:
methane, CH₄: 890 kJ/mol (CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O)
octane, C₈H₁₈: 5470 kJ/mol (each mole forms 8 mol CO₂)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide formed per megajoule (1000 kJ) of energy released for methane and for octane. Give your answers to 3 significant figures. [Mr: CO₂ = 44]
parts.working: M1 methane: 44 g CO₂ per 890 kJ; A1 44 ÷ 0.890 = 49.4 g; A1 octane: 8 × 44 = 352 g per 5470 kJ → 64.4 g.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage reduction in CO₂ per MJ when a power station switches from an octane-like fuel to natural gas.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why burning natural gas still adds to climate change.
parts.answer: It still releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas (and leaks of methane are also greenhouse gases).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for cracking decane, C₁₀H₂₂, into octane and ethene.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum mass of ethene, in kg, formed from 1.00 tonne of decane. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. [Mr: C₁₀H₂₂ = 142, C₂H₄ = 28]

parts.label: c
parts.text: All of this ethene is turned into poly(ethene). State the maximum mass of poly(ethene) and explain.
parts.answer: 197 kg; addition polymerisation forms only one product, so no mass is lost.
parts.working: B1 197 kg; B1 addition — no other product.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hexadecane is cracked: C₁₆H₃₄ → C₆H₁₄ + x C₂H₄ + C₄H₈. Find the value of x.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the homologous series of C₄H₈ and give the name of one unbranched isomer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Cracking can also give hydrogen. Complete: C₈H₁₈ → C₈H₁₆ + ____ and give one use of the gas.
parts.answer: H₂; fuel (e.g. in fuel cells) or making ammonia

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, in terms of molecules and forces, why bitumen is more viscous and has a higher boiling range than gasoline.
parts.answer: Bitumen has much longer hydrocarbon chains; there are stronger intermolecular forces between larger molecules; more energy is needed to separate them, and the long chains do not slide over each other easily.
parts.working: B1 longer chains / larger molecules; B1 stronger intermolecular forces; B1 more energy to overcome (boiling) / molecules tangle and resist flow (viscosity).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Bitumen leaves the column at the bottom as a liquid residue. Suggest why it is not vaporised.
parts.answer: Its boiling point is higher than the temperature at which petroleum enters the column.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a fraction is not a single compound.
parts.answer: Many hydrocarbons have boiling points within the same range and condense at the same level.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What are the products of the complete combustion of ethanol?
A carbon monoxide and water
B carbon dioxide and hydrogen
C carbon dioxide and water
D carbon and water
parts.working: Complete combustion in plenty of oxygen gives CO₂ and H₂O. A and D are products of incomplete combustion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two uses of ethanol.
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept: in hand sanitisers (as a solvent / antiseptic).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the balanced equation for the complete combustion of ethanol.

practice.stem: Hand sanitiser gels contain about 70% ethanol by volume.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the homologous series to which ethanol belongs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the functional group in ethanol and give its formula.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the molecular formula of ethanol.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one other use of ethanol.

practice.stem: A student dissolves sugar in water, adds yeast and keeps the flask at about 30 °C. A delivery tube from the flask dips into limewater, and the flask has no other opening.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is seen in the limewater after an hour. Name the gas responsible.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the flask is kept at about 30 °C and not at 60 °C.
parts.answer: 30 °C is warm enough for a reasonable rate; at 60 °C the enzymes in the yeast are denatured (yeast killed) and fermentation stops.
parts.working: B1 optimum temperature for yeast/enzymes; B1 enzymes denatured at high temperature.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why air must be kept out of the flask.
parts.answer: In air (oxygen) the ethanol would be oxidised to ethanoic acid / respiration would be aerobic, giving no ethanol.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name the method used to obtain fairly pure ethanol from the final mixture.

practice.stem: In some countries petrol is mixed with ethanol made by fermenting sugar cane.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why ethanol made from sugar cane is described as a renewable fuel.
parts.answer: Sugar cane can be grown again each year, so the supply will not run out.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the two products of the complete combustion of ethanol.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one disadvantage of using large areas of farmland to grow sugar cane for fuel.
parts.answer: Less land for growing food crops (food prices may rise) / forests cleared.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the structural formulae of butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the molecular formula that both compounds share.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the term used for compounds like these two alcohols.

practice.stem: Pakistan makes ethanol from sugar-cane molasses. Ethanol can also be made from ethene.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the conditions for making ethanol by fermentation.
parts.answer: Yeast; about 25–35 °C; absence of oxygen (anaerobic); aqueous sugar (glucose).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the conditions for making ethanol from ethene and steam.
parts.answer: about 300 °C; about 6000 kPa (60 atm); phosphoric acid catalyst

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one advantage of fermentation and one advantage of the hydration of ethene.
parts.answer: Fermentation: uses a renewable raw material (sugar cane) / low temperature; hydration: faster / continuous / produces pure ethanol.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is the structural formula of propan-2-ol?
A CH₃CH₂CH₂OH
B CH₃CH(OH)CH₃
C CH₃COCH₃
D CH₃CH₂COOH
parts.working: Propan-2-ol has three carbon atoms with the –OH on the middle (second) carbon. A is propan-1-ol (OH on the end carbon); C has no –OH group; D is propanoic acid.

practice.stem: Glucose is fermented: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. A student collects 1.8 dm³ of carbon dioxide at room temperature and pressure. [Mr: C₂H₅OH = 46, C₆H₁₂O₆ = 180; 1 mol of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in moles, of carbon dioxide collected.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of ethanol formed at the same time.
parts.working: M1 moles ethanol = moles CO₂ = 0.075; A1 0.075 × 46 = 3.45 g.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of glucose that was fermented.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the true mass of glucose fermented is probably larger than your answer to (c).
parts.answer: Some carbon dioxide dissolves in the solution / escapes, so less gas is collected than is made.

practice.stem: Propan-1-ol is burned in a spirit lamp.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Balance the equation for the complete combustion of propan-1-ol:
__C₃H₇OH + __O₂ → __CO₂ + __H₂O

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide formed when 6.0 g of propan-1-ol burns completely. [Mr: C₃H₇OH = 60, CO₂ = 44]

practice.stem: A chemical plant makes ethanol by the catalytic addition of steam to ethene.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum mass of ethanol, in tonnes, that can be made from 14 tonnes of ethene. [Mr: C₂H₄ = 28, C₂H₅OH = 46]

parts.label: c
parts.text: The plant actually produces 21.6 tonnes of ethanol. Calculate the percentage yield to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give one reason why ethanol from ethene is often purer than ethanol from fermentation.
parts.answer: The only product is ethanol; fermentation gives a dilute aqueous mixture that must be distilled.

practice.stem: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum mass of ethanol formed from 45 g of glucose. [Mr: glucose = 180, ethanol = 46]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide formed at room temperature and pressure, in dm³. [1 mol of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the fermentation stops when the ethanol concentration reaches about 15 %.
parts.answer: The yeast is killed (denatured) by the high ethanol concentration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An alcohol from the same homologous series as ethanol has Mr = 74. Use the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH to find its molecular formula. [Ar: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the equation for the complete combustion of this alcohol.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen, in dm³ at r.t.p., needed to burn 3.7 g of this alcohol completely. [1 mol of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of ethene, in dm³ at r.t.p., needed to make 1.15 kg of ethanol. [Mr: C₂H₅OH = 46; 1 mol of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]
parts.working: M1 1150 ÷ 46 = 25 mol ethanol; M1 25 mol ethene; A1 25 × 24 = 600 dm³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Fermentation is a batch process, but the hydration of ethene is continuous. Explain one advantage of a continuous process.
parts.answer: Product is made all the time without stopping to empty and refill, so output is higher / cheaper labour.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why many countries without oil reserves prefer fermentation, even though it is slower.
parts.answer: Uses a renewable raw material (crops such as sugar cane) available locally; does not need ethene from petroleum; lower temperature/energy.
parts.working: B1 renewable / local raw material; B1 no need for crude oil (ethene) / low energy conditions.

practice.stem: 0.92 g of an alcohol burns completely to give 1.76 g of carbon dioxide and 1.08 g of water. [Mr: CO₂ = 44, H₂O = 18; Ar: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the masses of carbon and hydrogen in the sample.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of oxygen in the sample and deduce the empirical formula.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The Mr of the alcohol is 46. Give its molecular formula and name.

practice.stem: Vinegar contains ethanoic acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is seen when magnesium ribbon is added to aqueous ethanoic acid, and name the products.
parts.answer: Fizzing / bubbles and the magnesium dissolves (slowly); magnesium ethanoate and hydrogen.
parts.working: B1 observation; B1 magnesium ethanoate; B1 hydrogen.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the salt formed when ethanoic acid reacts with sodium carbonate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Ethanoic acid is a weak acid. Explain what this means.
parts.answer: It is only partially dissociated (ionised) in water.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which group is the functional group of all carboxylic acids?
A –OH
B –COOH
C –COO– joining two carbon chains
D C=C
parts.working: Carboxylic acids contain the –COOH (carboxyl) group. A is the alcohol group; C is the ester linkage; D is the alkene group.

practice.stem: Kettles in hard-water areas become coated with calcium carbonate ('scale'). Vinegar, which contains ethanoic acid, can remove it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is seen when vinegar is added to the scale.
parts.answer: Fizzing / bubbles; the white solid dissolves.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the three products of the reaction between ethanoic acid and calcium carbonate.
parts.answer: Calcium ethanoate, water and carbon dioxide

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe a test for the gas produced.
parts.answer: Bubble it through limewater: turns milky.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the carboxylic acids with the formulae HCOOH and CH₃CH₂COOH.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the structural formula of butanoic acid.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the molecular formula of butanoic acid.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the general name for the series that contains these acids.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the salt formed when ethanoic acid reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the word equation for this reaction.
parts.answer: ethanoic acid + sodium hydroxide → sodium ethanoate + water

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the two products when zinc reacts with ethanoic acid.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the type of reaction in (a).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which ester is formed when ethanol reacts with propanoic acid?
A propyl ethanoate
B ethyl propanoate
C ethyl ethanoate
D propyl propanoate
parts.working: The alcohol gives the first part of the name (ethyl) and the acid gives the second part (propanoate). A reverses the two parts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the conditions needed to make an ester from an alcohol and a carboxylic acid.
parts.answer: Heat (warm); concentrated sulfuric acid as a catalyst.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the word equation for the reaction between methanol and ethanoic acid.
parts.answer: methanol + ethanoic acid ⇌ methyl ethanoate + water
parts.working: B1 methyl ethanoate; B1 water. Accept → arrow.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one use of esters.

practice.stem: Esters are used as flavourings in sweets and drinks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the ester formed from methanol and butanoic acid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the ester formed from ethanol and methanoic acid.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the structural formula of the ester formed from propan-1-ol and propanoic acid, and name it.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name the other product formed in every esterification.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the carboxylic acid and the alcohol used to make methyl propanoate, CH₃CH₂COOCH₃.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the molecular formula of methyl propanoate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by mass of oxygen in methyl propanoate. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. [Ar: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16]

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the catalyst used in esterification.

practice.stem: An open bottle of rice wine slowly turns sour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the wine turns sour.
parts.answer: Ethanol is oxidised by oxygen in the air, helped by bacteria (bacterial oxidation), to ethanoic acid, which tastes sour.
parts.working: B1 ethanol oxidised / bacteria; B1 ethanoic acid formed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Balance the equation: C₂H₅OH + __O₂ → CH₃COOH + __H₂O

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name a reagent used in the laboratory to carry out the same change, and state the colour change seen.
parts.answer: Acidified potassium manganate(VII); purple to colourless.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethanoic acid can be made by heating ethanol with acidified potassium manganate(VII). State the colour change and the type of reaction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name another method of making ethanoic acid from ethanol.
parts.answer: Bacterial oxidation / fermentation by bacteria (in air), as in making vinegar.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the maximum mass of ethanoic acid that can be made from 9.2 g of ethanol. [Mr: ethanol = 46, ethanoic acid = 60]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Propyl ethanoate smells of pears. Name the alcohol and the carboxylic acid used to make it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the structural formula of propyl ethanoate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the molecular formula of propyl ethanoate and calculate its relative molecular mass. [Ar: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16]

practice.stem:
A food company tests vinegar. 25.0 cm³ of the vinegar is diluted with water to 250 cm³. 25.0 cm³ of the diluted solution needs 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide for neutralisation.
CH₃COOH + NaOH → CH₃COONa + H₂O

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of ethanoic acid in the diluted vinegar, in mol/dm³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of ethanoic acid in the original vinegar in mol/dm³ and in g/dm³. [Mr: CH₃COOH = 60]

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name a suitable indicator and give its colour change at the end-point.
parts.answer: Thymolphthalein: colourless to blue (or phenolphthalein: colourless to pink).

practice.stem: A student heats ethanoic acid with excess ethanol and a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum mass of ethyl ethanoate that can be made from 6.0 g of ethanoic acid. [Mr: CH₃COOH = 60, CH₃COOC₂H₅ = 88]

parts.label: c
parts.text: The student obtains 5.5 g. Calculate the percentage yield.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give one reason why the yield is well below 100%.
parts.answer: The reaction is reversible (does not go to completion) / product lost in separation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An unbranched carboxylic acid has Mr = 88. Identify it by name and give its structural formula. [Ar: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16]
parts.working: M1 CₙH₂ₙ₊₁COOH: 14n + 46 = 88, n = 3; A1 butanoic acid.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
The acid reacts with sodium carbonate:
2C₃H₇COOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2C₃H₇COONa + H₂O + CO₂
Calculate the mass of sodium carbonate needed to react with 4.4 g of the acid. [Mr: Na₂CO₃ = 106]

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide formed, in cm³ at r.t.p. [1 mol of gas occupies 24 dm³]

practice.stem: Two unlabelled bottles contain hexane and hexene.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a chemical test to show which liquid is hexene.
parts.answer: Add bromine water; hexene turns it from orange to colourless, hexane leaves it orange.
parts.working: B1 bromine water; B1 orange to colourless with hexene.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why hexene is described as unsaturated.
parts.answer: It contains a C=C double bond.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the general formula of the alkenes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the alkene with the formula C₃H₆ and give its structural formula.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the functional group present in all alkenes.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why alkenes are described as unsaturated.
parts.answer: Their molecules contain a carbon–carbon double bond.

practice.stem:
A student bubbles three gases, X, Y and Z, through separate tubes of bromine water and shakes each tube.
Gas X: orange → colourless
Gas Y: stays orange
Gas Z: orange → colourless

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which gases contain an alkene? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: X and Z; they decolourise the orange bromine water.
parts.working: B1 X and Z; B1 bromine water turned from orange to colourless.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest the identity of gas Y from the list methane, ethene, propene.
parts.working: B1: the only alkane in the list, so no reaction with bromine water.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the tubes are shaken after the gas is added.
parts.answer: To mix the gas with the bromine water so that it can react / dissolve.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the product when propene reacts with hydrogen.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the catalyst used for this reaction.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the equation for this reaction.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the reaction is called an addition reaction.
parts.answer: The two reactants join to form a single product (hydrogen adds across the C=C).
parts.working: B1 only one product / atoms added across the double bond.

practice.stem: Ethene, C₂H₄, is made by cracking and is a starting material for many products.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why alkenes are more reactive than alkanes.
parts.answer: Alkenes have a C=C double bond; one of the bonds in the double bond can break so that other atoms add on. Alkanes have only single bonds.
parts.working: B1 C=C present in alkenes (unsaturated); B1 atoms can add across the double bond / alkanes saturated with only single bonds.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two products made from ethene that are useful.
parts.answer: Any two of: ethanol, poly(ethene), 1,2-dibromoethane / other addition products.
parts.working: B1 each, e.g. ethanol (with steam), poly(ethene) (addition polymerisation).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the product when ethene reacts with hydrogen, and state the catalyst.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the product when ethene reacts with steam.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the product when ethene reacts with bromine.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the type of reaction in (a), (b) and (c).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Ethanol is manufactured by reacting ethene with steam. Which conditions are used?
A 300 °C, 6000 kPa and an acid catalyst
B 30 °C, 100 kPa and yeast
C 450 °C, 20 000 kPa and an iron catalyst
D room temperature and ultraviolet light
parts.answer: A 300 °C, 6000 kPa and an acid catalyst
parts.working: Catalytic addition of steam to ethene: about 300 °C, 6000 kPa (60 atm), acid (phosphoric acid) catalyst. B is fermentation of sugar; C is the Haber process; D is substitution of alkanes with chlorine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: But-1-ene and but-2-ene both react with bromine. Give the molecular formula of the product formed from either alkene.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the relative molecular mass of this product. [Ar: C = 12, H = 1, Br = 80]

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the structural formula of the product from but-2-ene.
parts.working: B1 Br atoms on carbons 2 and 3.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State what is seen when but-2-ene is bubbled into bromine water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction of ethene with bromine.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of bromine that reacts exactly with 2.8 g of ethene. [Ar: C = 12, H = 1, Br = 80]

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of product formed.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name the product formed.

practice.stem: Hydrocarbon X has a relative molecular mass of 56. It decolourises aqueous bromine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the general formula of the alkenes to show that the molecular formula of X is C₄H₈. [Ar: C = 12, H = 1]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two unbranched alkenes with this molecular formula and give their structural formulae.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the name given to compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural formulae.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Propene reacts with bromine. What is the molecular formula of the product?
A C₃H₅Br
B C₃H₆Br₂
C C₃H₇Br
D C₃H₈Br₂
parts.working: Addition across the C=C bond adds both bromine atoms and keeps all six H atoms: C₃H₆ + Br₂ → C₃H₆Br₂. A would be a substitution product.

practice.stem: Propene reacts with hydrogen when passed over a heated nickel catalyst.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 50 cm³ of propene and 80 cm³ of hydrogen are passed over the heated catalyst until no further change. All volumes are measured at the same temperature and pressure. Calculate the total volume of gas at the end and name the gases present.
parts.answer: 80 cm³: 50 cm³ propane and 30 cm³ hydrogen.
parts.working: M1 1 : 1 volume ratio, so 50 cm³ H₂ reacts (propene limiting); M1 30 cm³ H₂ left and 50 cm³ propane formed; A1 total 80 cm³.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe a test to show that no propene is left in the final mixture.
parts.answer: Bubble the gas through bromine water: it stays orange (no decolourisation).
parts.working: B1 bromine water; B1 remains orange.

practice.stem: 1.40 g of an alkene reacts exactly with 3.20 g of bromine, Br₂. [Ar: Br = 80, C = 12, H = 1]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in moles, of bromine that reacted.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Each mole of alkene reacts with one mole of bromine. Calculate the relative molecular mass of the alkene.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Deduce the molecular formula of the alkene.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The student repeated the experiment with 1.40 g of a different hydrocarbon with the same Mr. The bromine stayed orange. Suggest why.
parts.answer: That hydrocarbon has no C=C double bond (it is saturated).

practice.stem: Vegetable oils contain unsaturated molecules. In making banaspati (a solid cooking fat), oil is reacted so that some or all of its C=C bonds are removed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the reagent and catalyst needed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Each molecule of the oil contains three C=C double bonds. Calculate the volume of hydrogen, in dm³ at r.t.p., needed to react completely with 0.50 mol of the oil. [1 mol of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe a test to show that a sample of the product still contains some C=C bonds.
parts.answer: Shake with bromine water; if it turns from orange to colourless, C=C bonds are still present.
parts.working: B1 bromine water; B1 decolourised if C=C present.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction of but-2-ene with steam.
parts.working: B1 (C₄H₈ + H₂O → C₄H₉OH accepted with structural formulae).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the product in (a).

parts.label: c
parts.text: But-1-ene reacts with steam to give a mixture of two alcohols. Name both alcohols and explain why two products are possible.
parts.answer: Butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol; the C=C is at the end of the chain, so the –OH can add to either carbon of the double bond (C1 or C2), giving different products. In but-2-ene both carbons of the C=C are equivalent.
parts.working: B1 butan-1-ol; B1 butan-2-ol; B1 OH can attach to either carbon atom of the C=C (the two ends are different).

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the type of reaction.

practice.stem: LPG cylinders used for cooking in many Pakistani homes contain propane.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the balanced equation for the complete combustion of propane.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the toxic gas produced if the supply of air to the cooker is limited.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Apart from combustion, alkanes are generally unreactive. Explain why, in terms of bonding.
parts.answer: They contain only single C–C and C–H bonds (saturated).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement about the alkanes is correct?
A They are saturated hydrocarbons that contain only single covalent bonds.
B They decolourise aqueous bromine at room temperature.
C Each molecule contains at least one C=C double bond.
D They have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ.
parts.answer: A They are saturated hydrocarbons that contain only single covalent bonds.
parts.working: Alkanes are saturated: every carbon forms four single bonds, general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. B and C describe alkenes (unsaturated, C=C); D is the alkene general formula.

practice.stem: Many homes in Pakistan cook with natural gas supplied through pipelines.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Natural gas piped to homes is mainly methane, CH₄. Methane is a hydrocarbon. State what is meant by a hydrocarbon.
parts.answer: A compound containing hydrogen and carbon only.
parts.working: B1: compound of carbon and hydrogen ONLY ("only" needed).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why methane is described as saturated.
parts.answer: It contains only single bonds between atoms (no C=C double bonds).
parts.working: B1: only single (C–C/C–H) bonds; no double bonds.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the number of covalent bonds in one molecule of methane.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name the two products of the complete combustion of methane.

practice.stem:
Boiling points of some unbranched alkanes:
methane −162 °C; ethane −89 °C; propane −42 °C; butane −1 °C; pentane 36 °C; hexane 69 °C; heptane 98 °C

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which of the alkanes in the table are liquids at 25 °C?
parts.working: B1: all three (boiling points above 25 °C; melting points well below 25 °C).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the trend in boiling point as the number of carbon atoms increases.
parts.answer: The boiling point increases as the number of carbon atoms increases.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hexane has six carbon atoms. Give its molecular formula and calculate its relative molecular mass. [Ar: C = 12, H = 1]

practice.stem: A camping stove burns butane gas.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the molecular formula of butane.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Balance the equation for the complete combustion of butane:
__C₄H₁₀ + __O₂ → __CO₂ + __H₂O
parts.working: B1 correct formulae ratio C:CO₂ and H:H₂O (2, 8, 10); B1 13 O₂.

parts.label: c
parts.text: When the air hole of the stove is partly blocked, the flame becomes yellow and a black solid forms on the pan. Name the black solid and one toxic gas formed.
parts.working: B1 carbon/soot; B1 carbon monoxide (incomplete combustion in a limited supply of oxygen).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the type of reaction between methane and chlorine.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the condition needed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction that forms chloromethane.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain the role of the UV light.
parts.answer: It provides the energy to break the Cl–Cl bond (start the reaction).

practice.stem: A mixture of ethane and chlorine is left in sunlight.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the type of reaction that takes place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction in which one hydrogen atom of ethane is replaced.
parts.working: B1 C₂H₅Cl; B1 HCl and balanced.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what the ultraviolet light in sunlight provides for this reaction.
parts.answer: The activation energy (energy to start the reaction by breaking the Cl–Cl bond).
parts.working: B1 activation energy / energy to break bonds in Cl₂.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name the organic product in (b) and give its structural formula.

practice.stem: A domestic gas cylinder contains 11.8 kg of liquefied gas. Assume the gas is pure propane.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the balanced equation for the complete combustion of propane.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A family uses one full 11.8 kg cylinder of propane each month. Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide, in kg, released when 11.8 kg of propane burns completely. [Mr: C₃H₈ = 44, CO₂ = 44]
parts.working: M1 moles propane = 11 800 ÷ 44 = 268 mol; M1 moles CO₂ = 3 × 268 = 805 mol; A1 805 × 44 = 35 400 g = 35.4 kg (since both Mr are 44, mass of CO₂ = 3 × 11.8).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The relative molecular mass of an alkane is 72. Use the general formula of the alkanes to find its molecular formula. [Ar: C = 12, H = 1]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the molecular formula of the alkane with 20 carbon atoms and calculate its relative molecular mass.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the alkane with 20 carbon atoms has a much higher boiling point than the alkane in (a).
parts.answer: Larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces, so more energy is needed to separate the molecules.
parts.working: B1 stronger intermolecular forces (not covalent bonds); B1 more energy needed to overcome them.

practice.stem:
Data for two alkanes:
butane: melting point −138 °C, boiling point −1 °C
pentane: melting point −130 °C, boiling point 36 °C

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the physical state of each alkane at 20 °C.
parts.working: B1 both: butane bp below 20 °C; pentane between its mp and bp.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why butane, rather than pentane, is used in gas lighters.
parts.answer: Butane boils just below room temperature, so it is a liquid under pressure in the lighter but turns to a gas easily when released; pentane is a liquid at room temperature.
parts.working: B1 butane is a gas at room temperature / vaporises when released; B1 pentane is a liquid at room temperature (bp 36 °C).

parts.label: c
parts.text: When pentane boils, no covalent bonds are broken. Explain what is overcome when pentane boils.
parts.answer: The weak forces of attraction between the pentane molecules (intermolecular forces).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
50 cm³ of butane, C₄H₁₀, is burned completely in oxygen. All volumes are measured at the same temperature and pressure. What volume of oxygen is needed?
A 200 cm³
B 250 cm³
C 325 cm³
D 400 cm³
parts.working: 2C₄H₁₀ + 13O₂ → 8CO₂ + 10H₂O, so 1 volume of butane needs 6.5 volumes of O₂: 50 × 6.5 = 325 cm³. A is the volume of CO₂ formed.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
20 cm³ of ethane is mixed with 100 cm³ of oxygen and burned completely:
2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O
All volumes are measured at room temperature and pressure, where water is a liquid. Calculate the total volume of gas left after the reaction and give its composition.
parts.answer: 70 cm³: 40 cm³ carbon dioxide and 30 cm³ unreacted oxygen.
parts.working: M1 oxygen used = 20 × 7/2 = 70 cm³, so 30 cm³ O₂ left; M1 CO₂ = 20 × 2 = 40 cm³; A1 total 70 cm³ (water is liquid, volume ignored).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The remaining gas is shaken with aqueous sodium hydroxide. State the final volume of gas and explain your answer.
parts.answer: 30 cm³; the carbon dioxide (an acidic gas) is absorbed by the sodium hydroxide, leaving only oxygen.
parts.working: B1 30 cm³; B1 CO₂ reacts with / is absorbed by the alkali.

practice.stem: 0.29 g of a gaseous alkane is burned completely. It forms 0.88 g of carbon dioxide and 0.45 g of water. [Mr: CO₂ = 44, H₂O = 18; Ar: C = 12, H = 1]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of carbon and of hydrogen atoms in the products.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the sample contained only carbon and hydrogen.
parts.answer: Mass of C + H = 0.020 × 12 + 0.050 × 1 = 0.29 g, equal to the mass of the sample.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the empirical formula and the molecular formula of the alkane. Its relative molecular mass is 58.
parts.answer: Empirical formula C₂H₅; molecular formula C₄H₁₀
parts.working: B1 ratio 0.020 : 0.050 = 2 : 5, C₂H₅; B1 Mr of C₂H₅ = 29, 58 ÷ 29 = 2, so C₄H₁₀.

practice.stem: Methane reacts with chlorine in ultraviolet light: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum mass of chloromethane, CH₃Cl, that could be made from 4.0 g of methane. [Ar: C = 12, H = 1, Cl = 35.5]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Only 8.1 g of chloromethane was obtained. Calculate the percentage yield. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one chemical reason why the yield is less than 100%.
parts.answer: Some chloromethane reacts further with chlorine to form CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃ or CCl₄.
parts.working: B1 further substitution / other chlorinated products formed.

practice.stem: A poorly maintained heater in a closed room burns hexane in a limited supply of air.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Balance the equation for the incomplete combustion of hexane in which the only carbon product is carbon monoxide:
__C₆H₁₄ + __O₂ → __CO + __H₂O

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of carbon monoxide, in dm³ at room temperature and pressure, formed when 4.3 g of hexane burns in this way. [Mr: C₆H₁₄ = 86; 1 mol of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why carbon monoxide is dangerous to humans.
parts.answer: It is toxic: it combines with haemoglobin in the blood, so the blood carries less oxygen.
parts.working: B1 combines with haemoglobin; B1 reduces oxygen transport (can cause death). Also accept: colourless and odourless so not noticed.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An ion of iron is written as ⁵⁶₂₆Fe³⁺. How many protons, neutrons and electrons does this ion contain?
A 26 protons, 30 neutrons, 23 electrons
B 26 protons, 30 neutrons, 29 electrons
C 26 protons, 56 neutrons, 23 electrons
D 30 protons, 26 neutrons, 23 electrons
parts.working: Proton number 26; neutrons = 56 − 26 = 30; a 3+ ion has lost 3 electrons, so 26 − 3 = 23. B adds 3 electrons instead of removing them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete the following: an atom has a central ______ containing protons and ______, surrounded by ______ in shells.
parts.working: 2 marks for all three correct, 1 mark for two correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the electronic configuration of a magnesium atom (proton number 12).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Magnesium has three isotopes. State why all three isotopes react in the same way with dilute hydrochloric acid.
parts.answer: They have the same number of outer-shell electrons / the same electronic configuration.
parts.working: Chemical properties depend on electrons, not neutrons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the relative mass and relative charge of: (i) a proton, (ii) a neutron, (iii) an electron.
parts.answer: proton: mass 1, charge +1; neutron: mass 1, charge 0; electron: mass 1/1840 (negligible), charge −1
parts.working: 1 mark for each particle with both values correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which two of these particles are found in the nucleus.

practice.stem: Phosphorus is one of the three main nutrient elements in fertilisers used on wheat farms in Punjab. A phosphorus atom has 15 electrons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the electronic configuration of a phosphorus atom.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answer to (a) to state the group and the period of phosphorus in the Periodic Table.
parts.working: B1 group V (5 outer electrons); B1 period 3 (three shells).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the number of protons in the nucleus of a phosphorus atom.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An atom of element E has the electronic configuration 2,8,6. In which group and period of the Periodic Table is E?
A Group VI, Period 3
B Group III, Period 6
C Group VI, Period 2
D Group II, Period 3
parts.working: Three occupied shells → Period 3; six outer-shell electrons → Group VI (E is sulfur). C is wrong: Period 2 elements have only two shells.

practice.stem:
Four particles are described below.
Particle P: 8 protons, 8 neutrons, 8 electrons
Particle Q: 8 protons, 10 neutrons, 8 electrons
Particle R: 11 protons, 12 neutrons, 10 electrons
Particle S: 9 protons, 10 neutrons, 10 electrons

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which two particles are isotopes of the same element?
parts.working: B1: both have 8 protons but different numbers of neutrons (8 and 10).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which particle is a positive ion? Give its charge.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which particle is a negative ion? Name the element it comes from.
parts.working: B1 S (9 protons, 10 electrons); B1 proton number 9 = fluorine.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the nucleon number of particle Q.

practice.stem: Gallium is used in semiconductors for LED lights. A sample of gallium contains 60.1 % of gallium-69 and 39.9 % of gallium-71.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by the term isotopes.
parts.answer: Atoms of the same element (same number of protons / same proton number) with different numbers of neutrons (different nucleon numbers).
parts.working: B1 same proton number / same element; B1 different number of neutrons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the relative atomic mass of gallium. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the number of neutrons in one atom of gallium-71 (proton number 31).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which pair of atoms are isotopes of the same element? (Values given as nucleon number, proton number.)
A (40, 18) and (40, 20)
B (35, 17) and (37, 17)
C (14, 6) and (14, 7)
D (23, 11) and (24, 12)
parts.working: Isotopes have the same proton number but different nucleon numbers: 17 and 17 with 35 and 37. A has the same nucleon number but different proton numbers, so they are different elements.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Particle X has 17 protons, 20 neutrons and 18 electrons. Write the symbol of X, showing its nucleon number and charge.
parts.working: B1 Cl with nucleon number 37; B1 charge 1− (one more electron than protons).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Particle Y has 12 protons, 12 neutrons and 10 electrons. Write the symbol of Y, showing its nucleon number and charge.
parts.working: B1 Mg with nucleon number 24; B1 charge 2+.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the electronic configuration of a sulfide ion, S²⁻ (proton number of sulfur 16).

practice.stem: An ion X²⁻ contains 18 electrons and 16 neutrons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify element X. Explain your answer.
parts.working: M1 X²⁻ has gained 2 electrons, so the atom has 18 − 2 = 16 electrons = 16 protons; A1 proton number 16 = sulfur.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the nucleon number of this isotope of X.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the electronic configuration of the X²⁻ ion.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name the noble gas that has the same electronic configuration as X²⁻.

practice.stem: Lithium is used in the rechargeable batteries of mobile phones and electric rickshaws. Natural lithium contains 7.6 % lithium-6 and 92.4 % lithium-7.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of neutrons in an atom of lithium-6 and in an atom of lithium-7. (Proton number of lithium = 3.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the relative atomic mass of lithium. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why lithium-6 and lithium-7 have the same chemical properties.
parts.answer: They have the same number of electrons (3) and the same electronic configuration (2,1), with one outer-shell electron.
parts.working: B1 same number of electrons / same electronic configuration; B1 chemical reactions depend on (outer-shell) electrons, not neutrons.

practice.stem: Boron compounds are used in heat-resistant glass. Natural boron is a mixture of only two isotopes, boron-10 and boron-11. The relative atomic mass of boron is 10.81.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Let the percentage of boron-10 be x. Write an expression for the relative atomic mass of boron in terms of x.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of boron-10 atoms in natural boron.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the number of neutrons in an atom of boron-11. The proton number of boron is 5.

practice.stem:
A mass spectrometer in a university laboratory in Islamabad gives these results for a sample of magnesium:
magnesium-24: 78.99 %
magnesium-25: 10.00 %
magnesium-26: 11.01 %

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the relative atomic mass of magnesium. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of neutrons in one atom of magnesium-26. The proton number of magnesium is 12.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student says that magnesium-26 must be more reactive than magnesium-24 because it is heavier. Explain why the student is wrong.
parts.answer: Both isotopes have 12 electrons with the same arrangement (2 outer electrons), and reactivity depends on the electrons, not on the number of neutrons.
parts.working: B1 same electronic configuration / same number of outer electrons; B1 neutrons do not affect chemical reactions.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Chlorine has two isotopes, chlorine-35 and chlorine-37. Chlorine gas is made of Cl₂ molecules. How many different relative molecular masses can a Cl₂ molecule have?
A 2
B 3
C 4
D 6
parts.working: Possible pairs: ³⁵Cl–³⁵Cl = 70, ³⁵Cl–³⁷Cl = 72, ³⁷Cl–³⁷Cl = 74, so three masses. A ignores the mixed molecule; C counts ³⁵Cl–³⁷Cl and ³⁷Cl–³⁵Cl separately, but they are the same molecule.

practice.stem:
Argon is used to fill the bulbs of filament lamps. A sample of argon contains three isotopes:
argon-36: 0.337 %
argon-38: 0.063 %
argon-40: 99.600 %

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the relative atomic mass of argon to 4 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Potassium (proton number 19) has a relative atomic mass of 39.10, yet it comes after argon (proton number 18) in the Periodic Table. Explain why the Periodic Table puts potassium after argon.
parts.answer: Elements are arranged in order of proton number, not relative atomic mass; potassium has one more proton than argon (and fits Group I by its properties).
parts.working: B1 order is by proton number; B1 potassium has 19 protons, argon 18 / potassium has 1 outer electron like Group I.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why argon has a higher relative atomic mass than potassium even though it has fewer protons.
parts.answer: Almost all argon atoms are argon-40 (22 neutrons), the heaviest isotope, while most potassium atoms are potassium-39 (20 neutrons); argon's atoms on average contain more neutrons.
parts.working: B1 most abundant argon isotope is heavy (Ar-40 has 22 neutrons); B1 relative atomic mass is a weighted average depending on isotope abundance, so the extra neutrons outweigh the extra proton.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Calcium forms Ca²⁺ ions and nitrogen forms N³⁻ ions. What is the formula of calcium nitride?
A CaN
B Ca₂N₃
C Ca₃N₂
D CaN₂
parts.working: Charges must balance: 3 × (+2) = +6 and 2 × (−3) = −6, so Ca₃N₂. B swaps the numbers the wrong way round.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the electronic configurations of a lithium atom and a fluorine atom.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the formulae, with charges, of the two ions in lithium fluoride.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the type of bonding in lithium fluoride.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which pair of elements would combine to form an ionic compound?
A carbon and oxygen
B potassium and bromine
C nitrogen and hydrogen
D chlorine and oxygen
parts.working: Ionic bonding forms between a metal and a non-metal: potassium (metal) gives an electron to bromine (non-metal) → K⁺ and Br⁻. A, C and D are pairs of non-metals, which share electrons (covalent).

practice.stem: Calcium chloride is spread on some roads in cold mountain areas, such as near Murree, to stop ice forming.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the electronic configuration of a calcium atom (proton number 20) and a chlorine atom (proton number 17).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what happens to the electrons when calcium chloride forms from its elements.
parts.answer: Each calcium atom loses its two outer electrons, one to each of two chlorine atoms; Ca²⁺ and two Cl⁻ ions form.
parts.working: B1 calcium loses 2 electrons; B1 each chlorine gains 1 electron; B1 two chlorine atoms needed per calcium / ions Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻ formed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the formula of calcium chloride.

practice.stem:
Use these ions to write the formula of each compound:
Na⁺, Ca²⁺, Al³⁺, Fe³⁺, NH₄⁺, NO₃⁻, OH⁻, CO₃²⁻, SO₄²⁻

parts.label: a
parts.text: aluminium sulfate

parts.label: b
parts.text: ammonium carbonate

parts.label: c
parts.text: iron(III) hydroxide

parts.label: d
parts.text: calcium nitrate

practice.stem: Magnesium oxide is used to line the inside of furnaces in steel works.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe, in terms of electrons, how a magnesium atom and an oxygen atom form magnesium oxide. Give the electronic configurations of both ions formed.
parts.answer: Magnesium atom loses its two outer electrons, oxygen atom gains two electrons; Mg²⁺ is 2,8 and O²⁻ is 2,8.
parts.working: B1 two electrons transferred from Mg to O; B1 Mg²⁺ 2,8; B1 O²⁻ 2,8.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why magnesium oxide has a very high melting point.
parts.answer: It has a giant ionic lattice with strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions; a lot of energy is needed to overcome these forces.
parts.working: B1 strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions; B1 lots of energy needed to overcome them / giant lattice.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which ions all have the same electronic configuration as a neon atom?
A Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Cl⁻
B Li⁺, F⁻, O²⁻
C Na⁺, Al³⁺, O²⁻
D K⁺, Ca²⁺, S²⁻
parts.working: Na⁺, Al³⁺ and O²⁻ each have 10 electrons (2,8). A includes Cl⁻ (2,8,8); D are all 2,8,8 like argon; Li⁺ in B is 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the formula of aluminium oxide, which contains Al³⁺ and O²⁻ ions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total number of electrons transferred when the ions in one formula unit of aluminium oxide are formed from atoms.
parts.working: M1 each Al loses 3 electrons and there are 2 Al; A1 6 (= 3 O atoms × 2 electrons).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the formula of potassium sulfide.

practice.stem: Hospitals in Pakistan use a 'barium meal' of barium sulfate, BaSO₄, to show the stomach on X-ray images. Barium sulfate is an ionic compound.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the formulae of the two ions in barium sulfate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the structure of solid barium sulfate.
parts.answer: A giant lattice of Ba²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ ions, held together by strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
parts.working: B1 giant lattice of (alternating) positive and negative ions; B1 strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Barium sulfate does not conduct electricity when a solid, and it is insoluble in water, so a mixture of it with water does not conduct either. Explain why, and state the condition under which barium sulfate would conduct.
parts.answer: Its ions are fixed in the lattice and cannot move; as it does not dissolve, the ions are not freed in water; it would conduct when molten.
parts.working: B1 ions cannot move in the solid lattice; B1 insoluble so ions are not released into solution; B1 conducts when molten (melted).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Aluminium (Group III) reacts with nitrogen (Group V) to form aluminium nitride. Give the formulae of the two ions and of aluminium nitride.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of electrons transferred to form one formula unit of aluminium nitride.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Lithium (Group I) reacts with oxygen (Group VI). Give the formula of lithium oxide and the total number of electrons transferred to form one formula unit.
parts.working: B1 Li₂O; B1 2 (one from each lithium atom).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why both ions in lithium oxide have the electronic configuration of helium or neon.
parts.answer: Li⁺ (2) has helium's configuration and O²⁻ (2,8) has neon's: each ion has a full outer shell.
parts.working: B1 Li⁺ = 2 and O²⁻ = 2,8 / full outer shells.

practice.stem: Pink rock salt is mined at Khewra in the Salt Range of Punjab. It is mainly sodium chloride.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the arrangement of the particles in a crystal of rock salt (sodium chloride).
parts.answer: Giant ionic lattice: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions arranged in a regular repeating pattern, each ion surrounded by ions of opposite charge.
parts.working: B1 giant lattice/regular arrangement of ions; B1 alternating positive and negative ions (Na⁺ and Cl⁻).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why rock salt has a high melting point (801 °C).
parts.answer: Strong electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ions acts in all directions throughout the lattice; much energy is needed to overcome it.
parts.working: B1 strong (electrostatic) attraction between oppositely charged ions; B1 lots of energy needed to overcome many of these forces.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a solution of rock salt in water conducts electricity.
parts.answer: When it dissolves, the ions are free to move and carry charge.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity but molten sodium chloride does.
parts.answer: In the solid the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice and cannot move; when molten the ions are free to move and carry charge.
parts.working: B1 ions fixed in solid; B1 ions mobile when molten. (Reject 'electrons move'.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: The melting point of sodium chloride is 801 °C and the melting point of magnesium oxide is 2852 °C. Suggest why the melting point of magnesium oxide is much higher.
parts.answer: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ have larger charges than Na⁺ and Cl⁻, so the electrostatic attraction between the ions is stronger and needs more energy to overcome.
parts.working: B1 ions have charges 2+ / 2− compared with 1+ / 1−; B1 stronger attraction, more energy needed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the structure of solid sodium chloride.
parts.answer: A giant lattice of alternating Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in a regular repeating arrangement.
parts.working: B1 giant lattice; B1 regular alternating positive and negative ions.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Element X has the electronic configuration 2,8,3 and element Y has the electronic configuration 2,6. What is the formula of the compound formed between X and Y, and what type of bonding does it have?
A XY, ionic
B X₂Y₃, ionic
C X₃Y₂, ionic
D X₂Y₃, covalent
parts.working: X loses 3 electrons → X³⁺; Y gains 2 electrons → Y²⁻. Charges balance with 2 X³⁺ (+6) and 3 Y²⁻ (−6): X₂Y₃. X is a metal (aluminium) and Y a non-metal (oxygen), so the bonding is ionic. C swaps the numbers; D has the right formula but wrong bonding.

practice.stem: An ion of element Z has the symbol Z³⁺ and contains 10 electrons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify Z and give its electronic configuration as an atom.
parts.working: M1 Z³⁺ has 10 electrons, so the atom has 13 → aluminium; A1 2,8,3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Z reacts with sulfur (proton number 16). Give the formula of the compound formed and explain how you worked it out.
parts.working: B1 Al₂S₃ (Z₂S₃); B1 charge balance shown.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total number of electrons transferred when one formula unit of this compound forms from atoms.
parts.working: B1 2 aluminium atoms × 3 electrons = 6 (= 3 sulfur atoms × 2).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give the electronic configuration of the sulfide ion.

practice.stem: A student has a white solid, W, with a high melting point. She wants to show that W is an ionic compound.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student could use the conductivity of the molten solid to show that white solid W is ionic. Give the result expected.
parts.answer: Melt the solid in a crucible, dip in two inert (graphite) electrodes connected in a circuit with a power supply and lamp/ammeter; the lamp lights / current flows (and products form at the electrodes) for an ionic compound.
parts.working: B1 melt the solid; B1 electrodes + power supply + lamp/ammeter in series; B1 conducts when molten (but not as solid).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student suggests testing an aqueous solution of W instead. Explain why a solution that conducts does not prove that W is ionic.
parts.answer: Some covalent substances, such as hydrogen chloride, react with or form ions in water, so their solutions conduct too.
parts.working: B1 some covalent compounds form ions in water; B1 named example, e.g. HCl / an acid.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why solid W does not conduct even though it contains charged particles.
parts.answer: The ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice and cannot move.

practice.stem: Ammonia is used to make urea fertiliser at plants near Daharki.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In an ammonia molecule, NH₃, state the number of bonding pairs of electrons and the number of non-bonding (lone) pairs on the nitrogen atom.
parts.working: B1 3 bonding pairs; B1 1 lone pair (N has 5 outer electrons).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Ammonia boils at −33 °C. Explain, in terms of forces, why ammonia has a low boiling point.
parts.answer: The intermolecular forces between ammonia molecules are weak, so little energy is needed to separate the molecules.
parts.working: B1 weak intermolecular forces / forces between molecules; B1 little energy needed. Reject 'weak covalent bonds'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: When iodine crystals are warmed gently in a boiling tube, a purple vapour forms. Name the type of structure in solid iodine.
parts.answer: simple molecular (simple covalent molecules of I₂)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why iodine changes to a vapour at a low temperature.
parts.answer: The forces between I₂ molecules are weak intermolecular forces, which need little energy to overcome.
parts.working: B1 weak intermolecular forces; B1 little energy needed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict whether solid iodine conducts electricity. Give a reason.
parts.answer: No, it has no ions or free electrons to carry charge.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which substance is made of simple covalent molecules?
A diamond
B magnesium oxide
C methane
D copper
parts.working: Methane, CH₄, exists as small separate molecules. Diamond is giant covalent, magnesium oxide is ionic and copper is metallic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the type of bonding between the atoms in a water molecule.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of bonding pairs and non-bonding (lone) pairs of electrons on the oxygen atom in H₂O.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Water boils at 100 °C, a low temperature compared with sodium chloride. Explain why, in terms of forces.
parts.answer: Only weak intermolecular forces between water molecules have to be overcome; the covalent bonds inside the molecules are not broken.
parts.working: B1 weak intermolecular forces / forces between molecules; B1 covalent bonds are not broken on boiling.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the bonding in a molecule of hydrogen chloride, HCl.
parts.answer: A single covalent bond: the hydrogen atom and the chlorine atom each share one electron, forming a shared pair.
parts.working: B1 shared pair of electrons; B1 one electron from each atom / single bond.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the number of electrons in the outer shell of the chlorine atom in HCl, including the shared ones.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why hydrogen chloride is a gas at room temperature.
parts.answer: It is made of small molecules with weak intermolecular forces, which need little energy to overcome.
parts.working: B1 simple molecules / weak intermolecular forces; B1 little energy needed so low boiling point.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Chlorine exists as Cl₂ molecules. State the number of electrons shared between the two atoms.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of non-bonding pairs of electrons on each chlorine atom in Cl₂.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Chlorine is used to kill bacteria in drinking water in many cities. Predict whether liquid chlorine conducts electricity, and explain.
parts.answer: No; it contains molecules with no overall charge, so there are no ions or free electrons to carry the current.
parts.working: B1 does not conduct; B1 no mobile ions or (delocalised) electrons.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
How many electrons are shared between the atoms in one molecule of carbon dioxide, O=C=O?
A 4
B 6
C 8
D 16
parts.working: There are two double bonds; each double bond is 2 shared pairs = 4 electrons, so 2 × 4 = 8. A counts only the number of shared pairs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the total number of covalent bonds in one molecule of methanol, CH₃OH.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of non-bonding pairs of electrons on the oxygen atom in methanol.
parts.working: O has 6 outer electrons, 2 used in bonds.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why liquid methanol does not conduct electricity.
parts.answer: It is made of neutral molecules; there are no ions or free (delocalised) electrons to carry charge.
parts.working: B1 molecules / no ions; B1 no mobile charged particles.

practice.stem:
Liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), used for cooking in many Pakistani homes, is a mixture of propane and butane.
Boiling points: methane −162 °C, ethane −89 °C, propane −42 °C, butane −0.5 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the trend in boiling points of these alkanes.
parts.answer: The boiling point increases as the molecules get larger (more carbon atoms).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the trend.
parts.answer: Larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces, so more energy is needed to separate the molecules.
parts.working: B1 intermolecular forces increase with molecule size; B1 more energy needed to overcome them.

parts.label: c
parts.text: On a winter night in Murree the temperature falls to −5 °C. Predict the state of propane and of butane at this temperature and explain why gas cylinders containing much butane work poorly in cold weather.
parts.answer: Propane is a gas (−5 °C is above −42 °C); butane is a liquid (−5 °C is below −0.5 °C); liquid butane does not evaporate (boil) easily, so little gas comes out.
parts.working: B1 propane gas; B1 butane liquid; B1 butane does not boil/vaporise at −5 °C so too little gas reaches the burner.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of electrons shared between the two atoms in an oxygen molecule, O₂, and name the type of bond.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of non-bonding pairs on each oxygen atom.
parts.working: B1 6 outer electrons − 2 used in bonding = 4 = 2 pairs.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Oxygen is supplied to hospital patients as a compressed gas. Explain why oxygen molecules separate easily on release, while the O=O bond itself stays intact.
parts.answer: Forces between O₂ molecules are weak intermolecular forces, easily overcome; the covalent bond within the molecule is strong and is not broken by a change of state.
parts.working: B1 weak intermolecular forces; B1 strong covalent bond within molecule not broken.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the total number of electrons shared in covalent bonds in one ethanol molecule, CH₃CH₂OH.
parts.working: B1 8 bonds (5 C–H + 1 C–C + 1 C–O + 1 O–H), each a shared pair: 8 × 2 = 16.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hand sanitiser feels cold on the skin because ethanol evaporates quickly. Explain why ethanol evaporates easily at room temperature.
parts.answer: It has a simple molecular structure with weak intermolecular forces, so little energy is needed for molecules to escape.
parts.working: B1 weak forces between molecules; B1 little energy needed to overcome them.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Ethanol boils at 78 °C and water boils at 100 °C. Suggest what this tells you about the intermolecular forces in ethanol compared with those in water.
parts.answer: The intermolecular forces between ethanol molecules are weaker than those between water molecules.
parts.working: B1 weaker forces between ethanol molecules (less energy needed to separate them).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A nitrogen molecule contains a triple bond. State the number of electrons shared between the two atoms and the number of non-bonding pairs on each nitrogen atom.
parts.answer: 6 shared electrons; 1 non-bonding pair on each N
parts.working: B1 6; B1 one lone pair each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student writes: 'When liquid nitrogen boils, the covalent bonds between the nitrogen atoms break.' Explain why this statement is incorrect.
parts.answer: Boiling only overcomes the weak intermolecular forces between N₂ molecules; the covalent (triple) bonds inside each molecule are not broken.
parts.working: B1 intermolecular forces overcome; B1 covalent bonds remain / N₂ molecules stay intact.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why nitrogen gas is very unreactive.
parts.answer: The N≡N triple bond is very strong and needs a lot of energy to break.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which molecule has the greatest total number of non-bonding (lone) pairs of electrons?
A ammonia, NH₃
B water, H₂O
C methane, CH₄
D hydrogen chloride, HCl
parts.working: Lone pairs: NH₃ 1 (on N); H₂O 2 (on O); CH₄ 0; HCl 3 (Cl has 7 outer electrons, 1 used in the bond, 6 left = 3 pairs). B is the usual wrong choice: water has 2 lone pairs, fewer than the 3 on chlorine in HCl.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Phosphorus (Group V) forms phosphorus trichloride, PCl₃. State the number of bonding pairs and lone pairs around the phosphorus atom.
parts.working: B1 each: P has 5 outer electrons, 3 used in bonds, 2 left = 1 pair.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total number of non-bonding pairs of electrons in one PCl₃ molecule.
parts.working: M1 each Cl has 3 lone pairs → 9; A1 + 1 on P = 10.

parts.label: c
parts.text: PCl₃ is a liquid that boils at 76 °C. Explain why it has a low boiling point even though its P–Cl bonds are strong.
parts.answer: Boiling separates whole molecules by overcoming weak intermolecular forces; the strong covalent P–Cl bonds are not broken.
parts.working: B1 weak intermolecular forces overcome; B1 covalent bonds not broken.
