practice.stem: Hydrazine, N₂H₄, is a rocket fuel. Its molecule has a single N–N bond, and each nitrogen atom is also bonded to two hydrogen atoms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of covalent bonds in one hydrazine molecule and the total number of electrons shared.
parts.working: B1 5 bonds (4 N–H + 1 N–N); B1 10 electrons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Each nitrogen atom has one lone pair. Show that each nitrogen atom has 8 electrons in its outer shell.
parts.answer: Each N has 3 bonds (2 N–H, 1 N–N) = 3 shared pairs = 6 electrons, plus 1 lone pair = 2 electrons; total 8.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hydrazine melts at 2 °C and boils at 114 °C. Use this information to state its physical state at 25 °C and give one other property you would expect of hydrazine because of its structure.
parts.answer: Liquid; e.g. does not conduct electricity (no ions or free electrons).
parts.working: B1 liquid; B1 any correct simple-molecular property: poor conductor of electricity / low melting and boiling points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of diamond.
parts.answer: Each carbon atom is covalently bonded to four other carbon atoms in a giant three-dimensional (tetrahedral) lattice.
parts.working: B1 each C bonded to 4 others; B1 giant 3-D covalent lattice.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the structure of diamond to explain why it is used in drill tips for oil wells.
parts.answer: It is very hard because of many strong covalent bonds in a giant structure.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Graphite is used in pencils. Explain, in terms of its structure, why graphite is soft.
parts.answer: Graphite has layers of carbon atoms with weak forces between the layers, so the layers slide over each other.
parts.working: B1 layers; B1 weak forces between layers so layers slide.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which property does diamond have?
A It conducts electricity.
B It is very hard.
C It has a low melting point.
D It dissolves in water.
parts.working: Every carbon atom is joined to four others by strong covalent bonds in a rigid giant structure, so diamond is very hard. A is wrong: it has no delocalised electrons or ions.

practice.stem: Graphite rods are used as electrodes in the electrolysis of molten compounds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two properties of graphite that make it suitable for electrodes.
parts.answer: Conducts electricity; high melting point (also: unreactive/inert).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, in terms of structure, why graphite conducts electricity.
parts.answer: Each carbon atom bonds to only three others; the fourth outer electron is delocalised and can move through the structure.
parts.working: B1 three bonds per carbon; B1 delocalised (free) electrons can move.

practice.stem: Diamond and graphite are both forms of carbon with giant covalent structures. Compare them under each heading.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Number of covalent bonds formed by each carbon atom

parts.label: b
parts.text: Whether it conducts electricity

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hardness
parts.answer: diamond very hard; graphite soft / slippery

parts.label: d
parts.text: One use, linked to the property in (c)
parts.answer: diamond: cutting tools / drill tips; graphite: lubricant / pencils
parts.working: B1 one correct use for each.

practice.stem: Sand is mainly silicon(IV) oxide, SiO₂.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the type of structure of silicon(IV) oxide.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Bricks rich in silicon(IV) oxide are used to line the inside of furnaces. Explain, in terms of structure and bonding, why silicon(IV) oxide is suitable.
parts.answer: It has a giant covalent structure with many strong covalent bonds throughout; a very large amount of energy is needed to break them, so it has a very high melting point and does not melt in the furnace.
parts.working: B1 many strong covalent bonds in a giant structure; B1 lots of energy needed to break them → very high melting point.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one other physical property of silicon(IV) oxide.
parts.answer: Hard / does not conduct electricity / insoluble in water

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement about silicon(IV) oxide, SiO₂, is correct?
A It is made of separate SiO₂ molecules with weak forces between them.
B Each silicon atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms and each oxygen atom to two silicon atoms.
C It conducts electricity when molten because it contains ions.
D It has a low melting point because the Si–O bonds are weak.
parts.answer: B Each silicon atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms and each oxygen atom to two silicon atoms.
parts.working: SiO₂ is a giant covalent lattice: Si bonded to 4 O, each O to 2 Si, giving the 1 : 2 ratio. A describes a simple molecular structure like CO₂, which SiO₂ is not.

practice.stem: Marble quarries in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa cut stone with saw blades whose cutting edges contain small diamonds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Cutting marble makes the saw blade very hot. Explain, in terms of structure and bonding, why the diamonds are not melted or worn away.
parts.answer: Diamond is a giant covalent structure in which every carbon atom is joined to four others by strong covalent bonds; a very large amount of energy is needed to break these bonds, so diamond has a very high melting point and is extremely hard.
parts.working: B1 giant structure, each C covalently bonded to four others; B1 many strong bonds must be broken → very high melting point / very hard.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student suggests using diamond as an electrode. Explain why this would not work.
parts.answer: All four outer electrons of each carbon are used in bonding, so there are no delocalised electrons (or ions) to carry a current.
parts.working: B1 all outer electrons used in bonds; B1 no mobile charged particles.

practice.stem: Locksmiths in Peshawar puff powdered graphite into stiff padlocks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why powdered graphite is a good lubricant for a padlock.
parts.answer: Graphite has layers of carbon atoms; the forces between the layers are weak; the layers slide over each other easily.
parts.working: B1 layers; B1 weak forces between layers; B1 layers slide.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why graphite is better than oil for lubricating a padlock that is used outdoors in a dusty area.
parts.answer: Graphite is a dry solid, so dust does not stick to it (and it does not evaporate or drain away).

parts.label: a
parts.text: In silicon(IV) oxide each silicon atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms and each oxygen atom is bonded to two silicon atoms. Use this to explain why the formula is SiO₂.
parts.answer: Each oxygen is shared between two silicon atoms, so each Si has 4 × ½ = 2 oxygen atoms; ratio Si : O = 1 : 2.
parts.working: M1 each O shared by two Si; A1 4 ÷ 2 = 2 → SiO₂.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one similarity between the structure of silicon(IV) oxide and diamond.
parts.answer: Both are giant 3D covalent structures; each Si/C atom bonds tetrahedrally to four other atoms.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why silicon(IV) oxide does not conduct electricity even when molten.
parts.answer: It has no ions and no delocalised electrons.

practice.stem: A student draws a thick line on paper with a soft pencil (a mixture of graphite and clay). When the two ends of the line are connected to a 9 V battery and a small bulb, the bulb glows dimly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the bulb lights.
parts.answer: Pencil 'lead' contains graphite, which has delocalised electrons that can move along the line and carry the current.
parts.working: B1 graphite in pencil; B1 delocalised/mobile electrons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the bulb glows only dimly.
parts.answer: The line is thin and contains clay, which does not conduct, so the resistance is high / current is small.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the student could make the bulb glow more brightly.
parts.answer: Draw a thicker / shorter line or use a softer pencil with more graphite.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not.
parts.answer: In graphite each carbon uses only three outer electrons in bonding, so one electron per atom is delocalised and can move; in diamond all four outer electrons are in covalent bonds.
parts.working: B1 graphite has delocalised / mobile electrons (one per C); B1 diamond: all 4 electrons used in bonds, none free.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one similarity in the structure of diamond and silicon(IV) oxide.
parts.answer: Both are giant covalent (macromolecular) structures with every atom held by strong covalent bonds in 3-D.
parts.working: Accept: both have tetrahedral arrangement around the central atom.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why both diamond and silicon(IV) oxide have very high melting points.
parts.answer: Many strong covalent bonds must be broken to melt them; this needs a lot of energy.
parts.working: B1 many strong covalent bonds; B1 must be broken, needing much energy.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement about the structure of graphite is correct?
A Each carbon atom forms three covalent bonds, and the layers are held together by weak forces.
B Each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds, and the layers are held together by weak forces.
C Each carbon atom forms three covalent bonds, and the layers are joined by strong covalent bonds.
D Each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds, and every outer electron is used in bonding.
parts.answer: A Each carbon atom forms three covalent bonds, and the layers are held together by weak forces.
parts.working: In graphite each carbon bonds to three others in hexagonal layers; the fourth outer electron is delocalised; the layers are held by weak forces, so they slide. B and D describe diamond-like four bonds; C would make graphite hard.

practice.stem: A 0.600 g diamond is heated strongly in pure oxygen. It burns completely and only carbon dioxide is formed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the complete combustion of diamond.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide formed. [Ar: C = 12, O = 16]

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide formed at room temperature and pressure (1 mol of gas occupies 24 dm³).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain how this result supports the idea that diamond is an element.
parts.answer: The only product is carbon dioxide and its mass matches that expected from 0.600 g of carbon, so diamond contains only carbon atoms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State how many of the four outer electrons of each carbon atom in graphite are delocalised.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of delocalised electrons in 1.20 g of graphite. [Ar: C = 12; Avogadro constant = 6.02 × 10²³ /mol]

parts.label: c
parts.text: Both diamond and graphite have very high melting points. Explain why, even though graphite is soft.
parts.answer: Melting either one needs many strong covalent bonds to be broken; graphite's softness comes only from weak forces between layers, which are not what holds each layer together.
parts.working: B1 many strong covalent bonds broken on melting; B1 softness due to weak forces between layers only.

practice.stem:
Substance Q is used to coat cutting tools.
Melting point: about 2970 °C
Hardness: scratches glass and steel
Electrical conductivity: none as a solid; none when molten
Solubility in water: insoluble

parts.label: a
parts.text: Deduce the type of structure of Q. Give two pieces of evidence from the data.
parts.answer: Giant covalent: very high melting point (strong bonds throughout) and does not conduct even when molten (so not ionic or metallic); very hard.
parts.working: B1 giant covalent; B1 high melting point / hard; B1 non-conductor when molten.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Q cannot be an ionic compound.
parts.answer: An ionic compound would conduct when molten because its ions would be free to move.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Q cannot be a metal.
parts.answer: A metal conducts as a solid because it has delocalised electrons; Q does not.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sodium chloride is a solid at room temperature but hydrogen chloride is a gas. State the type of bonding in each compound.
parts.answer: sodium chloride: ionic; hydrogen chloride: covalent

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference in their states at room temperature.
parts.answer: Sodium chloride has a giant lattice with strong electrostatic attraction between ions, needing much energy to break; hydrogen chloride is made of small molecules with weak intermolecular forces, needing little energy to separate.
parts.working: B1 NaCl giant ionic lattice, strong forces between ions; B1 HCl simple molecules, weak intermolecular forces; B1 comparison of energy needed.

practice.stem: State the type of structure of each substance. Choose from: giant ionic, giant covalent, metallic, simple molecular.

parts.label: a
parts.text: sodium chloride

parts.label: b
parts.text: diamond

parts.label: c
parts.text: copper

parts.label: d
parts.text: water

practice.stem:
Properties of four substances:
J: melting point 770 °C; solid conducts: no; liquid conducts: yes; aqueous solution conducts: yes
K: melting point 1610 °C; solid conducts: no; liquid conducts: no; insoluble
L: melting point 1455 °C; solid conducts: yes; liquid conducts: yes; insoluble
M: melting point 44 °C; solid conducts: no; liquid conducts: no; insoluble

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which substance is a metal? Give a reason.
parts.answer: L; it conducts when solid (and when liquid).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which substance is ionic? Give a reason.
parts.answer: J; conducts when molten or dissolved but not when solid.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which substance has a simple molecular structure? Give a reason.
parts.answer: M; low melting point and never conducts.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Which substance is giant covalent?

practice.stem: A teacher in a village school tests two solutions with a battery and a bulb. A solution of table salt lights the bulb. A solution of sugar does not.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the salt solution conducts electricity.
parts.answer: Sodium chloride is ionic; when it dissolves the ions are free to move and carry charge.
parts.working: B1 ions; B1 free to move.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the sugar solution does not conduct.
parts.answer: Sugar is a covalent (simple molecular) substance; its molecules have no charge, so there are no ions in the solution.

practice.stem: For each substance, state its type of structure and give one physical property that results from it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: graphite
parts.answer: Giant covalent; e.g. conducts electricity / high melting point / soft

parts.label: b
parts.text: magnesium
parts.answer: Metallic; e.g. conducts electricity / malleable / high melting point

parts.label: c
parts.text: carbon dioxide
parts.answer: Simple molecular; e.g. gas at room temperature / low boiling point / does not conduct

parts.label: d
parts.text: potassium oxide
parts.answer: Giant ionic; e.g. high melting point / conducts when molten

practice.stem:
Properties of four substances:
W: melting point 801 °C; conducts when solid: no; when molten: yes; dissolved in water: yes
X: melting point −95 °C; conducts when solid: no; when liquid: no; insoluble in water
Y: melting point 1083 °C; conducts when solid: yes; when molten: yes; insoluble in water
Z: melting point 1710 °C; conducts when solid: no; when molten: no; insoluble in water

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the type of structure in each of W, X, Y and Z. Choose from: giant ionic, simple molecular, giant metallic, giant covalent.
parts.answer: W giant ionic; X simple molecular; Y giant metallic; Z giant covalent

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why W conducts electricity when dissolved in water but not when solid.
parts.answer: In solution its ions are free to move; in the solid the ions are fixed in the lattice.
parts.working: B1 ions move in solution; B1 ions fixed in solid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ice melts at 0 °C but sand does not melt even in the hottest part of the Thar Desert. Explain this difference in terms of structure and bonding.
parts.answer: Ice is made of simple molecules held by weak intermolecular forces, which need little energy to overcome. Sand (SiO₂) is giant covalent: melting needs many strong covalent bonds to be broken, which needs a very high temperature.
parts.working: B1 ice simple molecular; B1 weak intermolecular forces; B1 SiO₂ giant covalent; B1 strong covalent bonds broken on melting.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Place these substances in order of increasing melting point: sodium chloride, iodine, silicon(IV) oxide, chlorine.
parts.answer: chlorine < iodine < sodium chloride < silicon(IV) oxide
parts.working: B2 all correct; B1 one adjacent pair swapped.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why chlorine and iodine are lowest.
parts.answer: Simple molecules with weak intermolecular forces.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Both sodium chloride and silicon(IV) oxide have high melting points. For each, state what must be overcome or broken when it melts.
parts.answer: SiO₂: many strong covalent bonds throughout the giant structure are broken; NaCl: strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions is overcome.
parts.working: B1 SiO₂: covalent bonds broken; B1 NaCl: electrostatic attraction between ions overcome.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student says: 'All substances with very high melting points are ionic.' Give two named substances that show this statement is wrong, and state the structure of each.
parts.answer: e.g. diamond / graphite / silicon(IV) oxide (giant covalent); iron / copper / tungsten (metallic)
parts.working: B1 each named substance with correct structure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe a test that would show whether a high-melting solid is ionic, and give the result for an ionic solid.
parts.answer: Test whether it conducts as a solid and when molten: an ionic solid does not conduct as a solid but does conduct when molten.
parts.working: B1 conductivity of solid and molten sample; B1 correct result.

practice.stem: For each substance, state whether it conducts electricity and name the particles responsible (or say why it does not).

parts.label: a
parts.text: solid copper

parts.label: b
parts.text: solid graphite

parts.label: c
parts.text: solid potassium bromide
parts.answer: Does not conduct – ions fixed in the lattice.

parts.label: d
parts.text: molten potassium bromide

parts.label: e
parts.text: liquid sulfur
parts.answer: Does not conduct – simple molecules, no ions or free electrons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Carbon and silicon are both in Group IV. Carbon dioxide turns directly to a gas at −78 °C, but silicon(IV) oxide melts at about 1700 °C. Explain this difference in terms of structure and bonding.
parts.answer: CO₂ is simple molecular: weak intermolecular forces between CO₂ molecules are overcome, needing little energy. SiO₂ is giant covalent: many strong covalent bonds between Si and O atoms must be broken, needing much energy.
parts.working: B1 CO₂ simple molecules; B1 weak intermolecular forces overcome; B1 SiO₂ giant covalent lattice; B1 strong covalent bonds broken.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict whether silicon(IV) oxide conducts electricity when molten. Give a reason.
parts.answer: No; it has no ions or delocalised electrons.

practice.stem:
Melting points of some Period 3 chlorides:
NaCl 801 °C
MgCl₂ 714 °C
AlCl₃ turns to vapour at about 180 °C
SiCl₄ −69 °C
PCl₃ −94 °C

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe and explain the change in structure and bonding across the chlorides from sodium to phosphorus.
parts.answer: NaCl and MgCl₂ are giant ionic (high melting points); SiCl₄ and PCl₃ are simple covalent molecules with weak intermolecular forces (low melting points); the bonding changes from ionic to covalent as the element becomes a non-metal.
parts.working: B1 Na/Mg chlorides ionic, giant; B1 Si/P chlorides simple molecular, weak intermolecular forces; B1 change from metal to non-metal → ionic to covalent.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict which of the five chlorides conduct electricity when molten. Explain.
parts.answer: NaCl and MgCl₂ only: they contain ions that become mobile; SiCl₄ and PCl₃ (and AlCl₃) consist of molecules.

practice.stem:
Melting points of some oxides:
Na₂O 1132 °C
MgO 2852 °C
SiO₂ 1710 °C
SO₂ −72 °C

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the type of structure of each oxide.
parts.answer: Na₂O and MgO giant ionic; SiO₂ giant covalent; SO₂ simple molecular
parts.working: B1 Na₂O/MgO ionic; B1 SiO₂ giant covalent; B1 SO₂ simple molecular.

parts.label: b
parts.text: SiO₂ and SO₂ are both covalent oxides of non-metals. Explain why their melting points differ by more than 1700 °C.
parts.answer: Melting SiO₂ breaks strong covalent bonds throughout the giant structure; melting SO₂ only overcomes weak forces between small molecules.
parts.working: B1 SiO₂: covalent bonds broken; B1 SO₂: weak intermolecular forces.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the melting point of MgO is higher than that of Na₂O.
parts.answer: Mg²⁺ has a higher charge than Na⁺, so attraction between ions is stronger.

practice.stem:
Three elements:
X: very hard, colourless crystals; does not conduct; does not melt below 3500 °C
Y: grey-black crystals; melts at 114 °C and gives a purple vapour when warmed; does not conduct
Z: grey solid; melts at 1538 °C; conducts as a solid; attracted to a magnet

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify X, Y and Z and the type of structure of each.
parts.answer: X: diamond/carbon, giant covalent; Y: iodine, simple molecular; Z: iron, metallic

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Y has a much lower melting point than X, although both are non-metals.
parts.answer: Melting Y overcomes only weak forces between I₂ molecules; melting X breaks many strong covalent bonds.
parts.working: B1 Y weak intermolecular forces; B1 X strong covalent bonds broken.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Caesium (Group I) reacts with fluorine (Group VII) to form caesium fluoride. Predict its type of bonding, whether it has a high or low melting point, and whether it conducts when molten. Explain each prediction.
parts.answer: Ionic (metal + non-metal; Cs⁺ and F⁻); high melting point (strong attraction between oppositely charged ions in a giant lattice); conducts when molten (ions free to move).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Silicon reacts with fluorine to form silicon tetrafluoride, SiF₄, which contains separate SiF₄ molecules. Predict its state at room temperature and explain.
parts.answer: Gas (or very low boiling point): simple molecules with weak intermolecular forces.
parts.working: B1 gas; B1 weak intermolecular forces.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe metallic bonding.
parts.answer: A lattice of positive metal ions in a 'sea' of delocalised electrons; held together by electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons.
parts.working: B1 lattice of positive ions and delocalised electrons; B1 electrostatic attraction between them.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why metals are good electrical conductors.
parts.answer: The delocalised electrons can move through the structure and carry charge.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the description using words from the list: atoms, delocalised, electrons, molecules, negative, positive, strong, weak.
'A metal consists of a lattice of ______ ions in a "sea" of ______ electrons. There is a ______ attraction between the ions and the electrons.'

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what moves through a metal wire when it conducts electricity.

practice.stem: Traditional copper cooking pots are still made in the bazaars of Lahore.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the copper base of a cooking pot heats quickly and evenly.
parts.answer: Copper is a good thermal conductor because its delocalised electrons (and vibrating ions) pass energy quickly through the metal.
parts.working: B1 good thermal conductor; B1 delocalised electrons transfer energy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Copper can be pressed into the curved shape of a pot without breaking. Name this property and explain it.
parts.answer: Malleable; layers of copper ions slide over each other when force is applied, and the delocalised electrons keep holding the ions together.
parts.working: B1 malleable; B1 layers (of ions) slide; B1 metallic bonding is not broken / electrons still attract ions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the type of particle that carries the electric current in each case: (i) a copper wire; (ii) molten sodium chloride.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why copper conducts as a solid but sodium chloride does not.
parts.answer: Copper has delocalised electrons that are free to move; in solid sodium chloride the ions are fixed in the lattice.
parts.working: B1 mobile electrons in copper; B1 ions cannot move in solid NaCl.

practice.stem: Craftsmen in Lahore draw gold into very fine threads for zari embroidery on wedding clothes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the name of the property that allows gold to be drawn out into thin wires.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the structure of gold and use it to explain this property.
parts.answer: Regular layers of positive gold ions in a sea of delocalised electrons; when the metal is pulled, the layers slide over each other but the delocalised electrons still hold the ions together.
parts.working: B1 layers of positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons; B1 layers slide without the metallic bonding breaking.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one other physical property of gold that is typical of metals.
parts.answer: Shiny / good electrical or thermal conductor / malleable / high melting point

parts.label: a
parts.text: Copper is used for electrical wiring in houses. Explain in terms of structure why copper can be drawn into wires and why it conducts electricity.
parts.answer: Layers of copper ions can slide over each other (ductile); delocalised electrons move through the lattice and carry charge.
parts.working: B1 layers slide; B1 bonding not broken as layers slide / structure stays together; B1 delocalised electrons move.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why copper has a high melting point.
parts.answer: Strong electrostatic attraction between positive copper ions and delocalised electrons; much energy needed to overcome it.
parts.working: B1 strong attraction ions–electrons; B1 much energy needed.

practice.stem: Sodium, magnesium and aluminium are metals in Period 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the charge on the ions in the lattice of sodium, magnesium and aluminium.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of delocalised electrons per atom for each metal.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why aluminium is a better electrical conductor than sodium.
parts.answer: Aluminium gives more delocalised electrons per atom (3 vs 1), so there are more charge carriers.
parts.working: B1 more delocalised electrons per atom; B1 more charge carriers → better conductor.

practice.stem: A student wrote: 'In a metal, negative ions are held in a regular pattern by a sea of free protons. The attraction between them is weak.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two errors in the student's description and correct each one.
parts.answer: Error 1: the ions are positive, not negative. Error 2: the 'sea' is of delocalised electrons, not protons. (Also accept: the attraction is strong, not weak.)
parts.working: B1 + B1 for each error identified and corrected (any two).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the attraction in metallic bonding is described as non-directional.
parts.answer: The delocalised electrons are spread throughout the structure, so each ion is attracted equally in all directions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happens to the delocalised electrons in a copper wire when it is connected to a cell.
parts.answer: The delocalised electrons drift through the wire towards the positive terminal, forming a current.
parts.working: B1 electrons move; B1 towards positive terminal / in one direction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the copper ions do not move along the wire.
parts.answer: They are held in fixed positions in the lattice by the strong attraction to the delocalised electrons (they can only vibrate).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the wire is not used up or changed chemically when current flows.
parts.answer: Electrons flow in at one end as they flow out at the other; no ions are discharged and no new substance is formed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Mercury is a metal that is liquid at room temperature. Explain why liquid mercury still conducts electricity.
parts.answer: It still has delocalised electrons, which are free to move in the liquid as well as the solid.
parts.working: B1 delocalised electrons present; B1 free to move / carry charge.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why metals usually have high melting points.
parts.answer: There is strong electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons; much energy is needed to overcome it.
parts.working: B1 strong attraction between positive ions and delocalised electrons; B1 large amount of energy needed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest what the low melting point of mercury (−39 °C) tells you about the strength of its metallic bonding.
parts.answer: The attraction between its ions and delocalised electrons is relatively weak.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why metals such as aluminium can be hammered into thin sheets (are malleable).
parts.answer: The layers of positive ions can slide over each other while the delocalised electrons keep holding the structure together, so the metal changes shape without breaking.
parts.working: B1 layers of ions slide; B1 metallic bonding not broken / electrons still hold layers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The melting point of sodium is 98 °C and that of magnesium is 650 °C. Suggest why magnesium has the higher melting point.
parts.answer: Magnesium ions are Mg²⁺ (higher charge) and each atom gives two delocalised electrons, so the attraction between the ions and the delocalised electrons is stronger.
parts.working: B1 Mg²⁺ / more delocalised electrons per atom; B1 stronger electrostatic attraction, more energy needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of delocalised electrons each aluminium atom gives to the metallic structure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of delocalised electrons in a 2.70 g piece of aluminium foil. [Ar: Al = 27; Avogadro constant = 6.02 × 10²³ /mol] Give your answer in standard form to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Both a metal and an ionic compound contain positive ions. Explain why a metal conducts electricity when solid, but an ionic compound conducts only when molten or dissolved.
parts.answer: In a metal, delocalised electrons are free to move even in the solid; in an ionic solid the ions are held in fixed positions and there are no free electrons; on melting/dissolving the ions become free to move.
parts.working: B1 metal: delocalised electrons mobile in solid; B1 ionic solid: ions fixed, no free electrons; B1 molten/aqueous: ions free to move.

parts.label: b
parts.text: When a metal conducts, it is not chemically changed. When a molten ionic compound conducts, it is decomposed. Explain this difference.
parts.answer: In a metal, the charge is carried by electrons flowing through it; in an ionic melt, ions move to the electrodes and are discharged, forming new substances (electrolysis).
parts.working: B1 electron flow causes no chemical change; B1 ions discharged at electrodes → decomposition.

practice.stem: Melting points of some Group I metals: lithium 181 °C; sodium 98 °C; potassium 63 °C; rubidium 39 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the trend in melting point down Group I.
parts.answer: The melting point decreases down the group.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Each of these metals gives one delocalised electron per atom. Suggest, in terms of metallic bonding, why the melting point decreases down the group.
parts.answer: The ions get larger down the group, so the delocalised electrons are further from the positive nuclei; the attraction between the ions and the delocalised electrons is weaker, so less energy is needed to melt the metal.
parts.working: B1 ions larger / electrons further from the nucleus; B1 weaker attraction between ions and delocalised electrons → less energy needed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Potassium is soft enough to cut with a knife. Link this to your answer in (b).
parts.answer: Its weak metallic bonding means the layers of ions slide over each other very easily.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a piece of aluminium bends when hammered, but a crystal of sodium chloride shatters.
parts.answer: In aluminium, layers of positive ions slide and the delocalised electrons still hold them together, so the metal changes shape without breaking. In sodium chloride, a blow shifts layers so that ions of the same charge come next to each other; they repel, and the crystal splits.
parts.working: B1 metal layers slide; B1 delocalised electrons keep bonding non-directional/intact; B1 in ionic lattice, like charges brought together; B1 repulsion → shatters.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of these is a mixture?
A distilled water
B sea water
C sodium chloride
D copper
parts.working: Sea water contains water with several dissolved salts that are not chemically combined, so it is a mixture. Distilled water and sodium chloride are compounds; copper is an element.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which substance is a compound?
A air
B brass
C carbon dioxide
D oxygen
parts.working: Carbon dioxide contains carbon and oxygen chemically combined in a fixed ratio. Air and brass are mixtures; oxygen is an element.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term element.
parts.answer: A substance made of only one type of atom (cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical means).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define the term compound.
parts.answer: A substance containing two or more elements chemically combined (in a fixed ratio).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Classify each of these as an element, a compound or a mixture: tap water, iron, iron(II) sulfide, air, glucose.
parts.answer: tap water – mixture; iron – element; iron(II) sulfide – compound; air – mixture; glucose – compound
parts.working: B3 all five correct; B2 four; B1 two or three.

practice.stem: A student mixes iron filings and powdered sulfur.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student can separate the iron from the sulfur in the mixture.
parts.answer: Use a magnet; the iron is attracted.

parts.label: b
parts.text: When the mixture is heated it glows and forms a black solid. Name the black solid.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the iron cannot be removed from the black solid with a magnet.
parts.answer: Iron(II) sulfide is a compound: the iron is chemically combined with sulfur and the compound has different properties (it is not magnetic).
parts.working: B1 compound / chemically combined; B1 new substance with different properties.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give one other difference between the mixture and the black solid.
parts.answer: The mixture can have any proportions / is separated physically; the compound has a fixed composition / forms with an energy change.

practice.stem: Four boxes show particles. For each box, state whether it contains an element, a compound or a mixture.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Box A: many single atoms, all of the same kind

parts.label: b
parts.text: Box B: many molecules, each made of two identical atoms joined together

parts.label: c
parts.text: Box C: many identical molecules, each made of one atom of one kind joined to two atoms of another kind

parts.label: d
parts.text: Box D: some molecules made of two identical atoms and some single atoms of a different kind, not joined

practice.stem: Pure water boils at 100 °C at normal atmospheric pressure. A sample of tap water from a hard-water area boils at 100.4 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how this shows that the water from the tap is not a pure substance.
parts.answer: A pure substance has a fixed boiling point (100 °C for pure water at normal pressure); dissolved substances raise the boiling point, so the tap water is a mixture.
parts.working: B1 pure substances boil at a fixed temperature; B1 tap water contains dissolved substances / is a mixture.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the type of water that would boil at exactly 100 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which list shows an element, a compound and a mixture, in that order?
A copper, sea water, sodium chloride
B nitrogen, water, air
C steel, iron, iron oxide
D hydrogen, ammonia, nitrogen
parts.working: Nitrogen is an element, water is a compound, air is a mixture. A has the compound and mixture swapped; D ends with an element.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe one property of sodium and one property of chlorine.
parts.answer: Sodium: soft, reactive metal that reacts violently with water; chlorine: green/yellow-green toxic gas.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Sodium chloride is safe to eat. Use this example to explain what is meant by a compound.
parts.answer: The elements are chemically combined to form a new substance whose properties are completely different from those of the elements.
parts.working: B1 chemically combined; B1 different properties from its elements.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why sodium cannot be separated from sodium chloride by dissolving and filtering.
parts.answer: The sodium is chemically bonded (as ions); a chemical change/electrolysis is needed to separate it.

practice.stem: For each compound, state the number of different elements and the total number of atoms in one formula unit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ca(OH)₂
parts.working: B1 elements; B1 atoms (1 Ca + 2 O + 2 H).

parts.label: b
parts.text: (NH₄)₂SO₄

parts.label: c
parts.text: C₆H₁₂O₆

practice.stem: Air is about 78 % nitrogen and 21 % oxygen, with small amounts of argon, carbon dioxide and water vapour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State whether air is an element, a compound or a mixture.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two pieces of evidence that support your answer.
parts.answer: Its composition varies (e.g. water vapour, CO₂ near cities); it can be separated by physical means (fractional distillation of liquid air); its components keep their own properties; it has no fixed boiling point.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why brass is described as a mixture, while water is a compound.
parts.answer: Brass can contain different proportions of copper and zinc (not chemically combined); water always contains hydrogen and oxygen in a fixed ratio, chemically combined.
parts.working: B1 brass composition varies; B1 water fixed ratio / chemically combined.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Water always contains 1 g of hydrogen for every 8 g of oxygen. Calculate the mass of oxygen in 45 g of water.
parts.working: M1 oxygen = 8/9 of the mass; A1 8/9 × 45 = 40 g.

practice.stem: Two samples of a white solid were made by burning magnesium. Sample 1: 4.8 g of magnesium combined with 3.2 g of oxygen. Sample 2: 7.2 g of magnesium combined with 4.8 g of oxygen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio mass of magnesium : mass of oxygen for each sample, in its simplest form.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what these results show about the white solid.
parts.answer: Both samples have the same ratio, so the solid has a fixed composition: it is a compound (magnesium oxide), not a mixture.
parts.working: B1 same/fixed ratio; B1 so a compound.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by mass of magnesium in magnesium oxide, MgO. [Ar: Mg = 24, O = 16]

practice.stem: A student heats 5.6 g of iron powder with 4.0 g of sulfur powder. They react: Fe + S → FeS

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show which reactant is in excess, and calculate the mass of it left over. [Ar: S = 32, Fe = 56]
parts.answer: Sulfur is in excess by 0.80 g

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum mass of iron(II) sulfide formed. [Mr: FeS = 88]

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the student could show that no free iron remains in the product.
parts.answer: Hold a magnet near the product: it is not attracted.

practice.stem: Classify each substance as an element, a compound or a mixture and give a reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: ozone, O₃

parts.label: b
parts.text: steel
parts.answer: Mixture (alloy of iron with carbon/other elements).

parts.label: c
parts.text: dry ice (solid carbon dioxide)

parts.label: d
parts.text: hydrogen chloride gas

parts.label: e
parts.text: hydrochloric acid
parts.answer: Mixture – a solution of hydrogen chloride in water.

practice.stem: A student evaporates 250 cm³ of sea water collected at Clifton Beach, Karachi, to dryness and obtains 8.75 g of white solid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of dissolved solids in 1.00 dm³ of this sea water.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The solid left behind is white. Explain why it is still a mixture, not pure sodium chloride.
parts.answer: Sea water contains several dissolved salts (e.g. magnesium chloride, calcium sulfate) which all remain when the water evaporates.
parts.working: B1 more than one dissolved substance; B1 named example or 'all remain on evaporation'.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether sea water itself is an element, a compound or a mixture.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Magnesium ribbon reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid. Which change increases the rate of the reaction?
A using a larger volume of the same acid
B increasing the temperature of the acid
C using a wider beaker
D adding water to the acid
parts.answer: B increasing the temperature of the acid
parts.working: A higher temperature gives particles more energy, so more frequent and more successful collisions. A does not change concentration so the rate is unchanged.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a catalyst.
parts.answer: A substance that increases the rate of a reaction and is unchanged (chemically and in mass) at the end.
parts.working: B1 increases rate; B1 unchanged at the end.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes slowly into water and oxygen. Name a catalyst for this reaction.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe a test for the oxygen given off.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Zinc reacts with dilute sulfuric acid. Which change decreases the rate of reaction?
A using zinc powder instead of zinc granules
B increasing the temperature of the acid
C diluting the acid with water
D adding a catalyst
parts.answer: C diluting the acid with water
parts.working: Dilution reduces the concentration of acid, so there are fewer particles per unit volume and collisions are less frequent. A, B and D all increase the rate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a student can measure the rate of the reaction between sodium thiosulfate solution and dilute hydrochloric acid by observing a cross marked on paper under the flask.
parts.answer: Add the acid to the thiosulfate in a flask standing on a marked cross; start the timer and swirl; stop the timer when the cross can no longer be seen; the rate is 1 ÷ time.
parts.working: 1 mark: acid added to thiosulfate on a cross, timing starts; 1 mark: time stops when the cross disappears (precipitate of sulfur makes the solution cloudy); 1 mark: rate taken as 1 ÷ time and the experiment repeated with a different concentration (the total volume kept constant with water).

practice.stem: A student in Peshawar reacts marble chips (calcium carbonate) with excess dilute hydrochloric acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The student repeats the experiment using the same mass of powdered marble. Explain, in terms of particles, why the reaction is faster.
parts.answer: Powder has a larger surface area, so more particles of calcium carbonate are exposed and the frequency of collisions with acid particles increases.
parts.working: B1 larger surface area; B1 more collisions per unit time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student then uses hydrochloric acid of half the concentration with the original marble chips. Explain the effect on the rate.
parts.answer: The rate decreases, because there are fewer acid particles per unit volume, so collisions are less frequent.
parts.working: B1 slower; B1 fewer particles per unit volume, lower collision frequency.

practice.stem:
Zinc granules react with dilute hydrochloric acid. The hydrogen is collected in a gas syringe.
time / s: 0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180, 210, 240
volume / cm³: 0, 24, 42, 55, 63, 67, 69, 70, 70

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the total volume of gas produced.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average rate of reaction in the first 60 s, in cm³/s.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the rate of reaction decreases as the reaction goes on.
parts.answer: Reactants are used up (the concentration of the acid decreases), so there are fewer collisions per unit time.
parts.working: B1 reactant(s) used up / concentration of acid falls; B1 fewer collisions per second.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest the time at which the reaction stopped.
parts.working: First time the volume reaches 70 cm³ is 210 s; accept any time from 180 s to 210 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A flask containing marble chips and dilute hydrochloric acid is placed on a balance and its mass is recorded every minute. The acid is in excess. Which change would make the mass fall faster but give the same total loss in mass?
A using the same mass of powdered marble
B using a smaller mass of marble chips
C using a larger volume of the same acid
D using a cotton wool plug in the flask
parts.answer: A using the same mass of powdered marble
parts.working: Powder increases surface area, so the rate rises, and the same mass of marble gives the same mass of CO₂. B would give a smaller total loss.

practice.stem:
Calcium carbonate is added to dilute nitric acid in a conical flask on a balance.
mass of flask and contents at start = 152.40 g
mass after 5 minutes = 151.52 g (the reaction had stopped)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide lost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average rate of reaction over the 5 minutes, in g/min.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of carbon dioxide lost. [Mr of CO₂ = 44]

parts.label: d
parts.text: State why a loose cotton wool plug is placed in the neck of the flask.
parts.answer: To let the gas escape but stop acid spray / liquid being lost (which would give extra mass loss).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The graph of volume of gas against time for a reaction is steep at the start and then levels off. Which explains the levelling off?
A the reactant is used up, so its concentration falls
B the reaction becomes exothermic
C the catalyst is used up
D the particles become larger
parts.answer: A the reactant is used up, so its concentration falls
parts.working: As reactant is used up its concentration falls, so collisions become less frequent and the rate decreases to zero. B does not explain the slowing; a catalyst is not used up; particles do not grow.

practice.stem:
Magnesium carbonate reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid in an open flask standing on a balance. Carbon dioxide escapes and the mass falls: MgCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g).
Time / s: 0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150
Mass lost / g: 0.00, 0.40, 0.66, 0.80, 0.88, 0.88

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the total mass of carbon dioxide lost.
parts.working: The mass stops changing at 0.88 g, so this is the total mass of carbon dioxide released.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of reaction over the first 60 s, in g/s.
parts.working: rate = mass lost ÷ time = 0.66 ÷ 60 = 0.0110 g/s (1 mark for the method, 1 mark for the answer).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the mass stops changing after 120 s.
parts.answer: One reactant has been used up, so no more carbon dioxide is produced.
parts.working: accept: the limiting reactant is used up.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, in terms of particles, why increasing the pressure of a gas increases the rate of a reaction involving that gas.
parts.answer: There are more gas particles in the same volume, so collisions between particles are more frequent and the rate increases.
parts.working: 1 mark: more particles per unit volume; 1 mark: more frequent successful collisions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, in terms of collisions and activation energy, why increasing the temperature increases the rate of a reaction.
parts.answer: Particles gain kinetic energy and move faster, so they collide more often; a greater proportion of collisions have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy, so more collisions are successful.
parts.working: B1 more kinetic energy / faster particles; B1 more frequent collisions; B1 more particles with energy ≥ activation energy (more successful collisions).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why milk kept in a refrigerator goes sour more slowly than milk left out on a hot day in Multan.
parts.answer: Lower temperature slows the reactions (of bacteria / enzymes) that sour the milk.

practice.stem:
Sodium thiosulfate solution reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to form a cloudy mixture. A flask is placed on a cross drawn on paper and the time for the cross to disappear is measured. 10 cm³ of acid is used each time.
experiment 1: 50 cm³ thiosulfate, 0 cm³ water, 20 s
experiment 2: 40 cm³ thiosulfate, 10 cm³ water, 25 s
experiment 3: 30 cm³ thiosulfate, 20 cm³ water, 34 s
experiment 4: 20 cm³ thiosulfate, 30 cm³ water, 62 s
experiment 5: 10 cm³ thiosulfate, 40 cm³ water, 101 s

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of 1/time for experiment 1. Give the unit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result. Explain your choice.
parts.answer: Experiment 4 (20 cm³), 62 s; the pattern suggests about 50 s, as halving the concentration from experiment 2 should double the time.
parts.working: B1 experiment 4; B1 reason based on trend (expected ~50 s).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why water was added so that the total volume was always 50 cm³.
parts.answer: So that the volume of thiosulfate is proportional to its concentration, and the depth of liquid over the cross is the same (fair test).
parts.working: B1 concentration proportional to volume used; B1 same depth / fair test.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name the solid that makes the mixture cloudy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A reaction produces 0.0600 mol of gas in 2.5 minutes. Convert the time into seconds.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of reaction in mol/s.
parts.working: rate = 0.0600 ÷ 150 = 4.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol/s (1 mark for the method, 1 mark for the answer and unit).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes: 2H₂O₂(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g). Manganese(IV) oxide is added as a catalyst. Explain how the catalyst increases the rate of reaction.
parts.answer: The catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, so more particles have enough energy to react when they collide.
parts.working: 1 mark: alternative pathway with lower activation energy; 1 mark: more collisions have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of hydrogen peroxide needed to produce 240 cm³ of oxygen at r.t.p. [Ar: H = 1, O = 16]

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate is heated until it turns white. When the white solid has cooled, a few drops of water are added. What is observed and why?
A The solid stays white because the reaction cannot be reversed.
B The solid turns blue and gets warm because the reaction is reversible.
C The solid turns blue and gets cold because water is absorbed.
D The solid dissolves to form a colourless solution.
parts.answer: B The solid turns blue and gets warm because the reaction is reversible.
parts.working: CuSO₄·5H₂O ⇌ CuSO₄ + 5H₂O is reversible; the forward reaction is endothermic so the reverse (adding water) is exothermic and the solid gets warm. C has the energy change the wrong way round.

practice.stem: A reversible reaction is allowed to reach equilibrium in a closed system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a closed system.
parts.answer: A system in which no substances can enter or leave.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the equilibrium is described as dynamic.
parts.answer: The forward and reverse reactions are still happening, at the same rate.
parts.working: B1 both reactions continue; B1 at equal rates.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what is meant by the symbol ⇌.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of these is a reversible reaction?
A combustion of magnesium in air
B thermal decomposition of limestone in an open furnace
C hydrated cobalt(II) chloride changing colour on heating and turning back when water is added
D the reaction of sodium with water
parts.answer: C hydrated cobalt(II) chloride changing colour on heating and turning back when water is added
parts.working: Only C can be reversed by adding water and gives back the original product. A and B are not reversed in an open system; D (sodium with water) gives sodium hydroxide and hydrogen, which do not recombine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hydrated cobalt(II) chloride, CoCl₂·6H₂O, is heated. State its colour before heating.
parts.working: the hydrated salt is pink; the anhydrous salt is blue.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what happens when water is added to the blue anhydrous solid.
parts.answer: It turns pink (the hydrated salt forms again).
parts.working: the reverse reaction takes place when water is added.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether the forward reaction (hydrated salt → anhydrous salt + water) is endothermic or exothermic.
parts.working: heat is absorbed when the water is driven off, so the forward reaction takes in heat.

practice.stem:
Dinitrogen tetroxide (colourless) and nitrogen dioxide (brown) form an equilibrium in a sealed tube:
N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g)   the forward reaction is endothermic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The sealed tube is placed in hot water. State and explain what happens to the colour of the gas mixture.
parts.answer: It becomes darker brown, because the forward reaction is endothermic so the equilibrium shifts to the right, producing more NO₂.
parts.working: B1 darker brown; B1 equilibrium moves in endothermic direction / to the right.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The gas mixture is compressed in a gas syringe at constant temperature. State and explain how the position of equilibrium changes.
parts.answer: It moves to the left, because there are fewer moles of gas on the left (1 mol compared with 2 mol), so this reduces the pressure.
parts.working: B1 shifts left (towards N₂O₄); B1 fewer gas molecules on left.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Methanol is made by the reaction CO(g) + 2H₂(g) ⇌ CH₃OH(g). The forward reaction is exothermic. Which conditions give the highest equilibrium yield of methanol?
A high temperature and high pressure
B high temperature and low pressure
C low temperature and high pressure
D low temperature and low pressure
parts.answer: C low temperature and high pressure
parts.working: Low temperature favours the exothermic forward reaction; high pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles (3 → 1). A would give a faster rate, but a lower yield.

practice.stem:
In aqueous solution, yellow chromate(VI) ions and orange dichromate(VI) ions form an equilibrium:
2CrO₄²⁻(aq) + 2H⁺(aq) ⇌ Cr₂O₇²⁻(aq) + H₂O(l)
  yellow                          orange

parts.label: a
parts.text: Dilute sulfuric acid is added to the yellow solution. State and explain the colour change.
parts.answer: It turns orange, because adding H⁺ ions moves the equilibrium to the right, forming more Cr₂O₇²⁻.
parts.working: B1 orange; B1 more H⁺ moves equilibrium right.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Aqueous sodium hydroxide is then added to the orange solution. Suggest what is seen. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: It turns yellow again, because OH⁻ ions react with (remove) H⁺ ions, so the equilibrium moves to the left.
parts.working: B1 yellow; B1 H⁺ removed so equilibrium shifts left.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The reaction N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) is exothermic in the forward direction. Which change increases the yield of ammonia at equilibrium?
A raising the temperature
B adding an iron catalyst
C increasing the pressure
D decreasing the pressure
parts.working: There are 4 mol of gas on the left and 2 mol on the right, so higher pressure moves the position to the right. Higher temperature moves it left (exothermic forward); a catalyst speeds up both directions equally; lower pressure moves it left.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calcium carbonate decomposes reversibly in a closed container: CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g). Explain what happens to the position of equilibrium if carbon dioxide is removed from the container.
parts.answer: The equilibrium moves to the right, so more CaCO₃ decomposes and more CaO and CO₂ are formed.
parts.working: 1 mark: position moves to the right (forward reaction favoured); 1 mark: the reaction replaces the CO₂ removed, so more products form.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The forward reaction is endothermic. State and explain the effect of increasing the temperature on the position of equilibrium.
parts.answer: The position moves to the right, because the forward reaction absorbs heat and the system counteracts the increase in temperature.
parts.working: 1 mark: right; 1 mark: the endothermic forward reaction absorbs the extra heat.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The reaction X(g) ⇌ Y(g) has ΔH = +40 kJ/mol for the forward reaction. Predict and explain the effect of lowering the temperature on the position of equilibrium and on the yield of Y.
parts.answer: The position moves to the left, so the yield of Y decreases.
parts.working: 1 mark: position moves to the left (the exothermic reverse reaction is favoured); 1 mark: the yield of Y falls.

practice.stem:
Hydrogen and iodine react in a closed container:
H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g)

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two features of a system at dynamic equilibrium.
parts.answer: The rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction; the concentrations of reactants and products stay constant.
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept: closed system needed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State and explain the effect of increasing the pressure on the position of equilibrium.
parts.answer: No effect, because there are equal numbers of moles of gas on each side (2 and 2).
parts.working: B1 no change; B1 same number of gas moles on both sides.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the effect of increasing the pressure on the rate at which equilibrium is reached. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: The rate increases, because the gas particles are closer together, so there are more collisions per unit time.
parts.working: B1 faster; B1 higher collision frequency.

practice.stem:
A gas XY₃ is made by the reaction X₂(g) + 3Y₂(g) ⇌ 2XY₃(g). The percentage of XY₃ at equilibrium is:
200 °C: 50 % at 10 000 kPa; 70 % at 30 000 kPa
400 °C: 15 % at 10 000 kPa; 35 % at 30 000 kPa
600 °C: 3 % at 10 000 kPa; 9 % at 30 000 kPa

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the data to deduce whether the forward reaction is exothermic or endothermic. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Exothermic: the yield of XY₃ decreases as temperature increases, so the equilibrium shifts left (endothermic direction) when heated.
parts.working: B1 exothermic; B1 yield falls with increasing temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe and explain the effect of increasing the pressure on the yield.
parts.answer: Yield increases, because the equilibrium shifts to the right, the side with fewer moles of gas (2 compared with 4).
parts.working: B1 yield increases (data); B1 fewer gas moles on right.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the manufacturer chooses 400 °C rather than 200 °C, even though the yield is lower.
parts.answer: At 200 °C the rate is too slow; 400 °C gives an acceptable yield at a faster rate (compromise).
parts.working: B1 rate too slow at low temperature; B1 compromise between rate and yield.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the effect of adding a catalyst on the position of equilibrium.
parts.answer: No effect / the position does not change.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a catalyst is still used in many industrial equilibrium reactions.
parts.answer: It increases the rates of the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached more quickly, saving time and energy costs.
parts.working: B1 increases both rates equally; B1 equilibrium reached faster / lower temperature can be used.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how a catalyst increases the rate of a reaction.
parts.answer: It provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, so more collisions have enough energy to react.
parts.working: B1 lower activation energy / alternative route; B1 more particles have energy ≥ Ea / more successful collisions.

practice.stem: The reaction 2A(g) ⇌ Z(g) takes place in a closed container at constant temperature. The equilibrium yield of Z was measured at three pressures: 100 kPa gives 35%; 200 kPa gives 52%; 400 kPa gives 62%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the trend in the yield of Z.
parts.answer: The yield of Z increases as the pressure increases.
parts.working: The yield rises at each increase in pressure, but by less on the second increase (+17 percentage points, then +10).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain this trend in terms of the number of gas molecules on each side of the equation.
parts.answer: The product side has fewer gas molecules (1 mol) than the reactant side (2 mol), so higher pressure favours the forward reaction.
parts.working: 1 mark: fewer gas molecules on the product side; 1 mark: an increase in pressure moves the position of equilibrium towards the side with fewer molecules.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the effect of adding a catalyst to this equilibrium on the position of equilibrium and on the yield of Z.
parts.answer: No effect: the position of equilibrium and the yield of Z stay the same; the catalyst only makes equilibrium reached more quickly.
parts.working: A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so it does not change the position of equilibrium.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The equilibrium 2HI(g) ⇌ H₂(g) + I₂(g) is set up in a closed container. Explain why an increase in pressure has no effect on the position of equilibrium.
parts.answer: There are 2 mol of gas on each side, so the pressure change affects the forward and reverse reactions equally and the position does not change.
parts.working: 1 mark: the same number of gas molecules on each side; 1 mark: increasing pressure affects both directions equally, so no shift occurs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define oxidation in terms of (i) oxygen and (ii) electrons.
parts.answer: (i) gain of oxygen; (ii) loss of electrons

parts.label: b
parts.text: For the reaction CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O, name the substance that is reduced and the substance that is oxidised.
parts.answer: CuO (copper(II) oxide) is reduced; H₂ (hydrogen) is oxidised.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the oxidation number of sulfur in H₂SO₄?
A +2
B +4
C +6
D −2
parts.working: H = +1 (×2) and O = −2 (×4), so 2(+1) + S + 4(−2) = 0; S = +6. A, B and D do not satisfy the sum to zero.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the oxidation number of oxygen in hydrogen peroxide, H₂O₂.
parts.working: H₂O₂ has H = +1 each, so 2(+1) + 2(O) = 0 gives O = −1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the oxidation number of carbon in carbon dioxide, CO₂.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the oxidation number of nitrogen in the nitrate ion, NO₃⁻.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State whether Fe → Fe²⁺ is oxidation or reduction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether Cl₂ → 2Cl⁻ is oxidation or reduction.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether Mg²⁺ → Mg is oxidation or reduction.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the oxidation number of manganese in potassium manganate(VII), KMnO₄?
A +2
B +4
C +6
D +7
parts.working: K is +1 and four O are 4 × (−2) = −8, so Mn = +7, as shown by (VII) in the name. C (+6) is the oxidation number in a manganate(VI); A and B are other common oxidation numbers of manganese (Mn²⁺, MnO₂).

practice.stem:
Zinc powder is added to blue copper(II) sulfate solution. The blue colour fades and a pink-brown solid forms.
Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the ionic half-equation for the change to zinc.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the ionic half-equation for the change to copper(II) ions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify the oxidising agent and the reducing agent. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Oxidising agent: Cu²⁺ (it gains electrons / is reduced); reducing agent: Zn (it loses electrons / is oxidised).
parts.working: B1 Cu²⁺ oxidising agent; B1 Zn reducing agent; B1 explanation in terms of electron transfer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solution P is added to acidified potassium manganate(VII). The purple colour disappears. State what this shows about P.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Solution Q is added to aqueous potassium iodide. The colourless solution turns brown. State what this shows about Q, and name the substance causing the brown colour.
parts.answer: Q is an oxidising agent; iodine.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student adds an oxidising agent to acidified potassium manganate(VII). State what the student sees. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: No change / the solution stays purple, because acidified potassium manganate(VII) is itself an oxidising agent and is only decolourised by a reducing agent.
parts.working: B1 stays purple / no colour change; B1 KMnO₄ is an oxidising agent, it needs a reducing agent to react.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In the reaction Cu(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s), which statement is correct?
A copper is reduced
B silver ions are oxidised
C copper atoms lose electrons
D silver atoms lose electrons
parts.working: Copper goes from 0 to +2 (oxidised, loses electrons). Silver ions go from +1 to 0 (reduced, gain electrons). A and B reverse these, and D describes silver atoms being formed, not losing electrons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In the reaction Mg(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → MgSO₄(aq) + Cu(s), identify the oxidising agent.
parts.working: the oxidising agent is the species that is reduced, Cu²⁺ → Cu.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the half-equation for the oxidation of magnesium.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the half-equation for the reduction of copper(II) ions.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the colour change of the solution.
parts.working: Cu²⁺ ions are blue; Mg²⁺ ions are colourless, so the blue colour fades.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In the reaction Cl₂(g) + 2I⁻(aq) → 2Cl⁻(aq) + I₂(aq), give the oxidation number of iodine in I⁻ and in I₂.
parts.working: 1 mark for each: I⁻ is −1; an element has oxidation number 0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which species is oxidised and which is reduced.
parts.answer: Iodide ions (I⁻) are oxidised; chlorine (Cl₂) is reduced.
parts.working: 1 mark each: I⁻ goes from −1 to 0 (loses electrons); Cl₂ goes from 0 to −1 (gains electrons).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The change Fe²⁺(aq) → Fe³⁺(aq) takes place. State whether this is oxidation or reduction, and give the change in oxidation number.
parts.answer: Oxidation; the oxidation number increases from +2 to +3 (by +1).
parts.working: 1 mark: oxidation (electron loss, Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻); 1 mark: oxidation number rises from +2 to +3.

practice.stem: Household bleach contains sodium chlorate(I), NaClO.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the oxidation number of chlorine in: (i) Cl₂, (ii) NaCl, (iii) NaClO, (iv) the chlorate ion ClO₃⁻.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Chlorine reacts with cold aqueous sodium hydroxide: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O. Use oxidation numbers to explain why this is a redox reaction.
parts.answer: Chlorine goes from 0 to −1 (reduced, in NaCl) and from 0 to +1 (oxidised, in NaClO); reduction and oxidation both occur.

practice.stem:
In the blast furnace, iron(III) oxide is reduced:
Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the oxidation number of iron in Fe₂O₃ and in Fe.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the oxidation number of carbon in CO and in CO₂.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to identify the reducing agent. State how many electrons are gained by each iron ion.
parts.answer: CO is the reducing agent (C is oxidised from +2 to +4); 3 electrons per iron ion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Acidified dichromate(VI) ions (Cr₂O₇²⁻) are orange. In a reaction they become Cr³⁺ ions (green). Give the oxidation number of chromium in Cr₂O₇²⁻.
parts.working: 2 Cr + 7(−2) = −2, so 2 Cr = +12 and each Cr = +6.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the ionic half-equation for the reduction of Cr₂O₇²⁻ to Cr³⁺ in acid.
parts.working: 1 mark for the correct species (Cr³⁺ and H₂O with H⁺ and electrons); 1 mark for balancing atoms and charge (14H⁺ and 6e⁻).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the oxidation number of nitrogen in each of: NH₃, NO, NO₂ and HNO₃.
parts.working: 1 mark each: NH₃: N + 3(+1) = 0 gives −3; NO: N + (−2) = 0 gives +2; NO₂: N + 2(−2) = 0 gives +4; HNO₃: 1 + N + 3(−2) = 0 gives +5.

practice.stem: Ammonia is manufactured by the Haber process at fertiliser plants in Pakistan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the balanced symbol equation for the Haber process, including the reversible sign.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the sources of the nitrogen and of the hydrogen.
parts.answer: Nitrogen from the air; hydrogen from methane (natural gas) reacting with steam.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the temperature, pressure and catalyst used.
parts.answer: about 450 °C; about 20 000 kPa (200 atm); iron catalyst

practice.stem: The Contact process is used to make sulfuric acid. In the converter: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g); the forward reaction is exothermic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the source of the oxygen used in the converter.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the catalyst used in the converter.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State and explain the effect of increasing the temperature on the equilibrium yield of sulfur trioxide.
parts.answer: The yield decreases, because the forward reaction is exothermic, so the equilibrium shifts to the left (the endothermic direction).
parts.working: B1 yield decreases; B1 forward reaction exothermic / equilibrium moves in endothermic direction.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the final product of the Contact process and give its formula.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which raw material is the source of nitrogen in the Haber process?
A air
B natural gas
C limestone
D sulfur
parts.working: Nitrogen is obtained from air by fractional distillation of liquid air. Natural gas supplies hydrogen; limestone and sulfur are not sources of nitrogen in this process.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the substance burned to form sulfur dioxide in the Contact process.
parts.working: sulfur burns in air (or oxygen) to give sulfur dioxide.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the substance that absorbs sulfur trioxide to form the acid.
parts.working: SO₃ is absorbed into concentrated sulfuric acid to form oleum, which is then diluted.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why sulfur trioxide is not dissolved directly in water.
parts.answer: Reacting SO₃ with water forms a fine mist (acid droplets) that is difficult to condense and collect, and the reaction is slow and dangerous.
parts.working: accept: a mist forms; it is inefficient and difficult to control.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State why unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled in the Haber process.
parts.answer: To save raw materials and make the process more economical (more of the reactants are used).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how ammonia is separated from the unreacted gases.
parts.answer: The gas mixture is cooled, so the ammonia turns into a liquid and is removed.
parts.working: ammonia has a higher boiling point and liquefies when cooled, while N₂ and H₂ remain gases.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two ways in which the sulfur dioxide for the Contact process is obtained.
parts.answer: Burning sulfur in air; roasting sulfide ores (e.g. zinc sulfide, iron pyrites) in air.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction in the converter, and state the conditions used.
parts.answer: 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃; about 450 °C, about 200 kPa (2 atm), vanadium(V) oxide catalyst
parts.working: B1 equation with ⇌; B1 temperature and pressure; B1 V₂O₅.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Higher pressure would increase the yield, but only about 200 kPa is used. Suggest why.
parts.answer: The yield is already high at low pressure, so the extra cost of high-pressure equipment is not worth it.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which set of conditions is used in the Haber process?
A 200 °C, 200 kPa, vanadium(V) oxide
B 450 °C, 200 kPa, iron
C 450 °C, 20 000 kPa, iron
D 1000 °C, 20 000 kPa, nickel
parts.working: The Haber process uses about 450 °C, 20 000 kPa and an iron catalyst. B uses the Contact process pressure.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which substance is the catalyst in the Contact process?
A iron
B vanadium(V) oxide
C platinum
D nickel
parts.working: The Contact process uses vanadium(V) oxide at about 450 °C. Iron is the catalyst in the Haber process; platinum and nickel are not the catalyst of the modern Contact process.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ammonia is made by the Haber process: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. Calculate the mass of hydrogen needed to make 680 kg of ammonia. [Ar: N = 14, H = 1]
parts.working: Mr NH₃ = 17; moles NH₃ = 680 ÷ 17 = 40 kmol (1 mark); H₂ needed = 1.5 × 40 = 60 kmol (1 mark); mass H₂ = 60 × 2 = 120 kg (1 mark).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Haber process is operated at 200 atm rather than at a higher pressure. Explain why a much higher pressure is not used.
parts.answer: Higher pressure would need stronger, more expensive equipment and more energy to compress the gases, which increases cost and the risk of accidents.
parts.working: 1 mark: equipment must be stronger and more expensive; 1 mark: more energy is needed to compress the gases (cost and safety).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ammonia reacts with nitric acid: NH₃ + HNO₃ → NH₄NO₃. Calculate the mass of ammonium nitrate that can be made from 1.7 tonnes of ammonia. [Ar: H = 1, N = 14, O = 16]
parts.working: moles NH₃ = 1.7 × 10⁶ ÷ 17 = 100 000 mol; NH₄NO₃ = 100 000 mol; Mr = 80; mass = 8.0 × 10⁶ g = 8.0 tonnes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The forward reaction in the Haber process is exothermic. Explain why a temperature of about 450 °C is used rather than a lower temperature.
parts.answer: A lower temperature would give a higher equilibrium yield, but the rate would be too slow; 450 °C is a compromise giving a reasonable yield at an acceptable rate.
parts.working: B1 lower T gives higher yield; B1 but rate too slow; B1 compromise.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a pressure higher than 20 000 kPa is not used.
parts.answer: Higher pressure would increase yield but equipment would be very expensive to build and run, and it is more dangerous.
parts.working: B1 cost of equipment / energy; B1 safety.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Only about 15 % of the gases react in each pass through the reactor. Suggest what happens to the unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen.
parts.answer: They are recycled (passed back over the catalyst).

practice.stem: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum mass of ammonia, in tonnes, that could be made from 1.40 tonnes of nitrogen. [Ar: N = 14, H = 1]

parts.label: b
parts.text: In one pass through the reactor only 15 % of this mass is formed. Calculate the mass of ammonia formed in one pass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A plant uses 1.60 tonnes of sulfur to make sulfuric acid. Calculate the number of kmol of sulfur used. [Ar: S = 32]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assuming all the sulfur converts to sulfuric acid (1 S → 1 H₂SO₄), calculate the theoretical mass of sulfuric acid in tonnes. [Mr H₂SO₄ = 98]
parts.working: moles H₂SO₄ = 50.0 kmol; mass = 50.0 × 98 = 4900 kg = 4.90 tonnes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The actual yield is 95%. Calculate the actual mass of sulfuric acid formed, in tonnes.
parts.working: actual mass = 4.90 × 0.95 = 4.655 tonnes, which is 4.66 tonnes to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A plant uses 4.20 tonnes of hydrogen in the Haber process: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. Calculate the number of kmol of hydrogen used. [Ar: H = 1]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the theoretical mass of ammonia, in tonnes. [Mr NH₃ = 17]
parts.working: 3 mol H₂ give 2 mol NH₃, so NH₃ = 2/3 × 2100 = 1400 kmol (1 mark); mass = 1400 × 17 = 23 800 kg = 23.8 tonnes (1 mark).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The actual mass of ammonia is 19.0 tonnes. Calculate the percentage yield to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: percentage yield = 19.0 ÷ 23.8 × 100 = 79.8% (1 mark for the method, 1 mark for the answer).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of these is a chemical change?
A ice melting in a glass of water
B sugar dissolving in tea
C an iron gate rusting
D water boiling in a kettle
parts.working: Rusting forms a new substance (hydrated iron(III) oxide). The others are physical changes that only change the state or mix substances.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two differences between a physical change and a chemical change.
parts.answer: A chemical change forms a new substance, a physical change does not; physical changes are usually easily reversed, chemical changes usually are not.
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept: chemical change usually has a large energy change.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Classify each of the following as a physical or chemical change: (i) burning natural gas in a cooking stove, (ii) iodine subliming, (iii) frying an egg, (iv) dissolving salt in water.
parts.working: 2 marks for all four correct, 1 mark for three correct.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of these is a physical change?
A souring of milk
B melting of wax
C toasting of bread
D tarnishing of silver
parts.working: Melting changes only the state of the wax; no new substance is formed and it can be reversed by cooling. A, C and D each form new substances (lactic acid, a toasted product and silver sulfide).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Dissolving sugar in water. Classify the change as physical or chemical.
parts.working: no new substance is formed; the sugar can be recovered by evaporation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Milk going sour. Classify the change as physical or chemical.
parts.working: bacteria produce acid, a new substance.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Crushing an aluminium can. Classify the change as physical or chemical.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Burning paper. Classify the change as physical or chemical.
parts.working: new substances (ash, carbon dioxide, water vapour) are formed.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Steam condensing to water. Classify the change as physical or chemical.
parts.working: only the state changes; it can be reversed by heating.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student heats a spoonful of sugar strongly until it turns black. Give two observations that show a new substance has been formed.
parts.answer: The sugar turns black (carbon is formed); steam or water vapour forms and a burnt smell is produced.
