parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of copper(II) oxide used and the mass of copper expected.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction and state which substance is reduced.
parts.answer: CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O; copper(II) oxide is reduced.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Iron from the blast furnace contains about 4 % carbon. State one property of this iron that makes it unsuitable for most uses.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how this iron is converted into steel. Include the role of oxygen and of calcium oxide.
parts.answer: Oxygen is blown into the molten iron; it oxidises carbon to carbon monoxide/carbon dioxide gas which escapes; it also oxidises impurities such as silicon and phosphorus to acidic oxides; calcium oxide (a basic oxide) is added and reacts with these acidic oxides to form slag, which is removed.
parts.working: B1 oxygen blown into molten iron; B1 carbon removed as CO/CO₂; B1 impurities form acidic oxides; B1 CaO neutralises them to form slag.

practice.stem: Iron and aluminium are the two most widely used metals in Pakistan's construction industry.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the reduction of iron(III) oxide by carbon monoxide.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, using the reactivity series, why iron can be extracted by reduction with carbon but aluminium cannot.
parts.answer: Carbon is more reactive than iron, so it (or CO) can remove oxygen from iron oxide; aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot reduce aluminium oxide.
parts.working: B1 C above Fe; B1 Al above C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how aluminium is extracted instead, and give one reason why this costs more than extracting iron.
parts.answer: Electrolysis of aluminium oxide dissolved in molten cryolite; it uses a very large amount of electricity (high temperature, anodes replaced).
parts.working: B1 electrolysis (of molten Al₂O₃ in cryolite); B1 large electricity cost.

practice.stem: Aluminium is extracted by electrolysis of aluminium oxide dissolved in molten cryolite. [Ar: O = 16, Al = 27]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the ionic half-equation for the reaction at the anode.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum mass of aluminium that can be obtained from 51 tonnes of aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃.
parts.working: M1 Mr Al₂O₃ = 102, Al = 54 per formula; A1 51 × 54 ÷ 102 = 27 t

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the process is described as a redox reaction.
parts.answer: Aluminium ions gain electrons (reduction) at the cathode; oxide ions lose electrons (oxidation) at the anode.
parts.working: B1 reduction at cathode; B1 oxidation at anode.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why aluminium smelters are often built near hydroelectric power stations.
parts.answer: Electrolysis needs very large amounts of electricity; hydroelectric power is cheap (and renewable).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the oxidation number of iron in Fe₂O₃ and in Fe.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the oxidation number of carbon in CO and in CO₂.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to identify the oxidising agent and the reducing agent in the reaction Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. Explain.
parts.answer: Fe₂O₃ is the oxidising agent (iron's oxidation number decreases; it is reduced); CO is the reducing agent (carbon's oxidation number increases; it is oxidised).
parts.working: B1 Fe₂O₃ oxidising agent with reason; B1 CO reducing agent with reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The overall reaction in the cell is 2Al₂O₃ → 4Al + 3O₂. Calculate the number of moles of oxygen formed when 108 kg of aluminium is produced.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assume all the oxygen reacts with the carbon anode to form carbon dioxide: C + O₂ → CO₂. Calculate the mass of carbon used, in kg.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name one environmental problem caused by this anode reaction.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas / contributes to climate change.

practice.stem:
A student heated a mixture of each metal oxide with powdered carbon in a crucible for ten minutes.
Copper(II) oxide: pink-brown solid formed
Lead(II) oxide: silvery beads of metal formed
Magnesium oxide: no change
Aluminium oxide: no change
[Ar: O = 16, Pb = 207]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the results to place carbon in the reactivity series relative to copper, lead, magnesium and aluminium.
parts.answer: Order (most reactive first): magnesium/aluminium > carbon > lead > copper
parts.working: B1 carbon above lead and copper; B1 carbon below magnesium and aluminium.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of lead that could be obtained from 2.23 g of lead(II) oxide, PbO.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction of lead(II) oxide with carbon, forming carbon dioxide.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why aluminium oxide gave no reaction with carbon.
parts.answer: Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot reduce its oxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Aluminium is extracted by electrolysis: 2Al₂O₃ → 4Al + 3O₂. What is the maximum mass of aluminium that can be obtained from 51 tonnes of aluminium oxide? [Ar: O = 16, Al = 27]
A 13.5 tonnes
B 27 tonnes
C 51 tonnes
D 54 tonnes
parts.working: Mr Al₂O₃ = 102, so 102 t gives 54 t Al; 51 t gives 27 t. D forgets that 51 t is only half of 102 t; A halves twice.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A metal reacts vigorously with cold water, floats and moves about on the surface, and gives off hydrogen. Which metal could it be?
A copper
B iron
C sodium
D zinc
parts.working: Only Group I metals such as sodium react vigorously with cold water. Zinc and iron react only with steam (iron slowly); copper does not react.

practice.stem:
Observations:
Calcium: fizzes steadily in cold water.
Magnesium: very slow reaction with cold water; burns brightly when heated in steam.
Iron: no reaction with cold water; reacts slowly when heated strongly in steam.
Copper: no reaction with water or steam.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Put the four metals in order of reactivity, most reactive first.
parts.working: 2 marks all correct; 1 mark one pair swapped.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the gas formed when calcium reacts with water and describe a test for it.
parts.answer: Hydrogen; a lighted splint gives a squeaky pop.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the word equation for magnesium reacting with steam.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which metal does NOT react with dilute hydrochloric acid?
A magnesium
B zinc
C iron
D copper
parts.working: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it does not displace hydrogen from acids. Magnesium, zinc and iron are above hydrogen and give off hydrogen.

practice.stem: A student puts a strip of magnesium ribbon into blue aqueous copper(II) sulfate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two things the student would see.
parts.answer: Blue colour of the solution fades / becomes colourless; pink-brown (red-brown) solid forms on the magnesium; (magnesium gets smaller; solution warms).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a word equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: magnesium + copper(II) sulfate → magnesium sulfate + copper

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the reaction happens.
parts.answer: Magnesium is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from its compound.

practice.stem: The order of reactivity is: magnesium > zinc > copper > silver. Predict whether there is a reaction in each mixture.

parts.label: a
parts.text: zinc + copper(II) nitrate

parts.label: b
parts.text: copper + magnesium nitrate

parts.label: c
parts.text: magnesium + zinc nitrate

parts.label: d
parts.text: copper + silver nitrate

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which mixture would react?
A copper + magnesium sulfate solution
B zinc + copper(II) sulfate solution
C silver + iron(II) sulfate solution
D iron + zinc sulfate solution
parts.working: A metal displaces a less reactive metal from a solution of its salt. Zinc is above copper. In A, C and D the metal is less reactive than the metal in the salt.

practice.stem:
Each metal was added to solutions of the nitrates of the other metals. ✓ = reaction, ✗ = no reaction.
Metal W: with X nitrate ✓, with Y nitrate ✗, with Z nitrate ✓
Metal X: with W nitrate ✗, with Y nitrate ✗, with Z nitrate ✗
Metal Y: with W nitrate ✓, with X nitrate ✓, with Z nitrate ✓
Metal Z: with W nitrate ✗, with X nitrate ✓, with Y nitrate ✗

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the results to put metals W, X, Y and Z in order of reactivity, most reactive first.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Metal Y is magnesium and metal X is copper. Write the ionic equation for the reaction of magnesium with copper(II) ions.
parts.working: B1 species; B1 balanced with state symbols.

parts.label: c
parts.text: In the reaction in (b), state which species is oxidised. Explain in terms of electrons.
parts.answer: Magnesium is oxidised because it loses electrons (Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻).

practice.stem:
Equal masses of four metal powders were added separately to 50 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. The volume of hydrogen collected in a gas syringe in the first 60 seconds was recorded.
Magnesium: 48 cm³
Zinc: 21 cm³
Iron: 6 cm³
Copper: 0 cm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average rate of gas production, in cm³/s, for magnesium, zinc and iron.
parts.answer: Mg 0.80 cm³/s; Zn 0.35 cm³/s; Fe 0.10 cm³/s

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the order of reactivity shown by the results.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why copper gave no gas.
parts.answer: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it cannot displace hydrogen from the acid.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two variables that must be controlled.
parts.answer: Mass/surface area of metal; volume and concentration of acid; temperature.

practice.stem:
Excess powder of each metal was stirred into 25 cm³ of the same aqueous copper(II) sulfate in a polystyrene cup.
Temperature rise: magnesium 9.5 °C; zinc 5.8 °C; iron 3.6 °C; silver 0.0 °C

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the results to put magnesium, zinc, iron and silver in order of reactivity, most reactive first.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the temperature rise can be used to compare reactivity.
parts.answer: Displacement is exothermic; the more reactive the metal compared with copper, the more energy is released, so the greater the temperature rise.
parts.working: B1 reaction is exothermic; B1 bigger difference in reactivity → more energy released.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two variables that must be kept the same to make the test fair.
parts.answer: Volume and concentration of copper(II) sulfate; mass (moles) and particle size of metal powder; starting temperature; insulated cup.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why there was no temperature change with silver.
parts.answer: Silver is less reactive than copper, so no reaction occurs.

practice.stem: The thermite reaction is used to weld railway tracks: 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify which substance is oxidised and which is reduced. Explain.
parts.answer: Aluminium is oxidised (gains oxygen / loses electrons); iron(III) oxide is reduced (loses oxygen).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the reaction happens, using the reactivity series.
parts.answer: Aluminium is more reactive than iron, so it takes the oxygen from iron(III) oxide.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of iron formed from 8.0 g of iron(III) oxide. [Ar: O = 16, Fe = 56]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the order of reactivity of metals in terms of their ions.
parts.answer: More reactive metals lose electrons more easily to form positive ions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Aluminium is high in the reactivity series, yet aluminium cooking pots do not react with water. Explain why.
parts.answer: Aluminium is covered by a thin, unreactive layer of aluminium oxide which protects the metal underneath.
parts.working: B1 oxide layer; B1 prevents contact / unreactive.

parts.label: c
parts.text: An iron nail is placed in aqueous copper(II) sulfate. Describe two observations and write the ionic equation.
parts.answer: Pink-brown copper coats the nail; blue solution fades (turns pale green). Fe(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Fe²⁺(aq) + Cu(s)
parts.working: B1 copper deposit; B1 colour change; B1 equation.

practice.stem: A metal M forms M²⁺ ions. M displaces iron from aqueous iron(II) sulfate but does not react with aqueous zinc sulfate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the ionic equation for the reaction of M with iron(II) ions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Place M in the reactivity series relative to zinc, iron and copper.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict whether M would react when heated with copper(II) oxide. Explain.
parts.answer: Yes; M is more reactive than copper so it removes oxygen from copper(II) oxide.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Predict whether the oxide of M could be reduced by heating it with carbon. Explain.
parts.answer: Yes; M is below zinc (which can be extracted with carbon), so M is less reactive than carbon.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Copper wire is placed in aqueous silver nitrate. Which ionic equation is correct?
A Cu + Ag⁺ → Cu²⁺ + Ag
B Cu + 2Ag⁺ → Cu²⁺ + 2Ag
C Cu²⁺ + 2Ag → Cu + 2Ag⁺
D Cu + 2Ag⁺ → Cu⁺ + Ag₂
parts.working: Copper is more reactive than silver and loses 2 electrons; two Ag⁺ ions each gain one electron. A is unbalanced for charge (+1 vs +2); C is the reverse reaction, which does not happen.

practice.stem: A strip of lead is placed in aqueous silver nitrate. Shiny crystals of silver grow on the lead: Pb + 2AgNO₃ → Pb(NO₃)₂ + 2Ag

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the ionic equation for the reaction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the reducing agent.
parts.working: B1 it gives electrons to Ag⁺.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the maximum mass of silver that can form when 4.14 g of lead reacts completely. [Ar: Ag = 108, Pb = 207]

practice.stem:
Results for three metals, W, X and Y:
W reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid, giving hydrogen.
X does not react with dilute hydrochloric acid, and does not react with aqueous copper(II) sulfate.
Y does not react with dilute hydrochloric acid, but a brown coating forms on it in aqueous copper(II) sulfate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Place W, X, Y, hydrogen and copper in order of reactivity, most reactive first.
parts.working: B2 fully correct; B1 one error. W reacts with acid (above H). Y does not react with acid (below H) but displaces copper (above Cu). X does not displace copper (below Cu).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict whether X reacts with aqueous Y nitrate. Explain.
parts.answer: No; X is less reactive than Y.

parts.label: c
parts.text: W forms W²⁺ ions. Write an ionic equation for W reacting with hydrogen ions in dilute acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Overhead power cables are made of aluminium wrapped round a steel core. Which properties make aluminium suitable?
A high density and good electrical conductivity
B low density and good electrical conductivity
C low density and poor electrical conductivity
D high melting point and magnetic
parts.answer: B low density and good electrical conductivity
parts.working: Aluminium conducts electricity well and has a low density, so the cables are light. The steel core adds strength.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three physical properties of metals.
parts.answer: Good conductors of heat; good conductors of electricity; malleable; ductile; high melting/boiling points; shiny.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Metals react with oxygen to form oxides. State the type of oxide formed by most metals and how it reacts with acids.
parts.answer: Basic oxides; they react with acids to form a salt and water.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one physical property in which non-metals generally differ from metals.
parts.answer: Poor conductors / brittle when solid / low melting points.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement describes how most metals react?
A They form acidic oxides with oxygen.
B They form basic oxides with oxygen.
C They gain electrons to form negative ions.
D They react with water to form acids.
parts.answer: B They form basic oxides with oxygen.
parts.working: Metal oxides are generally basic (they neutralise acids). A describes non-metals; C – metals lose electrons to form positive ions.

practice.stem: Choose the best metal from this list for each use: aluminium, copper, gold, iron, sodium.

parts.label: a
parts.text: hot-water pipes in a house
parts.working: B1 (does not corrode, easily bent, unreactive with water).

parts.label: b
parts.text: thin cooking foil

parts.label: c
parts.text: cheap, strong beams for buildings (when protected from rust)

parts.label: d
parts.text: electrical contacts in a mobile phone that must never corrode

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a word equation for the reaction of zinc with dilute sulfuric acid.
parts.answer: zinc + sulfuric acid → zinc sulfate + hydrogen

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the test for the gas produced.
parts.answer: A lighted splint gives a squeaky pop.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the type of compound formed from the metal.

practice.stem:
Two samples of elements:
Sample A: shiny grey solid; conducts electricity; melting point 1455 °C; bends without breaking
Sample B: dull yellow solid; does not conduct; melting point 115 °C; crumbles when hit

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which sample is a metal? Give two pieces of evidence.
parts.answer: A; shiny, conducts electricity, high melting point, bends (malleable)
parts.working: B1 A; B1 + B1 any two pieces of evidence.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Sample B is an element. Suggest which element it could be.
parts.working: B1 yellow, brittle, low melting point non-metal.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Copper is used for electrical wiring in houses. Give two properties of copper that make it suitable.
parts.answer: Good electrical conductor; ductile (can be drawn into wires).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Aluminium is used to make aircraft bodies. Give two reasons.
parts.answer: Low density; strong (as an alloy); resists corrosion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Aluminium is also used for food containers and foil. Explain why it does not corrode easily.
parts.answer: It has a protective oxide layer.

practice.stem: Mobile phones contain many different metals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why gold is used to coat the electrical connectors in mobile phones, although copper is cheaper.
parts.answer: Gold is a good conductor and very unreactive, so it never corrodes or forms an oxide layer that would stop the current; copper slowly oxidises.
parts.working: B1 good conductor; B1 unreactive / does not corrode.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two properties that make aluminium suitable for drinks cans.
parts.answer: Low density (light); resists corrosion; malleable; non-toxic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Magnesium ribbon burns in air with a bright white flame. Write the equation for the reaction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Copper does not burn, but a copper foil heated in a Bunsen flame becomes coated with a black solid. Name the black solid and write its equation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Magnesium oxide dissolves slightly in water. Predict the pH of the solution and explain.
parts.answer: About pH 9–10 (above 7); metal oxides are basic / form alkaline hydroxide.

practice.stem: A small piece of calcium is dropped into cold water. It sinks, fizzes steadily and the water becomes cloudy and alkaline.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the gas formed and give the formula of the solution formed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a balanced equation for the reaction.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict how magnesium would compare with calcium if dropped into cold water, and give a reason.
parts.answer: Very slow reaction (few bubbles) – magnesium is less reactive than calcium.

practice.stem:
A metal block from a ladder has a mass of 54.0 g and a volume of 20.0 cm³.
Densities in g/cm³: aluminium 2.70; zinc 7.13; iron 7.87; copper 8.96; lead 11.3

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the density of the metal.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the table to identify the metal.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one property, other than density, that makes this metal suitable for ladders.
parts.answer: Resists corrosion / strong for its weight.

practice.stem:
Data for four metals:
Metal P: density 2.7 g/cm³, relative electrical conductivity 61, melting point 660 °C, resists corrosion, low cost
Metal Q: density 8.9 g/cm³, relative electrical conductivity 100, melting point 1085 °C, resists corrosion, medium cost
Metal R: density 7.9 g/cm³, relative electrical conductivity 17, melting point 1538 °C, rusts, very low cost
Metal S: density 4.5 g/cm³, relative electrical conductivity 4, melting point 1668 °C, resists corrosion, high cost

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of a 500 cm³ bracket made of each metal.
parts.working: 2 marks all four; 1 mark two or three (mass = density × volume).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which metal would be best for electrical cables carried on pylons? Explain using the data.
parts.answer: P; good conductivity and lowest density (and cheap) so cables are light.
parts.working: B1 P; B1 reason using data.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which metal would be best for a part of a jet engine that becomes very hot and must stay strong? Explain.
parts.answer: S; highest melting point, does not corrode and fairly low density.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why Q is used for house wiring even though it is more dense than P.
parts.answer: It is a better electrical conductor (thinner wires can be used).

practice.stem:
Data for four metals:
Aluminium: relative strength 1; cost low; resists corrosion; non-toxic; easily bent
Copper: relative strength 2; cost high; resists corrosion; non-toxic; easily bent
Lead: relative strength 0.2; cost medium; resists corrosion; toxic; very easily bent
Iron: relative strength 4; cost lowest; rusts; non-toxic; hard to bend

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which metal should be chosen for drinking-water pipes? Use the data to justify your choice and to reject the other metals.
parts.answer: Copper: resists corrosion, is easily bent and is non-toxic. Iron rusts; lead is toxic (dissolves slowly into drinking water); aluminium is too weak / less suitable for pipes.
parts.working: B1 copper; B1 non-toxic and resists corrosion / easily bent; B1 reason for rejecting lead (toxic) or iron (rusts).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which metal should be chosen for a cheap, strong garden gate? State how its main disadvantage can be overcome.
parts.answer: Iron (steel): it is the strongest and cheapest; it rusts, so it must be painted (or galvanised).
parts.working: B1 iron/steel with strength and cost; B1 paint/galvanise to stop rusting.

practice.stem: Zinc oxide, used in sunscreen creams, dissolves in dilute hydrochloric acid and also in aqueous sodium hydroxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the type of oxide that reacts with both acids and alkalis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a balanced equation for zinc oxide reacting with hydrochloric acid.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name one other metal oxide that behaves in the same way.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Most metal oxides are basic. State how a basic oxide differs from zinc oxide in its reaction with aqueous sodium hydroxide.
parts.answer: A basic oxide does not react with sodium hydroxide.

practice.stem: Household wiring uses copper cable whose core has a cross-sectional area of 2.5 mm².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of copper in 100 m of the core, in cm³. (1 m = 100 cm, 1 mm² = 0.01 cm²)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of copper in kg. (Density of copper = 8.96 g/cm³.)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain, in terms of structure, why copper can be drawn into long wires.
parts.answer: It is ductile: layers of ions slide over each other without breaking the metallic bonding.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define an alloy.
parts.answer: A mixture of a metal with other elements (metals or non-metals).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why an alloy is usually harder and stronger than the pure metal it is made from.
parts.answer: In the pure metal, atoms are the same size and arranged in layers that slide easily; in the alloy, atoms of different sizes disrupt the layers; so the layers cannot slide over each other easily.
parts.working: B1 pure metal layers slide; B1 different-sized atoms in alloy; B1 layers can no longer slide easily.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one use of brass and the property it depends on.
parts.answer: Musical instruments / door fittings / electrical plugs – hard and resists corrosion (or attractive).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which substance is an alloy?
A aluminium
B graphite
C iron
D stainless steel
parts.working: Stainless steel is a mixture of iron with chromium, nickel and carbon. Aluminium and iron are pure metals; graphite is a form of carbon.

practice.stem:
Four particle diagrams are described in words.
W: identical circles packed in regular rows.
X: regular rows of large circles, with a few smaller circles of a different kind in place of some large ones.
Y: separate pairs of joined circles spread far apart.
Z: two kinds of circle, labelled + and −, alternating in regular rows.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which diagram, W, X, Y or Z, represents an alloy?
parts.working: B1 metal atoms in layers with some atoms of a different size.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which diagram represents a pure metal?

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which diagram represents an ionic compound? Give a reason.
parts.answer: Z – it contains alternating positive and negative ions.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Use diagrams W and X to explain why an alloy is harder than the pure metal.
parts.answer: In W the identical atoms are in regular layers that slide easily; in X the different-sized atoms disrupt the layers so they cannot slide easily.
parts.working: B1 layers slide in pure metal; B1 different-sized atoms stop layers sliding.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two uses of stainless steel in a kitchen.
parts.answer: Cutlery; sinks; cooking pans; kitchen surfaces

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the property of stainless steel that makes it suitable for these uses.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why stainless steel is described as an alloy.
parts.answer: It is a mixture of a metal (iron) with other elements (chromium, nickel, carbon).
parts.working: B1 mixture of iron with other elements.

practice.stem: Pure tin melts at 232 °C. A lead-free solder made of tin with small amounts of silver and copper melts at about 217 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State why solder is described as an alloy.
parts.answer: It is a mixture of a metal (tin) with other elements (silver, copper).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a low melting point is useful for solder used to join parts of electronic circuits.
parts.answer: It melts easily with a soldering iron without damaging the components.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the melting-point information shows that solder is not pure tin.
parts.answer: A pure substance has a fixed melting point (tin 232 °C); solder melts at a different (lower) temperature, so it is a mixture.
parts.working: B1 pure substances have a fixed melting point; B1 different value → not pure / mixture.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which metals are mixed to make brass?
A copper and tin
B copper and zinc
C iron and carbon
D iron and chromium
parts.working: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc. Copper and tin make bronze (A).

practice.stem: A teacher models a metal with a tray of identical marbles packed in rows. She then replaces a few marbles with larger ones, scattered through the tray.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the description to explain why the tray of mixed marbles is harder to push into a new shape.
parts.answer: In the pure metal the layers of identical atoms slide easily. In the alloy the different-sized atoms disrupt the regular layers, so the layers cannot slide over each other easily; the alloy is harder and stronger.
parts.working: B1 pure metal layers slide; B1 different-sized atoms distort layers; B1 sliding is harder → harder/stronger.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one limitation of using marbles as a model of an alloy.
parts.answer: No delocalised electrons/charges shown; real particles are ions; only 2D; real atoms vibrate.

practice.stem: Gold jewellery is usually made from gold alloyed with copper and silver.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 18-carat gold contains 75 % gold by mass. Calculate the mass of gold in a 12.0 g ring.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 22-carat gold, popular in Pakistan, is 22/24 gold by mass. Calculate the mass of pure gold in one tola (11.66 g) of 22-carat gold. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why pure (24-carat) gold is rarely used for rings.
parts.answer: Pure gold is soft and wears / bends easily; the alloy is harder.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin. Suggest why bronze, not pure copper, is used to make statues that stand outdoors.
parts.answer: Bronze is harder/stronger and more resistant to wear and corrosion than pure copper.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A bronze statue of mass 450 kg contains 88 % copper and 12 % tin. Calculate the mass of tin in it.

practice.stem:
A metallurgy student measured the relative hardness of copper–zinc alloys.
% zinc: 0, 10, 20, 30, 40
Relative hardness: 40, 55, 68, 80, 92

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship between the percentage of zinc and the hardness.
parts.answer: Hardness increases as the percentage of zinc increases.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the data to estimate the hardness of brass containing 25 % zinc.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why adding zinc makes copper harder.
parts.answer: Zinc atoms are a different size from copper atoms; they disrupt the layers of copper ions so the layers cannot slide easily.
parts.working: B1 different-sized atoms; B1 layers less able to slide.

practice.stem: The city of Sialkot exports surgical instruments made of stainless steel.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the main metal in stainless steel and two other elements added to it.
parts.answer: Iron; chromium and nickel (and a little carbon).
parts.working: B1 iron; B1 two of chromium, nickel, carbon.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of chromium and the mass of nickel in a 250 g instrument made of 18/8 stainless steel (18 % chromium and 8 % nickel by mass).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why stainless steel, rather than mild steel, is chosen for surgical instruments.
parts.answer: Stainless steel resists corrosion (does not rust) and is hard/strong; instruments must stay clean and can be sterilised repeatedly.
parts.working: B1 resists corrosion; B1 link to use (hygiene/sterilising).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give one use of mild steel.

practice.stem: An aluminium alloy used in aircraft contains 4.4 % copper and 1.5 % magnesium by mass; the rest is aluminium.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of each element in a 2.50 kg aircraft part made from this alloy.
parts.answer: copper 110 g; magnesium 37.5 g; aluminium 2352.5 g (2.35 kg)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why aircraft are made from this alloy rather than from pure aluminium or from steel.
parts.answer: The alloy is much stronger than pure aluminium but keeps a low density (lighter than steel, which is very dense).
parts.working: B1 stronger than pure Al; B1 lower density than steel.

practice.stem: A 5.00 g sample of brass shavings is added to excess dilute hydrochloric acid. The zinc reacts (Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂) but the copper does not. 0.600 dm³ of hydrogen is collected at room temperature and pressure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why only the zinc reacts.
parts.answer: Zinc is above hydrogen in the reactivity series; copper is below it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of zinc in the sample. [Ar: Zn = 65; 1 mol of gas occupies 24 dm³]

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by mass of zinc in the brass.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe how the student could obtain the copper from the mixture at the end.
parts.answer: Filter, then wash with water and dry the residue.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Stainless steel contains chromium. Suggest how chromium helps the steel resist corrosion.
parts.answer: Chromium reacts with oxygen to form a thin, tough, unreactive oxide layer on the surface that stops air and water reaching the iron (and re-forms if scratched).
parts.working: B1 chromium oxide layer; B1 barrier that protects iron.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Copper used for wiring is very pure. Suggest why an alloy of copper would be a poorer electrical conductor.
parts.answer: Atoms of other elements disrupt the regular lattice, which makes it harder for delocalised electrons to flow (higher resistance).
parts.working: B1 irregular lattice; B1 electron flow hindered.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a student could compare the hardness of sheets of copper and brass of the same thickness, using a steel ball and a 1 kg mass dropped from a fixed height.
parts.answer: Place the steel ball on each metal sheet, drop the 1 kg mass from the same height on to it, then measure the diameter (or depth) of the dent. The smaller dent shows the harder metal.
parts.working: B1 same height/mass for each; B1 measure dent diameter/depth; B1 smaller dent = harder.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two variables that must be kept constant.
parts.answer: Thickness of sheets; size of ball; mass; height; surface the sheet rests on.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the reliability of the results could be improved.
parts.answer: Repeat several times on different parts of each sheet and take an average.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which substances must both be present for iron to rust?
A oxygen and water
B carbon dioxide and water
C nitrogen and oxygen
D oxygen and salt
parts.working: Rusting needs both oxygen and water. Salt speeds rusting up but is not needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which method protects an underground steel gas pipeline by sacrificial protection?
A painting the pipe
B coating the pipe with grease
C attaching blocks of magnesium to the pipe
D wrapping the pipe in plastic
parts.answer: C attaching blocks of magnesium to the pipe
parts.working: Magnesium is more reactive than iron, so it corrodes (is oxidised) instead of the steel. A, B and D are barrier methods only.

practice.stem: Many people in Karachi ride bicycles. Steel bicycle parts rust quickly near the sea.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the substance that forms when iron rusts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why bicycles rust faster in Karachi than in an inland city.
parts.answer: Salty, damp sea air / salt speeds up rusting.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest a suitable way to stop rusting of (i) the bicycle chain and (ii) the bicycle frame. Give a reason for each choice.
parts.answer: (i) oil or grease – it keeps out water and air but still lets the chain move; (ii) paint – it is a lasting barrier and looks good.
parts.working: B1 method + B1 reason for each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a word equation for the rusting of iron.
parts.answer: iron + oxygen + water → hydrated iron(III) oxide

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how a shiny iron nail looks after rusting.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why rusting is described as an oxidation reaction.
parts.answer: Iron gains oxygen (iron atoms lose electrons).

practice.stem: Steel wire for garden fences is often sold with a coating of green plastic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the plastic coating stops the steel wire from rusting.
parts.answer: It is a barrier that keeps oxygen (air) and water away from the steel.
parts.working: B1 barrier; B1 oxygen and water kept out.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one advantage of a plastic coating over paint for wire that is bent into a fence.
parts.answer: The plastic is flexible, so it does not crack or flake off when the wire bends (lasts longer, no repainting).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Steel bicycle handlebars are often electroplated with chromium. Give one reason, other than preventing rusting, for using chromium.

practice.stem:
Four identical iron nails were set up for one week:
Tube A: nail in tap water, open to air. Mass increase 0.12 g.
Tube B: nail in boiled water with a layer of oil on top. Mass increase 0.00 g.
Tube C: nail in air with anhydrous calcium chloride, stoppered. Mass increase 0.00 g.
Tube D: nail in salt water, open to air. Mass increase 0.21 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In which tubes did the nails rust?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the nail in tube B did not rust.
parts.answer: Boiling removes dissolved oxygen (air); the oil layer stops oxygen dissolving back in.
parts.working: B1 boiling removes oxygen; B1 oil stops air.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the nail in tube C did not rust.
parts.answer: Anhydrous calcium chloride absorbs water vapour, so the air is dry.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the mass increase was in tube D than in tube A. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Suggest why car bodies rust faster in coastal cities such as Karachi.
parts.answer: Salt (sodium chloride) from sea spray speeds up rusting.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how painting a steel gate prevents rusting.
parts.answer: It forms a barrier that keeps water and oxygen away from the iron.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the metal used to galvanise steel roof sheets.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A galvanised roof sheet is scratched, exposing the steel. Explain why the steel still does not rust.
parts.answer: Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it corrodes/is oxidised instead of the iron (sacrificial protection).
parts.working: B1 zinc more reactive; B1 zinc oxidised in preference to iron.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why a scratched painted gate does rust.
parts.answer: The paint is only a barrier; once broken, water and oxygen reach the iron.

practice.stem: Damp iron wool was pushed to the top of a measuring tube containing 50.0 cm³ of air. The tube was stood upside-down in water. After a week, the volume of gas had fallen to 39.6 cm³ and stopped changing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of oxygen in the air from these results.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the water rises up the tube.
parts.answer: The iron uses up the oxygen as it rusts, so the gas pressure inside falls and water is pushed up into the tube.
parts.working: B1 oxygen used up in rusting; B1 lower pressure / volume of gas decreases.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the iron wool is damp.
parts.answer: Water is needed for rusting / it speeds up the reaction.

practice.stem: Two steel cans are scratched: one is coated with zinc and the other with tin. Both are left outside for a month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the scratched zinc-coated can does not rust.
parts.answer: Zinc is more reactive than iron, so zinc corrodes (is oxidised) instead; this is sacrificial protection.
parts.working: B1 zinc more reactive; B1 zinc corrodes instead of iron.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the scratched tin-coated can rusts quickly at the scratch.
parts.answer: Tin is less reactive than iron, so it cannot protect iron sacrificially; once the barrier is broken, the iron corrodes (even faster than unplated iron).
parts.working: B1 tin less reactive than iron; B1 only a barrier, so exposed iron rusts.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why tin, not zinc, is used to coat the inside of food cans.
parts.answer: Tin is less reactive / does not react with food acids (zinc compounds could get into food).

practice.stem:
An underground steel water tank can be protected from rusting in two ways.
Method 1: coat the tank with bitumen, a thick waterproof tar.
Method 2: connect the tank by wires to buried blocks of magnesium.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how each method prevents the tank from rusting.
parts.answer: Method 1: the bitumen is a barrier that keeps water and oxygen away from the steel. Method 2: magnesium is more reactive than iron, so it is oxidised (corrodes) instead of the iron – sacrificial protection.
parts.working: B1 barrier excludes water/oxygen; B1 magnesium more reactive, corrodes instead of iron.

parts.label: b
parts.text: During installation, stones scrape off some of the bitumen. Explain which method still protects the scraped areas.
parts.answer: Method 2: the magnesium still corrodes in preference to the exposed iron; a broken barrier no longer protects.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Aluminium is also more reactive than iron, but blocks of aluminium protect steel much less well than magnesium. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Aluminium is covered by a thin, unreactive layer of aluminium oxide, which stops it reacting / corroding.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Aluminium is more reactive than iron, yet aluminium window frames do not corrode. Explain why.
parts.answer: Aluminium is covered by a thin, tough layer of aluminium oxide that sticks to the surface and stops air and water reaching the metal underneath.
parts.working: B1 oxide layer; B1 unreactive / impermeable / protects metal underneath.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why rust does not protect iron in the same way.
parts.answer: Rust is porous and flakes off, so fresh iron is constantly exposed to air and water.
parts.working: B1 flakes off / porous; B1 iron underneath exposed.

practice.stem: Blocks of zinc are bolted to the steel hulls of ships in Karachi port, below the waterline.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the type of protection given by the blocks.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the half-equation for the reaction of the zinc blocks and explain why it protects the steel.
parts.answer: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻; zinc loses electrons more easily than iron, so it is oxidised instead of the iron.

parts.label: c
parts.text: An engineer suggests using copper blocks instead. Explain why this would not work.
parts.answer: Copper is less reactive than iron, so the iron would be oxidised instead (rusting faster).
parts.working: B1 copper less reactive; B1 iron corrodes.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the chemical name of rust.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Explain why the zinc blocks must be replaced from time to time.
parts.answer: They are used up as the zinc corrodes.

practice.stem: A sample of rust has the formula Fe₂O₃·xH₂O. When 3.56 g of the rust is heated until all the water is removed, 3.20 g of Fe₂O₃ remains.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of water lost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of Fe₂O₃ and of H₂O. [Mr: Fe₂O₃ = 160, H₂O = 18]

parts.label: c
parts.text: Deduce the value of x.

practice.stem: Four identical iron nails are placed in salt water for a week: one alone, one wrapped with a strip of copper, one wrapped with zinc and one wrapped with magnesium.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the order in which the nails rust, starting with the most rusty. Explain your prediction.
parts.answer: Nail with copper > nail alone > nail with zinc ≈ nail with magnesium (little or no rust). Copper is less reactive, so iron corrodes faster; zinc and magnesium are more reactive and corrode instead (sacrificial protection).
parts.working: B1 copper nail most rusted; B1 Mg and Zn nails least/not rusted; B1 explanation in terms of reactivity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why salt water is used rather than tap water.
parts.answer: It speeds up rusting so the results appear sooner.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one control needed to make the comparison fair.
parts.answer: Identical nails / same volume of the same salt water / same time / same temperature / a nail with no metal attached.

practice.stem: Treat rusting as the reaction 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃ (ignoring water). An iron nail of mass 5.60 g is left to rust.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of Fe₂O₃ that would form if the 5.60 g nail rusted completely. [Ar: O = 16, Fe = 56]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen, at room temperature and pressure, used in (a). (1 mol of gas occupies 24 dm³.)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the mass of real rust formed would be greater than your answer to (a).
parts.answer: Rust is hydrated; it also contains water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the colour and physical state at room temperature of: (i) chlorine, (ii) bromine, (iii) iodine.
parts.answer: (i) pale yellow-green gas; (ii) red-brown liquid; (iii) grey-black solid

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the trend in density down Group VII.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the electronic configuration of a chlorine atom.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the charge on the ion formed by chlorine, and explain why it has this charge.
parts.answer: 1−; the atom gains one electron to get a full outer shell.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the formulae of the compounds formed when chlorine reacts with (i) magnesium and (ii) hydrogen.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which halogen is a liquid at room temperature and pressure?
A fluorine
B chlorine
C bromine
D iodine
parts.working: Bromine is a red-brown liquid. Fluorine and chlorine are gases, and iodine is a solid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the colour of the solution produced when chlorine is bubbled into aqueous potassium bromide.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the ionic equation for the reaction.
parts.working: 1 mark: correct ions and products. 1 mark: balanced.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one safety precaution when working with chlorine water, and explain why it is needed.
parts.answer: Work in a fume cupboard (or with good ventilation). Chlorine is toxic and irritates the lungs and eyes.
parts.working: 1 mark: precaution (fume cupboard, eye protection). 1 mark: chlorine is toxic or irritant.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which mixture of aqueous solutions reacts to produce a halogen?
A bromine and potassium chloride
B iodine and potassium bromide
C chlorine and potassium bromide
D iodine and potassium chloride
parts.working: A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one from its halide: chlorine displaces bromine. In A bromine is less reactive than chlorine, so no reaction.

practice.stem: Chlorine water is added to aqueous potassium iodide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the colour change seen.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the ionic equation for the reaction.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify the species that is oxidised. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Iodide ions; they lose electrons (oxidation number goes from −1 to 0).

practice.stem:
Three solutions A, B and C each contain one sodium halide. A student adds dilute nitric acid and then aqueous silver nitrate to each, and in separate tests adds chlorine water.
solution A: white precipitate; no change with chlorine water
solution B: yellow precipitate; solution turns brown with chlorine water
solution C: cream precipitate; solution turns orange with chlorine water

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the halide ion in each solution.
parts.answer: A: chloride (Cl⁻); B: iodide (I⁻); C: bromide (Br⁻)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why chlorine water causes no visible change with solution A.
parts.answer: Chlorine cannot displace chloride (no reaction) — the halogen and halide are the same.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why dilute nitric acid is added before the aqueous silver nitrate.
parts.answer: To remove (react with) carbonate ions, which would also give a precipitate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the reactivity of the halogens with hydrogen changes down Group VII.
parts.answer: Reactivity decreases down the group. Fluorine reacts explosively in the dark, chlorine reacts with hydrogen in light or heat, and iodine reacts only slowly and needs heating.
parts.working: 1 mark: decreases down the group. 1 mark: correct examples (fluorine explosive, iodine slow).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the product formed when chlorine reacts with hydrogen.

practice.stem: Results of mixing halogen solutions with halide solutions (in test tubes): chlorine water + potassium bromide: orange; chlorine water + potassium iodide: brown; bromine water + potassium iodide: brown; bromine water + sodium chloride: no change; iodine solution + potassium bromide: no change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Place chlorine, bromine and iodine in order of reactivity, most reactive first.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why bromine water and sodium chloride solution show no change.
parts.answer: Bromine is less reactive than chlorine, so it cannot displace chloride ions from solution.
parts.working: 1 mark: bromine less reactive than chlorine. 1 mark: so it cannot displace chloride ions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict the result when chlorine water is added to sodium fluoride solution. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: No change. Fluorine is more reactive than chlorine, so chlorine cannot displace fluoride ions.
parts.working: 1 mark: no change. 1 mark: chlorine less reactive than fluorine, so no displacement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why small amounts of chlorine are added to drinking water.
parts.answer: Chlorine kills harmful bacteria and other microorganisms, so the water is safe to drink. Only a small amount is used so that it is not harmful to people.
parts.working: 1 mark: kills bacteria/microorganisms. 1 mark: makes water safe to drink. 1 mark: small amount used so it is not harmful to people.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Astatine is below iodine in Group VII. Predict its physical state and colour at room temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict whether bromine would react with aqueous sodium astatide. Give a reason.
parts.answer: Yes; bromine is more reactive than astatine, so it displaces astatine.
parts.working: B1 yes; B1 bromine more reactive.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain, in terms of electrons, why the halogens become less reactive down the group.
parts.answer: Atoms get larger with more shells; the outer shell is further from the nucleus (more shielding), so the attraction for an incoming electron is weaker and an electron is gained less easily.
parts.working: B1 more shells / larger atoms; B1 weaker attraction of nucleus for outer electrons; B1 less easily gains an electron.

practice.stem:
Melting points of the halogens:
fluorine −220 °C, chlorine −101 °C, bromine −7 °C, iodine 114 °C, astatine ?

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the trend in the melting points of the halogens.
parts.answer: Melting point increases down the group.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the melting point of astatine.
parts.working: The melting point rises by roughly 100–120 °C per element, so about 220–240 °C is expected; accept 200–320 °C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the trend in melting points in terms of forces.
parts.answer: Molecules get larger down the group, so the intermolecular forces get stronger and more energy is needed to overcome them.
parts.working: B1 larger molecules; B1 stronger intermolecular forces.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the balanced equation for the reaction of iron with chlorine to form iron(III) chloride.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the moles of iron in 5.60 g of iron (Ar: Fe = 56).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of chlorine needed to react with 5.60 g of iron (Ar: Cl = 35.5). Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the mass of iron(III) chloride formed (Mr: FeCl₃ = 162.5).

practice.stem: Explain why bromine is less reactive than chlorine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State how the number of electron shells in a bromine atom differs from a chlorine atom.
parts.answer: Bromine has 4 shells; chlorine has 3 shells.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the atomic size compares, and its effect on the attraction for an extra electron.
parts.answer: Bromine atoms are larger. The outer shell is further from the nucleus, so the nucleus attracts an incoming electron less strongly.
parts.working: 1 mark: bromine atom larger. 1 mark: weaker attraction for an extra electron.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the effect on the ease of gaining an electron.
parts.answer: Bromine is less likely to gain an electron, so it is less reactive than chlorine.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which property is typical of transition elements?
A low melting point
B low density
C they form coloured compounds
D they react vigorously with cold water
parts.working: Transition elements form coloured compounds, have high densities and high melting points. D describes Group I metals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three properties of transition elements that are not shown by Group I metals.
parts.answer: Any three of: high density; high melting point; form coloured compounds; act as catalysts (elements or compounds); have variable oxidation numbers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the transition element used as the catalyst in the Haber process.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which ion gives a blue aqueous solution?
A Ca²⁺
B Cu²⁺
C Mg²⁺
D Na⁺
parts.working: Hydrated copper(II) ions are blue. Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺ and Na⁺ are colourless in aqueous solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name a transition element used for each purpose: (i) electrical cables; (ii) the catalyst in the Haber process; (iii) stainless steel.
parts.answer: (i) copper; (ii) iron; (iii) chromium (nickel is also acceptable).
parts.working: 1 mark each for copper, iron and chromium (or nickel) in the correct order.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two ways in which the physical properties of iron differ from those of sodium.
parts.answer: Iron has a higher melting point; iron has a higher density.
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept: iron is harder / stronger.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Iron forms two chlorides, FeCl₂ and FeCl₃. Name each chloride, using Roman numerals.
parts.answer: FeCl₂ iron(II) chloride; FeCl₃ iron(III) chloride

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which property of transition elements is shown by the existence of these two chlorides?
parts.answer: They have variable oxidation numbers (more than one oxidation state).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the formula of iron(III) sulfate?
A FeSO₄
B Fe₃SO₄
C Fe₂(SO₄)₃
D Fe(SO₄)₃
parts.working: Fe³⁺ and SO₄²⁻: 2 × (+3) = +6 balances 3 × (−2) = −6. A is iron(II) sulfate.

practice.stem:
Aqueous sodium hydroxide is added drop by drop and then in excess to three solutions taken from a water pipe workshop in Sialkot.
solution J: light blue precipitate, insoluble in excess
solution K: green precipitate, insoluble in excess
solution L: red-brown precipitate, insoluble in excess

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the cation present in solution J, solution K and solution L.
parts.answer: J: Cu²⁺; K: Fe²⁺; L: Fe³⁺

parts.label: b
parts.text: The precipitate from solution K slowly turns brown at the surface when left in air. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Iron(II) is oxidised (by oxygen in the air) to iron(III).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the ionic equation, with state symbols, for the formation of the precipitate in solution J.
parts.working: B1 correct species and balancing; B1 state symbols.

practice.stem: A student adds 0.50 g of manganese(IV) oxide to aqueous hydrogen peroxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the balanced equation for the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen, in cm³ at room temperature and pressure, produced when 0.020 mol of hydrogen peroxide decomposes completely. [1 mol of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the student could show that the manganese(IV) oxide is a catalyst at the end of the experiment.
parts.answer: Filter off, wash and dry the solid and weigh it; its mass is the same as at the start.
parts.working: B1 filter, wash, dry; B1 mass unchanged.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the oxidation number of manganese in MnO₂.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the oxidation number of manganese in MnO₄⁻.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the oxidation number of iron in FeCl₃.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give the oxidation number of chromium in Cr₂O₇²⁻.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the formula of: (i) iron(III) oxide; (ii) copper(II) carbonate; (iii) chromium(III) sulfate; (iv) zinc hydroxide.
parts.working: 1 mark each: Fe₂O₃ (Fe³⁺ with O²⁻); CuCO₃ (Cu²⁺ with CO₃²⁻); Cr₂(SO₄)₃ (Cr³⁺ with SO₄²⁻); Zn(OH)₂ (Zn²⁺ with OH⁻).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why transition metals have higher melting points than Group I metals, in terms of metallic bonding.
parts.answer: Transition metals have more delocalised electrons per atom (outer s and d electrons). The metal ions are smaller and more closely packed. The electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons is stronger, so more energy is needed to melt them.
parts.working: 1 mark: more delocalised electrons per atom. 1 mark: smaller, more closely packed ions. 1 mark: stronger attraction between ions and delocalised electrons.

practice.stem: Chromium is a transition element used to make stainless steel.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the oxidation number of chromium in chromium(III) oxide, Cr₂O₃, and in potassium dichromate, K₂Cr₂O₇.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Chromium(III) oxide is green and potassium dichromate is orange. State one other general property of transition elements shown by these compounds.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the formula of chromium(III) chloride.

practice.stem:
Data for four metals:
sodium: melting point 98 °C, density 0.97 g/cm³
potassium: melting point 63 °C, density 0.86 g/cm³
iron: melting point 1538 °C, density 7.87 g/cm³
copper: melting point 1085 °C, density 8.96 g/cm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the data to identify the two transition elements. Give two reasons.
parts.answer: Iron and copper; they have much higher melting points and much higher densities than sodium and potassium.
parts.working: B1 Fe and Cu; B1 high melting points; B1 high densities.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why iron (as steel) rather than sodium is used for building bridges.
parts.answer: Iron is strong / hard and does not react with water like sodium does.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Copper(II) sulfate is blue but sodium sulfate is white. Which property of transition elements does this show?

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement explains why transition elements can act as catalysts?
A they are all gases at room temperature
B they have variable oxidation states, so they can gain and lose electrons during a reaction
C they have low melting points
D they are all less dense than water
parts.answer: B they have variable oxidation states, so they can gain and lose electrons during a reaction
parts.working: Transition elements can change oxidation state during a reaction, which lets them pass electrons on and speed up the reaction. A, C and D are false for most transition metals (most are solids with high melting points and high densities).

practice.stem: Chromium burns in excess oxygen to form chromium(III) oxide, Cr₂O₃: 4Cr + 3O₂ → 2Cr₂O₃

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the oxidation number of chromium in Cr₂O₃.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the moles of chromium in 1.52 g of chromium (Ar: Cr = 52).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of chromium(III) oxide formed when 1.52 g of chromium is burned completely in oxygen (Mr: Cr₂O₃ = 152). Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why transition elements can show more than one oxidation state.
parts.answer: They can lose different numbers of electrons from their outer s and d shells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two observations when a small piece of sodium is added to water.
parts.answer: Any two of: floats; melts into a ball; moves around on the surface; fizzes; gets smaller and disappears.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the balanced equation for the reaction.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Universal indicator is added to the solution at the end. Suggest the pH.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A metal is put into a Bunsen flame and gives a lilac flame. Which metal is it?
A lithium
B sodium
C potassium
D calcium
parts.working: Potassium gives a lilac flame. Lithium gives red, sodium gives yellow and calcium gives a brick-red flame.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is seen when a small piece of potassium is added to water.
parts.answer: The potassium moves about rapidly on the surface and may burst into a lilac flame. Hydrogen is given off. The solution becomes alkaline (for example, universal indicator turns purple or blue).
parts.working: 1 mark: moves rapidly on the surface. 1 mark: lilac flame or burning/fizzing. 1 mark: solution becomes alkaline.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the gas produced when sodium reacts with water, and describe the test for it.
parts.answer: Hydrogen. A lighted splint held at the mouth of the tube gives a squeaky pop.
parts.working: 1 mark: hydrogen. 1 mark: squeaky pop with a lighted splint.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which property increases going down Group I from lithium to potassium?
A melting point
B reactivity with water
C number of outer-shell electrons
D hardness
parts.working: Reactivity increases down Group I. Melting point and hardness decrease, and the number of outer electrons stays at one.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Rubidium is below potassium in Group I. Predict how rubidium reacts with water compared with potassium.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the formula of rubidium oxide and the formula of rubidium hydroxide.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why rubidium is stored under oil.
parts.answer: To stop it reacting with oxygen and water vapour in the air.

parts.label: a
parts.text: All Group I metals form ions with a 1+ charge. Explain why.
parts.answer: They have one electron in the outer shell, which is lost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, in terms of atomic structure, why potassium is more reactive than sodium.
parts.answer: Potassium atoms have more shells, so the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded; it is less strongly attracted and is lost more easily.
parts.working: B1 more shells / larger atom; B1 weaker attraction for outer electron; B1 electron lost more easily.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why Group I metals are stored under oil.
parts.answer: They react with oxygen in the air. They react with water vapour in the air. The oil keeps both air and water away from the metal.
parts.working: 1 mark: react with oxygen. 1 mark: react with water (moisture). 1 mark: oil excludes air and water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a balanced equation for the reaction of potassium with water.
parts.working: 1 mark: products KOH and H₂. 1 mark: balanced.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the colour that universal indicator or phenolphthalein would show in the solution formed.
parts.answer: Phenolphthalein turns pink (the solution is alkaline).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the trend in melting point down Group I from lithium to potassium.
parts.answer: The melting point decreases down the group.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain this trend in terms of metallic bonding.
parts.answer: The atoms become larger, so the attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons is weaker. Less energy is needed to melt the metal.
parts.working: 1 mark: weaker metallic bonding in larger atoms. 1 mark: less energy needed to melt.

practice.stem: A potassium atom has the electronic configuration 2,8,8,1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the ion formed by a potassium atom, with its charge.
parts.answer: K⁺ (a potassium ion with a 1+ charge)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the ion is formed.
parts.answer: The potassium atom loses its one outer electron to achieve a full outer shell.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the formula of potassium chloride.

practice.stem:
0.46 g of sodium reacts completely with water.
2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of sodium used. [Ar: Na = 23]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of hydrogen produced at room temperature and pressure, in cm³. [1 mol of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]
parts.working: M1 0.010 mol H₂ (2Na → H₂); A1 240 cm³.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The solution is made up to 250 cm³ with distilled water. Calculate the concentration of sodium hydroxide in mol/dm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Caesium burns in chlorine. Which row correctly describes the product?
A CsCl₂, covalent, insoluble in water
B CsCl, ionic, white solid that dissolves to form a neutral solution
C CsCl, covalent, coloured liquid
D Cs₂Cl, ionic, dissolves to form an alkaline solution
parts.answer: B CsCl, ionic, white solid that dissolves to form a neutral solution
parts.working: Cs⁺ and Cl⁻ give CsCl, an ionic white solid like NaCl; its solution is neutral. D wrongly predicts an alkaline solution, which forms only when the metal reacts with water.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Equal moles (1 mol) of lithium, sodium and potassium are each reacted with an excess of water. Which statement is correct?
A lithium produces the most hydrogen
B sodium produces the most hydrogen
C potassium produces the most hydrogen
D all three produce the same amount of hydrogen
parts.answer: D all three produce the same amount of hydrogen
parts.working: 2M + 2H₂O → 2MOH + H₂, so 1 mol of any Group I metal gives 0.5 mol of hydrogen. The amount of hydrogen depends on the moles of metal, not on how vigorous the reaction is.

practice.stem: 0.14 g of lithium reacts completely with excess water: 2Li + 2H₂O → 2LiOH + H₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the moles of lithium in 0.14 g (Ar: Li = 7).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the moles of hydrogen formed.
parts.working: 1 mark: the ratio Li : H₂ is 2 : 1, so 0.0200 ÷ 2 = 0.0100 mol.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the volume of hydrogen formed at room temperature and pressure (1 mol occupies 24 dm³). Give your answer in cm³.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the mass of lithium hydroxide formed (Mr: LiOH = 24).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What do elements in the same group of the Periodic Table have in common?
A the same number of electron shells
B the same number of outer-shell electrons
C the same nucleon number
D the same number of neutrons
parts.answer: B the same number of outer-shell electrons
parts.working: Elements in a group have the same number of outer electrons, which is why they have similar chemical properties. A describes elements in the same period.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An element has the electronic configuration 2,8,6. State its group and period.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the element.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether it is a metal or a non-metal and give the formula of the ion it forms.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Chlorine is in Period 3 of the Periodic Table. Which statement explains this?
A it has three electrons
B it has three occupied electron shells
C it has three protons in its nucleus
D it has three outer electrons
parts.answer: B it has three occupied electron shells
parts.working: The period number equals the number of occupied electron shells. Chlorine (2,8,7) has three shells. Chlorine has 17 protons and 7 outer electrons, so A, C and D are wrong.

practice.stem: Magnesium has the electronic configuration 2,8,2. Chlorine has the electronic configuration 2,8,7.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the group that each element is in.
parts.answer: Magnesium: Group II; chlorine: Group VII.
parts.working: 1 mark: Mg is in Group II (2 outer electrons). 1 mark: Cl is in Group VII (7 outer electrons).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why magnesium and chlorine form ions with different charges.
parts.answer: Magnesium loses its two outer electrons to form Mg²⁺. Chlorine gains one electron to form Cl⁻, which gives it a full outer shell.
parts.working: 1 mark: Mg loses 2 electrons to form Mg²⁺. 1 mark: Cl gains 1 electron to form Cl⁻ (full outer shell).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the formula of the compound formed between magnesium and chlorine.
parts.working: 1 mark: Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ combine in the ratio 1 : 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why elements in the same group have similar chemical properties.
parts.answer: They have the same number of outer electrons.
parts.working: 1 mark: same number of outer electrons. 1 mark: chemical reactions involve the outer electrons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the change in metallic character across Period 3 from sodium to argon.
parts.answer: Changes from metals to non-metals (metallic character decreases).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the nature (acidic or basic) of the oxides of elements on the left and on the right of Period 3. Give one example of each.
parts.answer: Left: basic, e.g. Na₂O or MgO; right: acidic, e.g. SO₂ or P₄O₁₀.
parts.working: B1 basic; B1 correct example; B1 acidic; B1 correct example.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An element forms an ion with a 3+ charge. Its atom has three occupied electron shells. Which element is it?
A boron
B aluminium
C gallium
D phosphorus
parts.working: Aluminium (2,8,3) is in Group III and Period 3 and loses 3 electrons. Boron is in Group III but has only two shells.

practice.stem:
Electronic configurations of four elements:
D 2,2
E 2,8,7
F 2,8,8,1
G 2,8

parts.label: a
parts.text: Place each element in the Periodic Table by stating its group and period.
parts.answer: D: Group II, Period 2; E: Group VII, Period 3; F: Group I, Period 4; G: Group 0 (VIII), Period 2

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which two elements would react together most vigorously? Give a reason.
parts.answer: F and E; F is a very reactive metal (low in Group I) and E is a reactive non-metal (Group VII), so F gives its electron to E readily.
parts.working: B1 F and E; B1 reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Going across Period 2 from lithium to neon, which statement is correct?
A the atomic radius increases
B the number of outer electrons increases from 1 to 8
C the number of electron shells increases
D the metallic character increases
parts.answer: B the number of outer electrons increases from 1 to 8
parts.working: Lithium (2,1) has 1 outer electron and neon (2,8) has 8. Across a period the number of shells stays the same, the atomic radius decreases, and the metallic character decreases.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the trend in atomic radius across Period 3 from sodium to chlorine.
parts.answer: The atomic radius decreases across the period.
parts.working: 1 mark: decreases. 1 mark: the number of shells stays the same (3) while the nuclear charge increases.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the trend in terms of the nuclear charge and attraction for the outer electrons.
parts.answer: The number of protons increases, so the nucleus has a greater positive charge. The outer electrons are pulled in more strongly, so the atoms get smaller.
parts.working: 1 mark: nuclear charge increases. 1 mark: stronger attraction pulls the outer electrons closer.

practice.stem: Period 2 contains lithium, beryllium, boron, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine and neon.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the element in Period 2 and Group IV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the number of outer electrons in nitrogen.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the group number of oxygen.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why neon is placed in Group 0.
parts.answer: It has a full outer shell of 8 electrons, like the other noble gases.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An element has atomic number 35. State its group, its period and whether it is a metal or a non-metal.
parts.answer: Group VII; Period 4; non-metal (it is bromine).
parts.working: 1 mark: Group VII (7 outer electrons). 1 mark: Period 4 (four shells). 1 mark: non-metal.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Element X is in Group II and Period 4. Give its electronic configuration and name it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the formula of the compound formed between X and chlorine, and between X and oxygen.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict the type of bonding in the chloride of X. Give a reason.
parts.answer: Ionic; X is a metal that loses two electrons and chlorine is a non-metal that gains an electron.
parts.working: B1 ionic; B1 metal + non-metal / electron transfer.

practice.stem: Element W has atomic number 16.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the electronic configuration of element W (atomic number 16).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State its group and period.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the formula of the compound W forms with hydrogen.
parts.working: 1 mark: W is sulfur, so H₂S.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give the symbol and charge of the ion it forms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why argon (Ar, relative atomic mass 39.95) is placed before potassium (K, relative atomic mass 39.10) in the Periodic Table.
parts.answer: Elements are arranged by atomic number. Argon has atomic number 18 and potassium has 19, so argon comes first. This keeps elements with similar properties in the same groups: argon is a noble gas and potassium is a Group I metal.
parts.working: 1 mark: arrangement by atomic number (Ar 18, K 19). 1 mark: relative atomic mass would put K first, which would break the grouping. 1 mark: keeps elements with similar properties in groups.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the noble gases are unreactive.
parts.answer: They have a full outer shell of electrons (stable configuration).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one use of argon and one use of helium, and give the property that makes each suitable.
parts.answer: Argon: filling light bulbs / lamps, because it is unreactive (inert); helium: filling balloons / airships, because it has a low density and is unreactive.
parts.working: B1 argon use; B1 property; B1 helium use; B1 property.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why neon exists as single atoms, whereas chlorine exists as Cl₂ molecules.
parts.answer: Neon has a full outer shell, so it does not need to gain, lose or share electrons. Chlorine atoms share a pair of electrons to fill their outer shells, forming a molecule.
parts.working: 1 mark: neon has a full outer shell. 1 mark: chlorine atoms share electrons to form covalent bonds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State why neon is suitable for use in advertising signs.
parts.answer: It is unreactive and non-flammable, so it is safe.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what happens when electricity passes through neon gas.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one use of argon in welding and explain why it is used.
parts.answer: It shields the hot metal from air, so the metal does not oxidise. Argon is unreactive, so it does not react with the hot metal.
parts.working: 1 mark: shields hot metal from oxygen. 1 mark: argon is unreactive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Argon has the electronic configuration 2,8,8. State its group and period.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why helium is used to fill balloons rather than hydrogen.
parts.answer: Helium is non-flammable, so it is safer. Helium is less dense than air, so the balloon rises.
parts.working: 1 mark: helium is non-flammable. 1 mark: less dense than air so the balloon floats.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Argon makes up about 0.9 % of air. A student says argon exists as Ar₂ molecules. Explain why this is wrong.
parts.answer: Argon has a full outer shell (2,8,8), so it does not form bonds; it exists as single atoms (monatomic).
parts.working: B1 full outer shell / stable; B1 monatomic, no bonds.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the electronic configuration of argon.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the group in which the noble gases are found.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of outer electrons in a helium atom.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why helium is placed in Group 0 even though it has only two outer electrons.
parts.answer: Its outer shell is full, as it is the first shell, so it behaves like the other noble gases.
parts.working: 1 mark: outer shell full (first shell holds 2). 1 mark: unreactive, like the other noble gases.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why argon is used to fill light bulbs with tungsten filaments.
parts.answer: Argon is unreactive, so it does not react with the hot filament. It does not burn, so the filament is not oxidised. This stops the filament from burning out at high temperature.
parts.working: 1 mark: argon is unreactive. 1 mark: it does not burn or oxidise the filament. 1 mark: the filament lasts longer at high temperature.

practice.stem: The density of helium at room temperature and pressure is 0.18 g/dm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of helium in a balloon of volume 2.0 dm³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of helium in the 2.0 dm³ balloon (1 mol occupies 24 dm³ at room temperature and pressure). Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

practice.stem: Krypton is a noble gas.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the electronic configuration of krypton (atomic number 36).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the period and group of krypton.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the noble gas with the lowest boiling point.

practice.stem:
Boiling points of the noble gases:
helium −269 °C, neon −246 °C, argon −186 °C, krypton −153 °C, xenon −108 °C, radon ?

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the trend in boiling points down the group.
parts.answer: Boiling point increases down the group.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the boiling point of radon and its state at room temperature.
parts.working: B1 value in range; B1 gas.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why boiling point increases down the group.
parts.answer: Atoms are larger (more electrons), so the forces between atoms are stronger and need more energy to overcome.
parts.working: B1 larger atoms; B1 stronger forces between atoms.

practice.stem: Xenon is a noble gas in Period 5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of electrons in an atom of xenon (atomic number 54).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the electronic configuration of xenon.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the number of outer electrons and explain why xenon is in Group 0.
parts.answer: 8 outer electrons. Its outer shell is full, like the other noble gases.
parts.working: 1 mark: 8 outer electrons. 1 mark: full outer shell.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why heavier noble gases are slightly more reactive than lighter ones.
parts.answer: The outer electrons of heavier atoms are further from the nucleus and are held less strongly, so they are slightly easier to share or lose.

practice.stem: Compare the electronic structures of helium and sodium.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the electron structure of helium and of sodium.
parts.answer: Helium has a full outer shell of 2 electrons. Sodium has 1 outer electron.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why helium is unreactive and sodium is reactive.
parts.answer: Helium does not lose, gain or share electrons because its outer shell is full. Sodium loses its one outer electron easily to form Na⁺.
parts.working: 1 mark: helium has no need to react. 1 mark: sodium loses its outer electron to form an ion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of argon in 1.00 dm³ of argon at room temperature and pressure (1 mol occupies 24 dm³).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of 1.00 dm³ of argon (Ar = 40). Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why is chlorine added to the domestic water supply?
A to remove tastes and odours
B to remove insoluble solids
