C to kill microbes
D to make the water neutral
parts.working: Chlorination kills harmful microbes (bacteria). Carbon removes tastes and odours; sedimentation and filtration remove solids.

practice.stem: River water is treated before it is supplied to homes in Rawalpindi.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the stages used to remove insoluble solids from the water.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the substance used to remove tastes and odours.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the purpose of chlorination.

practice.stem: A student pours muddy water from a pond through a homemade filter: a plastic bottle containing layers of gravel, sand and powdered charcoal.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the appearance of the water changes after passing through the filter.
parts.answer: It changes from cloudy/muddy to clear (colourless).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the purpose of the layer of charcoal in the filter.
parts.answer: To remove tastes and odours (and some coloured substances).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the filtered water is still not safe to drink.
parts.answer: It may still contain microbes (and dissolved harmful substances).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest a simple way to make the filtered water safe to drink at home.
parts.answer: Boil it (or add a chlorine tablet).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A few drops of a colourless liquid are added to anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride paper. The paper changes colour, showing water is present. What is the colour change?
A blue to pink
B pink to blue
C white to blue
D blue to white
parts.working: Anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride is blue and turns pink with water. White to blue is the change for anhydrous copper(II) sulfate.

practice.stem: Water from the Indus is treated before it is piped to homes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Put these stages in the order used at the treatment works: chlorination, filtration, sedimentation, treatment with carbon.
parts.working: B2 all correct; B1 sedimentation before filtration and chlorination last.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Match each stage to its purpose: (i) sedimentation, (ii) filtration, (iii) carbon, (iv) chlorination.
parts.answer: (i) heavy insoluble particles settle out; (ii) removes smaller insoluble particles; (iii) removes tastes and odours; (iv) kills microbes.

practice.stem:
A student measures the melting and boiling points of three water samples at normal pressure.
Sample A: melts −1.5 °C, boils 100.6 °C
Sample B: melts 0.0 °C, boils 100.0 °C
Sample C: melts −0.4 °C, boils 100.2 °C

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which sample(s) could be pure water? Explain.
parts.answer: Sample B only; it melts at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the presence of a dissolved salt affects the melting point and the boiling point of water, using the data.
parts.answer: Melting point is lowered (below 0 °C); boiling point is raised (above 100 °C).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the piece of apparatus used to measure these temperatures.

practice.stem: Water from natural sources contains many substances.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name one substance in river water that is beneficial to aquatic life.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why each of the following is harmful in water: (i) metal compounds, (ii) sewage, (iii) plastics.
parts.answer: (i) some metal compounds are toxic; (ii) contains harmful microbes that cause disease; (iii) harm aquatic life, e.g. animals swallow or get trapped in them.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how nitrates and phosphates from fertilisers can harm life in a lake.
parts.answer: They lead to deoxygenation of the water (excess algae grow, die and are decomposed by bacteria that use up oxygen), so fish and other aquatic life die.
parts.working: B1 deoxygenation/oxygen used up; B1 aquatic life dies.

practice.stem: A student tests a sample of water from a hand pump.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a chemical test that shows the sample contains water.
parts.answer: Add anhydrous copper(II) sulfate; it turns from white to blue.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 250 cm³ of the sample is evaporated to dryness in a weighed evaporating basin. The mass of solid left is 0.085 g. Calculate the mass of dissolved solids in 1.00 dm³ of the water.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the evaporating basin must be weighed after it has cooled.
parts.answer: A hot basin causes air currents that give an inaccurate reading (and may damage the balance).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which test shows that a colourless liquid is pure water?
A It turns anhydrous copper(II) sulfate blue.
B It turns anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride pink.
C It boils at exactly 100 °C at normal atmospheric pressure.
D It has a pH of 7.
parts.answer: C It boils at exactly 100 °C at normal atmospheric pressure.
parts.working: A pure substance has a fixed boiling point; pure water boils at 100 °C. A and B show only that water is present, not that it is pure; many solutions also have pH 7.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A liquid turns anhydrous copper(II) sulfate blue. It boils at 101.5 °C at normal atmospheric pressure. What can be concluded?
A It contains water but is not pure water.
B It is pure water.
C It contains no water.
D It is a pure substance, but is not water.
parts.answer: A It contains water but is not pure water.
parts.working: The colour change shows water is present; pure water boils at exactly 100 °C at normal pressure, so dissolved impurities have raised the boiling point. B is wrong because the boiling point is not 100 °C; C and D contradict the copper(II) sulfate result.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why distilled water, not tap water, is used to make up solutions for tests in the laboratory.
parts.answer: Tap water contains dissolved ions/substances (e.g. chloride from chlorination) that could react and give false results.
parts.working: B1 impurities/ions; B1 interfere with tests.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe a test to show tap water contains chloride ions, giving the result.
parts.answer: Add dilute nitric acid then aqueous silver nitrate; white precipitate.
parts.working: B1 acidified silver nitrate; B1 white precipitate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how distilled water is obtained from tap water.
parts.answer: Boil the water and condense the steam (distillation).

practice.stem:
Dissolved oxygen is measured along a river near a town's sewage outlet.
P (upstream of outlet): 9.0 mg/dm³
Q (just after outlet): 3.6 mg/dm³
R (2 km downstream): 5.4 mg/dm³
S (5 km downstream): 7.8 mg/dm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the dissolved oxygen changes along the river.
parts.answer: Falls sharply just after the outlet (from 9.0 to 3.6 mg/dm³), then rises gradually further downstream.
parts.working: B1 falls after outlet; B1 recovers downstream.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in dissolved oxygen between point P and point Q.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why untreated sewage lowers the dissolved oxygen.
parts.answer: Bacteria/microbes decompose the sewage using up dissolved oxygen.
parts.working: B1 bacteria decompose; B1 use oxygen.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give one other reason why untreated sewage in water is harmful to humans.
parts.answer: It contains harmful microbes that cause disease.

practice.stem: A water treatment works adds 0.5 mg of chlorine to every 1 dm³ of water. It supplies 4.0 × 10⁶ dm³ of water per day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of chlorine, in kg, needed each day.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why water that has passed through sand filters still needs chlorination before drinking.
parts.answer: Filtration removes insoluble solids but not microbes (bacteria are small enough to pass through / are not all removed).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why too much chlorine should not be added.
parts.answer: Chlorine is toxic / gives an unpleasant taste.

practice.stem: A plant on the coast near Gwadar makes drinking water by distilling seawater. Each day it takes in 12 000 m³ of seawater containing 35 g of dissolved salt per dm³ and produces 5000 m³ of fresh water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of dissolved salt, in tonnes, entering the plant each day.

parts.label: b
parts.text: All of this salt leaves in the waste brine. Calculate the concentration of salt in the brine in g/dm³. [1 m³ = 1000 dm³]

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why making drinking water this way is expensive.
parts.answer: Large amounts of energy are needed to boil the water.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one test to show the product water contains no dissolved salt.
parts.answer: Evaporate a sample to dryness: no solid residue (or boiling point exactly 100 °C).

practice.stem: A 2.5 dm³ sample of tap water from an old building contains 0.035 mg of lead compounds (measured as lead). The safe limit is 0.010 mg/dm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of lead in the sample in mg/dm³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: How many times greater is this than the limit?

parts.label: c
parts.text: Some metal compounds in water are beneficial and others are harmful. Explain this statement.
parts.answer: Some provide essential minerals for life (e.g. calcium/magnesium ions); others such as lead compounds are toxic.
parts.working: B1 essential minerals; B1 toxic metals.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest a source of the lead in the tap water.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the main source of sulfur dioxide in the air?
A the decomposition of vegetation
B the combustion of fossil fuels that contain sulfur compounds
C the reaction of nitrogen and oxygen in car engines
D photosynthesis
parts.answer: B the combustion of fossil fuels that contain sulfur compounds
parts.working: Fuels such as coal and some oils contain sulfur compounds, which burn to form SO₂. C is the source of oxides of nitrogen, not sulfur dioxide.

practice.stem: Traffic in large cities such as Karachi releases several air pollutants.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Carbon monoxide: give its source and one adverse effect.
parts.answer: Incomplete combustion of carbon-containing fuels; toxic (reduces the blood's ability to carry oxygen).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Particulates: give one source and one adverse effect.
parts.answer: Incomplete combustion of carbon-containing fuels (e.g. diesel engines, burning crop waste); increased risk of respiratory problems and cancer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Oxides of nitrogen: give one adverse effect.
parts.answer: Acid rain / photochemical smog / respiratory problems.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which pollutant gas is formed when nitrogen and oxygen from the air react at the high temperature inside a car engine?
A nitrogen monoxide
B carbon monoxide
C sulfur dioxide
D methane
parts.working: N₂ + O₂ → 2NO at high temperature in the engine. Carbon monoxide comes from incomplete combustion of the fuel, sulfur dioxide from sulfur impurities in fuel; methane is not formed in the engine.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which pollutant is correctly matched with one of its adverse effects?
A methane – climate change
B sulfur dioxide – combines with haemoglobin in the blood
C particulates – depletion of oxygen in rivers
D carbon dioxide – photochemical smog
parts.working: Methane is a greenhouse gas. B describes carbon monoxide; sulfur dioxide causes acid rain. Particulates cause respiratory problems and cancer; photochemical smog comes from oxides of nitrogen.

practice.stem: Catalytic converters are fitted to car exhausts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how nitrogen monoxide, NO, is formed in a car engine.
parts.answer: Nitrogen and oxygen from the air react at the high temperature inside the engine.
parts.working: B1 N₂ + O₂ from air; B1 high temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Complete and balance the equation for the reaction in the catalytic converter: __CO + __NO → __CO₂ + N₂

parts.label: c
parts.text: In this reaction, state which substance is reduced. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Nitrogen monoxide; it loses oxygen (to form N₂).
parts.working: B1 NO; B1 loses oxygen / oxidation number of N decreases from +2 to 0.

practice.stem: A coal-fired power station releases sulfur dioxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how sulfur dioxide from the power station leads to acid rain.
parts.answer: Sulfur dioxide dissolves in rainwater / reacts with water and oxygen to form sulfuric acid.
parts.working: B1 dissolves in water; B1 acid (sulfurous/sulfuric) forms.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two effects of acid rain.
parts.answer: Damages buildings and statues made of limestone/marble; corrodes metal structures; harms trees; makes lakes acidic and kills fish.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Flue gas desulfurisation uses calcium oxide. Write the equation for the reaction of calcium oxide with sulfur dioxide to form calcium sulfite.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give one other way to reduce sulfur dioxide emissions.
parts.answer: Use low-sulfur fuels / remove sulfur from fuels before burning.

practice.stem:
Students in a village near brick kilns collect rainwater at different distances from the kilns and measure its pH.
Site: A, B, C, D, E
Distance from kilns / km: 0.5, 1.5, 3.0, 5.0, 8.0
pH of rainwater: 4.2, 4.6, 4.0, 5.3, 5.6

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the pH of the rainwater changes with distance from the brick kilns.
parts.answer: The pH increases (rain is less acidic) as the distance increases.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest which pollutant gas from the kilns lowers the pH of the rain.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify the result that does not fit the pattern.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one way the students could make their results more reliable.
parts.answer: Collect several samples at each site / on different days and take an average; use a pH meter rather than indicator.

practice.stem: Each winter Lahore suffers from smog. Sources include vehicle exhausts, factories and the burning of rice straw on farms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two pollutants released by vehicles, factories and burning straw that cause breathing (respiratory) problems during smog.
parts.answer: Any two of: particulates; oxides of nitrogen; sulfur dioxide.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: particulates; oxides of nitrogen (NO/NO₂); sulfur dioxide. Do not accept carbon dioxide.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Burning rice straw in a limited supply of air produces carbon monoxide. Explain why carbon monoxide forms.
parts.answer: Incomplete combustion: there is not enough oxygen to convert all the carbon into carbon dioxide.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two actions that could reduce smog in the city.
parts.answer: Ban crop-residue burning / use the straw for animal feed or compost; fit catalytic converters; use public transport; control factory emissions; switch to cleaner fuels.

practice.stem: Most new cars sold in Pakistan are fitted with catalytic converters.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name one metal used as a catalyst in a catalytic converter.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the catalyst is coated thinly onto a ceramic honeycomb.
parts.answer: Gives a very large surface area, so the gases contact more catalyst and react faster; uses less expensive metal.
parts.working: B1 large surface area; B1 faster reaction / less metal needed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the converter removes few pollutants in the first few minutes of a journey.
parts.answer: The catalyst is cold; it only works well once it reaches a high temperature.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name two gases, formed in the converter, that leave the exhaust pipe.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide and nitrogen (also water vapour)

practice.stem: Monitoring stations in Islamabad measure oxides of nitrogen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the concentration of oxides of nitrogen is highest close to busy roads.
parts.answer: Car engines are very hot, so nitrogen and oxygen from the air react to form oxides of nitrogen, which are released in the exhaust.
parts.working: B1 high temperature in engine; B1 N₂ and O₂ (from air) react.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two adverse effects of oxides of nitrogen.
parts.answer: Any two: acid rain; photochemical smog; respiratory problems.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Acid rain contains nitric acid. Write the balanced equation for the reaction of nitric acid with the calcium carbonate in a marble statue.

practice.stem: Catalytic converters also oxidise unburned hydrocarbons such as octane. 1 mol of gas occupies 24 dm³ at room temperature and pressure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Balance the equation for the complete combustion of octane in the converter: __C₈H₁₈ + __O₂ → __CO₂ + __H₂O

parts.label: b
parts.text: A car without a converter releases 2.4 dm³ of carbon monoxide per km at room temperature and pressure. Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide formed when this carbon monoxide is fully oxidised. Mr CO₂ = 44.
parts.working: M1 mol CO = 2.4 ÷ 24 = 0.10; M1 2CO + O₂ → 2CO₂ so mol CO₂ = 0.10; A1 × 44 = 4.4 g.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Catalytic converters do not reduce the release of carbon dioxide. Explain why.
parts.answer: They convert CO and unburned hydrocarbons into carbon dioxide (and water), so CO₂ output is not reduced (may increase).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statements about catalytic converters are correct?
1 Carbon monoxide is oxidised to carbon dioxide.
2 Oxides of nitrogen are reduced to nitrogen.
3 They reduce the amount of carbon dioxide released.
4 They contain transition-metal catalysts such as platinum and rhodium.
A 1 and 2 only
B 1, 2 and 4
C 2 and 3 only
D 1, 3 and 4
parts.working: 1, 2 and 4 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: converters turn CO and hydrocarbons into CO₂, so they do not reduce carbon dioxide output.

practice.stem: A coal sample contains 2.0% sulfur by mass. Ar: S = 32, O = 16, Ca = 40.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of sulfur in 1000 tonnes of the coal.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of sulfur dioxide formed when this sulfur burns. S + O₂ → SO₂
parts.working: M1 Mr SO₂ = 64, S : SO₂ = 32 : 64; A1 40 tonnes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the minimum mass of calcium oxide needed to remove all of this sulfur dioxide. CaO + SO₂ → CaSO₃
parts.working: M1 mol ratio 1 : 1, so mass CaO = 40 × 56/64; A1 35 tonnes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Nitrogen dioxide forms nitric acid in the atmosphere. Balance the equation: __NO₂ + O₂ + __H₂O → __HNO₃

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum mass of nitric acid, in kg, formed from 92 kg of nitrogen dioxide. [Mr: NO₂ = 46, HNO₃ = 63]
parts.working: M1 92 ÷ 46 = 2.0 kmol NO₂ → 2.0 kmol HNO₃; A1 × 63 = 126 kg.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why nitrogen dioxide is an acidic oxide.
parts.answer: It is an oxide of a non-metal that reacts with water (and alkalis) to form an acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction between carbon monoxide and nitrogen monoxide in the converter.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A sample of exhaust gas contains 15 cm³ of CO and 10 cm³ of NO. They react completely according to your equation. Calculate the volume of each gas (CO, NO, CO₂, N₂) at the end. All volumes are at the same temperature and pressure.
parts.answer: CO 5 cm³; NO 0 cm³; CO₂ 10 cm³; N₂ 5 cm³
parts.working: M1 NO is limiting (1 : 1 ratio), 10 cm³ CO used, 5 cm³ CO left; M1 CO₂ = 10 cm³; A1 N₂ = 5 cm³.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify the oxidising agent in this reaction and explain.
parts.answer: Nitrogen monoxide; it gives oxygen to CO (CO is oxidised) and is itself reduced to N₂.
parts.working: B1 NO; B1 reason (loses oxygen / oxidation number of N falls from +2 to 0).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which two gases are greenhouse gases that contribute to climate change?
A carbon dioxide and methane
B nitrogen and oxygen
C argon and carbon dioxide
D oxygen and methane
parts.working: Carbon dioxide and methane absorb and re-emit thermal (infrared) energy. Nitrogen, oxygen and argon are not greenhouse gases.

practice.stem: Green plants make glucose by photosynthesis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the word equation for photosynthesis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the balanced symbol equation for photosynthesis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two conditions needed for photosynthesis.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere?
A photosynthesis
B respiration
C combustion of fossil fuels
D decomposition of dead plants
parts.working: Green plants take in CO₂ during photosynthesis. Respiration, combustion and decomposition all release CO₂.

practice.stem: Forests in the north of Pakistan are being cleared for timber and farmland.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two reasons why cutting down and burning large areas of forest increases the carbon dioxide in the air.
parts.answer: Fewer trees to remove CO₂ by photosynthesis; burning (or decay of) the wood releases CO₂.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one natural process that adds carbon dioxide to the atmosphere.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way to increase the removal of carbon dioxide from the air.

practice.stem: A student places pondweed in a beaker of water under a lamp. Bubbles of gas rise from the weed and are collected in an upturned test-tube.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a test to identify the gas collected.
parts.answer: Insert a glowing splint; it relights (gas is oxygen).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe and explain what happens to the rate of bubbling when the lamp is moved further away.
parts.answer: Fewer bubbles per minute; less light so less photosynthesis.
parts.working: B1 fewer bubbles; B1 light needed for photosynthesis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the green substance in the pondweed that absorbs light.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Write the word equation for photosynthesis.

practice.stem: The increase in greenhouse gases in the atmosphere is linked to climate change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how greenhouse gases cause the Earth's surface to warm.
parts.answer: Thermal energy (infrared radiation) is emitted by the Earth's surface; greenhouse gases absorb this energy; they re-emit it in all directions, including back towards the Earth, so less thermal energy escapes to space.
parts.working: B1 Earth emits thermal/infrared energy; B1 absorbed by greenhouse gases; B1 re-emitted back / reduced heat loss to space.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two possible effects of climate change on a country such as Pakistan.
parts.answer: Melting glaciers and more floods; more extreme heatwaves; droughts and water shortages; lower crop yields; rising sea levels affecting coastal areas.

practice.stem: Countries are trying to reduce emissions of carbon dioxide and methane.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two sources of methane in the atmosphere.
parts.answer: Digestion in animals such as cattle (waste gases); decomposition of vegetation / waste in landfill.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two ways of reducing carbon dioxide emissions.
parts.answer: Use renewable energy such as solar, wind or hydroelectric; plant trees (reforestation); use less fossil fuel / more public transport; use hydrogen or electric vehicles.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one way of reducing methane emissions.
parts.answer: Reduce livestock farming / eat less meat; reduce landfill (recycle, collect landfill gas).

practice.stem:
The concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, measured at a remote observatory:
Year: 1960, 1990, 2020
CO₂ / parts per million: 317, 354, 414

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in carbon dioxide concentration from 1960 to 2020. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average increase per year between 1990 and 2020.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two human activities responsible for this increase.
parts.answer: Burning fossil fuels (power stations, vehicles); deforestation (fewer trees for photosynthesis, and burning wood).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Put these statements in the correct order to explain the greenhouse effect:
P Greenhouse gases absorb thermal (infrared) energy and re-emit it in all directions, some back towards Earth.
Q The Earth's surface absorbs the energy and warms up.
R Energy from the Sun reaches the Earth, mostly as visible light.
S The warm surface emits thermal (infrared) energy.
parts.working: B2 all correct; B1 one pair swapped.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why an increase in greenhouse gases leads to a higher average temperature.
parts.answer: More thermal energy is absorbed and re-emitted back to Earth, so less escapes into space.
parts.working: B1 more absorbed/re-emitted; B1 less escapes.

practice.stem: Some cities are trying hydrogen-powered buses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the balanced equation for the combustion of hydrogen.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why using hydrogen instead of petrol in buses reduces climate change.
parts.answer: Hydrogen produces only water when it burns; no carbon dioxide (greenhouse gas) is released.
parts.working: B1 water only; B1 no CO₂.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one reason why hydrogen may not reduce carbon dioxide emissions overall.
parts.answer: Most hydrogen is made from fossil fuels (e.g. methane) or using electricity from fossil fuels, which releases CO₂.

practice.stem:
Average carbon dioxide concentration and global temperature difference from a long-term average (approximate values):
Year: 1980, 1990, 2000, 2010, 2020
CO₂ / ppm: 339, 354, 370, 390, 414
Temperature difference / °C: 0.26, 0.45, 0.39, 0.72, 1.01

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average increase in carbon dioxide concentration per decade from 1980 to 2020.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the relationship between the two sets of data.
parts.answer: As CO₂ concentration increases, the temperature difference generally increases (positive correlation).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify the decade in which the temperature did not follow the trend.
parts.answer: 1990 to 2000 (the temperature value fell from 0.45 to 0.39 °C).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why this data alone does not prove that carbon dioxide causes warming.
parts.answer: Correlation does not prove cause; other factors (e.g. methane, solar activity) also change.

practice.stem: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. Mr: CO₂ = 44, C₆H₁₂O₆ = 180. 1 mol of gas occupies 24 dm³ at room temperature and pressure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name one process in the carbon cycle that adds carbon dioxide to the atmosphere and one process that removes it.
parts.answer: Adds: respiration or combustion (or decomposition); removes: photosynthesis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of glucose made when 132 g of carbon dioxide is used in photosynthesis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen released, in dm³ at room temperature and pressure.

practice.stem: Biogas plants in rural Punjab collect methane from animal dung. Mr: CH₄ = 16, CO₂ = 44.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the balanced equation for the complete combustion of methane.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide, in kg, formed when 1.0 kg of methane burns completely. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Methane is a stronger greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide. Suggest why burning methane collected from a landfill site is better for the climate than letting it escape.
parts.answer: It converts methane into carbon dioxide, which has a smaller greenhouse effect per molecule (and the energy can replace another fuel).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the balanced equation for the complete combustion of octane, C₈H₁₈.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A car releases 120 g of CO₂ per km. Assuming the petrol is pure octane, calculate the mass of octane burned per km, to 3 significant figures. [Mr: CO₂ = 44, C₈H₁₈ = 114]

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of CO₂, in tonnes, the car releases in a year of 15 000 km.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A tree removes 22 kg of carbon dioxide from the air in one year. Using 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂, calculate the mass of glucose, in kg, it could make. [Mr: CO₂ = 44, C₆H₁₂O₆ = 180]

parts.label: b
parts.text: A car releases 1800 kg of carbon dioxide in a year. How many such trees would be needed to absorb this? Give a whole number.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why planting trees alone cannot solve climate change.
parts.answer: Trees take years to grow / land is limited / carbon is released again when trees die or burn.

practice.stem: Farmers in Punjab use NPK fertilisers on wheat fields.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the three elements that NPK fertilisers provide.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why farmers add these elements to soil.
parts.answer: For improved plant growth / higher crop yield.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name a compound that provides potassium, and one that provides both nitrogen and phosphorus.
parts.answer: Potassium chloride (or potassium sulfate); ammonium phosphate.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A farmer's soil test shows that it is short of phosphorus. Which compound should be added?
A ammonium phosphate
B potassium chloride
C ammonium nitrate
D calcium carbonate
parts.working: Ammonium phosphate supplies phosphorus (and nitrogen). Potassium chloride gives only potassium; ammonium nitrate gives only nitrogen; calcium carbonate only raises soil pH.

practice.stem: A bag of fertiliser sold in Faisalabad is labelled 'NPK 20-10-10'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: On this label the numbers are the percentages by mass of N, P and K. Calculate the mass of nitrogen in a 50 kg bag.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of phosphorus in the bag.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why farmers add fertilisers to fields where crops are harvested every year.
parts.answer: Each harvest removes the elements (N, P, K) taken up by the plants; fertilisers replace them so the next crop grows well / higher yield.
parts.working: B1 elements removed; B1 replaced for better growth.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two types of compound that provide nitrogen in fertilisers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the formula of ammonium sulfate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the formula of potassium nitrate and state which two essential elements it supplies.

practice.stem: A student tests a sample of a white fertiliser dissolved in distilled water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a test to show the fertiliser contains ammonium ions, and give the result.
parts.answer: Warm with aqueous sodium hydroxide; gas (ammonia) turns damp red litmus blue.
parts.working: B1 NaOH warm; B1 litmus blue.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe a test to show it contains sulfate ions, and give the result.
parts.answer: Add dilute nitric acid then aqueous barium nitrate (or chloride); white precipitate.
parts.working: B1 acidified Ba²⁺; B1 white precipitate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the fertiliser.

practice.stem: Three nitrogen fertilisers are sold: ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃ (Mr 80); urea, CO(NH₂)₂ (Mr 60); ammonium sulfate, (NH₄)₂SO₄ (Mr 132). Ar: N = 14.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in each fertiliser. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which fertiliser provides the most nitrogen per kilogram?

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why nitrogen fertilisers are needed even though air is 78% nitrogen.
parts.answer: Plants cannot use nitrogen gas directly; they need nitrogen in soluble compounds (nitrates/ammonium).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why fertilisers must be soluble in water.
parts.answer: Plants absorb the ions in solution through their roots.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one reason why farmers buy compound NPK fertilisers rather than three separate ones.
parts.answer: Supplies all three elements in one application (saves time/labour).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the relative formula mass of ammonium phosphate, (NH₄)₃PO₄. [Ar: N = 14, H = 1, P = 31, O = 16]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in ammonium phosphate, to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by mass of potassium in potassium nitrate, KNO₃, to 3 significant figures. [Ar: K = 39]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃, needed to supply 35 kg of nitrogen to a field. [Mr: NH₄NO₃ = 80]
parts.working: M1 80 kg contains 28 kg N; A1 35 × 80 ÷ 28 = 100 kg.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the farmer should not add much more than this.
parts.answer: Excess is washed into rivers (eutrophication) / waste of money.

practice.stem: Rice fields near a lake in Sindh are heavily fertilised.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how excess nitrate fertiliser from fields can lead to the death of fish in a lake.
parts.answer: Nitrates are soluble and wash into the lake; algae grow rapidly; algae die and are decomposed by bacteria; bacteria use up dissolved oxygen; fish die from lack of oxygen.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of these steps in order.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways farmers can reduce this problem.
parts.answer: Apply only the amount needed; avoid applying before heavy rain; keep strips of land unfertilised next to rivers.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which mixture of two compounds provides all three of the elements nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium?
A ammonium nitrate and ammonium sulfate
B ammonium phosphate and potassium chloride
C potassium nitrate and potassium chloride
D calcium phosphate and ammonium nitrate
parts.answer: B ammonium phosphate and potassium chloride
parts.working: Ammonium phosphate supplies N and P; potassium chloride supplies K. C has no phosphorus; D has no potassium; A supplies only nitrogen (and sulfur).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the neutralisation of aqueous ammonia by sulfuric acid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of 1.00 mol/dm³ sulfuric acid needed to neutralise 25.0 cm³ of 2.00 mol/dm³ ammonia.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the maximum mass of ammonium sulfate formed. [Mr: (NH₄)₂SO₄ = 132]

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe how pure dry crystals are obtained from the neutral solution.
parts.answer: Heat to evaporate some water until saturated (crystallisation point); cool and filter off crystals; wash and dry between filter papers.
parts.working: B1 evaporate/cool to crystallise; B1 filter and dry.

practice.stem: A fertiliser plant reacts ammonia with nitric acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum mass of ammonium nitrate, in tonnes, from 3.4 tonnes of ammonia. [Mr: NH₃ = 17, NH₄NO₃ = 80]

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of nitric acid, in tonnes, needed. [Mr: HNO₃ = 63]

parts.label: d
parts.text: The plant produces 15.2 tonnes. Calculate the percentage yield.

practice.stem: (Invented prices for this question.) A 50 kg bag of urea, CO(NH₂)₂, costs Rs 4500. A 50 kg bag of ammonium sulfate costs Rs 3000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in urea and in ammonium sulfate, to 3 significant figures. [Mr: CO(NH₂)₂ = 60, (NH₄)₂SO₄ = 132]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the cost of 1 kg of nitrogen from each fertiliser, to the nearest rupee.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason, other than cost, why a farmer might still choose ammonium sulfate.
parts.answer: It also supplies sulfur / makes soil slightly more acidic where needed.

practice.stem: A farmer mixes 25 kg of potassium nitrate, KNO₃, with 25 kg of ammonium phosphate, (NH₄)₃PO₄.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the masses of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium in the mixture, each to 3 significant figures. [Mr: KNO₃ = 101, (NH₄)₃PO₄ = 149; Ar: N = 14, P = 31, K = 39]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of each element in the 50 kg mixture to the nearest whole number, to give its NPK rating.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the approximate percentage of nitrogen in clean, dry air?
A 21%
B 50%
C 78%
D 99%
parts.working: Clean dry air is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen, with small amounts of argon and carbon dioxide. 21% is the oxygen value.

practice.stem: Clean, dry air is a mixture of gases.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the two main gases in clean, dry air and give their approximate percentages.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the noble gas that makes up most of the remaining 1%.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the compound present in clean air at about 0.04%.

practice.stem: A classroom contains 200 m³ of clean, dry air.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of nitrogen in the room.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen in the room.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the gas that makes up most of the remaining volume.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the oxygen percentage in a crowded, closed room may fall slightly.
parts.answer: People use oxygen in respiration (and release carbon dioxide).

practice.stem: Name the gas in clean air that matches each description.

parts.label: a
parts.text: needed for burning fuels

parts.label: b
parts.text: the most abundant gas in air

parts.label: c
parts.text: used by green plants in photosynthesis

parts.label: d
parts.text: a noble gas used to fill some light bulbs

practice.stem: A lit candle is placed on a floating cork under an upturned measuring jar standing in water. The candle soon goes out and the water rises up the jar.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the candle goes out.
parts.answer: The oxygen in the jar is used up (no longer enough to support burning).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the water level rises inside the jar.
parts.answer: Oxygen is removed, so gas pressure falls and water is pushed in to take its place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The water rose by 14% of the volume. Give two reasons why this method gives a value lower than the true oxygen percentage.
parts.answer: Candle goes out before all oxygen is used; carbon dioxide is formed which takes up volume (only partly dissolves); heated gas expands and some escapes at the start.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest a better method for finding the percentage of oxygen in air.
parts.answer: Pass a known volume of air repeatedly over heated copper (or use damp iron wool) and measure the volume decrease.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the approximate percentage of noble gases in clean, dry air.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the noble gases are unreactive.
parts.answer: Their atoms have full outer electron shells.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the most common noble gas in air and give one use.
parts.answer: Argon; filling light bulbs / inert atmosphere for welding.

practice.stem: 120 cm³ of air is passed backwards and forwards over heated copper powder until the volume stops changing. After cooling to room temperature, 94.8 cm³ of gas remains.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of oxygen in the air.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the colour change of the copper.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the balanced equation for the reaction of copper with oxygen.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the gas is allowed to cool before the final volume is measured.
parts.answer: Gases expand when hot, so the volume would be too large / the volume must be measured at the same temperature as the start.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A 500 cm³ sample of clean, dry air is used. Approximately what volume of oxygen does it contain?
A 105 cm³
B 390 cm³
C 50 cm³
D 21 cm³
parts.working: Oxygen is about 21% of clean, dry air: 0.21 × 500 = 105 cm³. B is the nitrogen volume (78%); D confuses the percentage with the volume.

practice.stem: 100 cm³ of air is passed back and forth between two gas syringes over a tube of heated copper. Readings after each set of passes, once cool: 92, 85, 81, 79, 79, 79 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of oxygen in the air sample.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the student continued until the reading did not change.
parts.answer: To make sure all the oxygen had reacted with the copper.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the colour change of the copper.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why each reading was taken after the apparatus had cooled.
parts.answer: Hot gas has expanded, so its volume would read too high.

practice.stem: A bedroom measures 4 m × 5 m × 3 m and is at room temperature and pressure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of the room in dm³. [1 m³ = 1000 dm³]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of oxygen in the room, in kg. Assume oxygen is 21% of the air. [Mr: O₂ = 32; 1 mol of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why tables of the composition of air are given for 'clean, dry air'.
parts.answer: The amount of water vapour varies from place to place and day to day; pollutants also vary, so they are left out to give fixed percentages.
parts.working: B1 water vapour varies; B1 pollutants vary/excluded.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why air in Karachi in summer usually contains more water vapour than air in Quetta in winter.
parts.answer: Karachi is warm and by the sea, so more water evaporates (warm air holds more water vapour).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe a chemical test to show that air contains water vapour.
parts.answer: Pass the air over (or leave out) anhydrous copper(II) sulfate: white turns blue (or cobalt(II) chloride paper blue to pink).

practice.stem: Damp iron wool is pushed to the closed end of a graduated tube containing 50.0 cm³ of air. The open end stands in a dish of water. After one week the volume of air in the tube is 39.6 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of oxygen in the air from these results.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the water rises up the tube.
parts.answer: The iron rusts, using up the oxygen in the air; the gas volume decreases so water is pushed up to replace it.
parts.working: B1 oxygen used in rusting; B1 volume of gas falls.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the apparatus is left for a week before the final reading.
parts.answer: Rusting is slow; time is needed for all the oxygen to be used up.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the result is slightly lower than 21%.
parts.answer: Not all the oxygen had reacted / the temperature or pressure changed / reading error.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average relative mass of the particles in air, to 3 significant figures, taking air as 78% N₂, 21% O₂ and 1% Ar by volume. [Ar: N = 14, O = 16, Ar = 40]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answer to explain why a balloon filled with helium (Ar = 4) rises in air.
parts.answer: Helium particles are much lighter (4 vs 29), so helium is less dense than air.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen in 240 cm³ of air (21% oxygen).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the minimum mass of copper needed to remove all of this oxygen: 2Cu + O₂ → 2CuO. [Ar: Cu = 63.5; 1 mol of gas occupies 24 000 cm³ at r.t.p.]

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the increase in mass of the solid in the tube.

practice.stem: All volumes are measured at the same temperature and pressure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the complete combustion of methane.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the minimum volume of air needed to burn 10 cm³ of methane completely. Air contains 21% oxygen. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: M1 oxygen needed = 20 cm³; A1 20 ÷ 0.21 = 95.2 cm³.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the volume of nitrogen in this air, to 3 significant figures, taking nitrogen as 78% of air, and explain why it is still present after burning.
parts.answer: 74.3 cm³; nitrogen is unreactive and does not take part in the combustion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Molten lead(II) bromide is electrolysed using graphite electrodes. What is formed at each electrode?
A cathode: lead; anode: bromine
B cathode: bromine; anode: lead
C cathode: hydrogen; anode: bromine
D cathode: lead; anode: oxygen
parts.working: Positive Pb²⁺ ions move to the cathode and gain electrons to form lead; Br⁻ ions move to the anode and lose electrons to form bromine. B swaps the electrodes; there is no water, so no hydrogen or oxygen can form.

practice.stem: Zinc chloride, ZnCl₂, is an ionic compound with a fairly low melting point.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term electrolysis.
parts.answer: The decomposition of an ionic compound, when molten or in aqueous solution, by the passage of an electric current.
parts.working: B1 decomposition/breakdown of ionic compound (molten or aqueous); B1 by electricity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the positive electrode.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why solid zinc chloride does not conduct electricity but molten zinc chloride does.
parts.answer: In the solid the ions are fixed in a lattice and cannot move; when molten the ions are free to move and carry charge.
parts.working: B1 solid: ions cannot move; B1 molten: ions mobile.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name the products at the cathode and at the anode when molten zinc chloride is electrolysed.

practice.stem: Dilute sulfuric acid is electrolysed using platinum electrodes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the gas formed at the cathode and the gas formed at the anode.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 36 cm³ of gas is collected at the cathode. State the volume of gas collected at the anode in the same time.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Complete the half-equation for the anode: 4OH⁻ → O₂ + ___ + ___

practice.stem: Concentrated aqueous sodium bromide is electrolysed using carbon electrodes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: List the four ions present in the solution.
parts.working: B1 for Na⁺ and Br⁻; B1 for H⁺ and OH⁻.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the product at each electrode.
parts.working: B1 each. Hydrogen, not sodium, because sodium is more reactive than hydrogen; bromide is discharged because the solution is concentrated.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe what is seen near the anode.
parts.answer: The solution turns orange (yellow-orange / orange-brown) as bromine forms.

practice.stem: A student electrolyses concentrated aqueous sodium chloride in an apparatus that collects the gas from each electrode in a separate tube.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is seen at each electrode.
parts.answer: Bubbles of gas at both electrodes; the gas at the anode is pale green / yellow-green.
parts.working: B1 bubbles at both; B1 pale green at anode.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student holds damp blue litmus paper at the top of the anode tube. State what happens.
parts.answer: It turns red and then is bleached (white).
parts.working: B1 bleached; accept red then white.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The volume of gas at the anode is a little less than at the cathode, although equal volumes are expected. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Some chlorine dissolves in the water/solution.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name the gas formed at the cathode.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which substance conducts electricity when molten but not when solid?
A copper
B sodium chloride
C sulfur
D graphite
parts.working: Sodium chloride is ionic: its ions cannot move in the solid but can move when molten. Copper and graphite conduct when solid; sulfur does not conduct in either state.

practice.stem: Name the two products formed when each molten compound is electrolysed with inert electrodes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: molten potassium iodide

parts.label: b
parts.text: molten calcium chloride

parts.label: c
parts.text: molten aluminium oxide

parts.label: d
parts.text: State at which electrode the metal is formed in each case and explain why.
parts.answer: The cathode; metal ions are positive and are attracted to the negative electrode, where they gain electrons.
parts.working: B1 cathode; B1 positive ions attracted / gain electrons.

practice.stem: Concentrated aqueous sodium chloride (brine) is electrolysed using inert electrodes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the product at the anode and describe a test for it.
parts.answer: Chlorine; it bleaches damp litmus paper.
parts.working: B1 chlorine; B1 bleaches damp (blue) litmus.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the ionic half-equation for the reaction at the cathode.
parts.working: B1 species; B1 balanced. Accept 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the compound left in solution at the end and explain why it is left.
parts.answer: Sodium hydroxide; H⁺ and Cl⁻ are removed, leaving Na⁺ and OH⁻ ions in solution.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why sodium is not produced at the cathode.
parts.answer: Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen ions are discharged instead.

practice.stem: Aqueous copper(II) sulfate is electrolysed using graphite electrodes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is seen at the cathode.
parts.answer: A pink-brown (copper-coloured) solid forms on it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what is seen at the anode, and name the product.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State and explain what happens to the colour of the solution.
parts.answer: The blue colour fades (becomes paler) because Cu²⁺ ions are removed from the solution as copper.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest what happens to the pH of the solution. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: pH decreases (becomes more acidic) because H⁺ ions are left in solution with sulfate ions — sulfuric acid forms.
parts.working: B1 decreases; B1 H⁺/sulfuric acid left.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Each aqueous solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes. Which one gives hydrogen at the cathode?
A aqueous copper(II) chloride
B aqueous silver nitrate
C aqueous potassium bromide
D aqueous copper(II) sulfate
parts.working: Potassium is more reactive than hydrogen, so H⁺ ions are discharged and hydrogen forms. Copper and silver are less reactive than hydrogen, so these metals are deposited instead.

practice.stem: Sodium metal is manufactured by electrolysing molten sodium chloride.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the half-equation for the reaction at the cathode.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the half-equation for the reaction at the anode.
parts.working: B1 species; B1 balanced with electrons.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which electrode reaction is oxidation. Explain your answer in terms of electrons.
parts.answer: The anode reaction; chloride ions lose electrons.
parts.working: B1 anode; B1 loss of electrons.

practice.stem: A student electrolyses aqueous potassium iodide with carbon electrodes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is seen at the cathode.
parts.working: B1 'a gas is given off' is not enough.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe a test for the gas at the cathode and give the result.
parts.working: B1 lighted splint; B1 squeaky pop.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A few drops of universal indicator were added to the solution before the electrolysis. State the colour of the solution near the cathode after a few minutes and explain why.
parts.answer: Blue/purple; hydroxide ions are left in solution as hydrogen is discharged, so the solution becomes alkaline.
parts.working: B1 blue/purple; B1 OH⁻ left / alkaline.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe the colour change near the anode.

practice.stem: Molten lead(II) bromide is electrolysed using graphite electrodes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the lead(II) bromide must be heated before a current flows.
parts.answer: Ions must be able to move; they are free to move only when molten.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the experiment is done in a fume cupboard.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the half-equation for the formation of lead.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe what is seen at the anode.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Aqueous copper(II) sulfate is electrolysed using carbon electrodes. Which statement is correct?
A The blue colour becomes darker.
B The mass of the anode decreases.
C Oxygen forms at the anode and the solution becomes more acidic.
D Hydrogen forms at the cathode.
parts.answer: C Oxygen forms at the anode and the solution becomes more acidic.
parts.working: OH⁻ ions are discharged at the anode as oxygen and H⁺ ions remain, so the solution becomes acidic. B happens only with copper anodes; copper (not hydrogen) forms at the cathode; the blue colour fades.

practice.stem: Aqueous sodium sulfate containing universal indicator (green) is electrolysed in a U-tube with inert electrodes. Hydrogen forms at the cathode and oxygen at the anode.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the colour near the anode and near the cathode after a few minutes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the colour near the anode.
parts.answer: OH⁻ ions are discharged as oxygen (4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻) so H⁺ ions are left in excess, making it acidic.
parts.working: B1 OH⁻ discharged/oxygen; B1 excess H⁺.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why sulfate ions are not discharged.
parts.answer: Hydroxide ions are discharged in preference to sulfate ions.

practice.stem: Aqueous copper(II) sulfate is electrolysed using copper electrodes. Ar: Cu = 64.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the half-equation for the reaction at the anode.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The anode loses 0.48 g. State the change in mass of the cathode.
parts.working: B1 copper atoms lost from anode = copper deposited on cathode.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of electrons that pass through the circuit. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the blue colour of the solution does not change.
parts.answer: Copper ions are formed at the anode at the same rate as they are removed at the cathode, so the concentration of Cu²⁺ stays the same.
parts.working: B1 Cu²⁺ made at anode; B1 removed at cathode at same rate.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Dilute aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed with inert electrodes. Which row shows the main products?
A cathode: hydrogen; anode: oxygen
B cathode: sodium; anode: chlorine
C cathode: hydrogen; anode: chlorine
D cathode: sodium; anode: oxygen
parts.working: In a dilute solution of a halide, OH⁻ (from water) is discharged at the anode giving oxygen; hydrogen forms at the cathode because sodium is more reactive than hydrogen. C is the result for the concentrated solution.

practice.stem: Name the product at the cathode and the product at the anode when each of the following is electrolysed with inert electrodes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Molten calcium bromide

parts.label: b
parts.text: Concentrated hydrochloric acid

parts.label: c
parts.text: Aqueous silver nitrate

parts.label: d
parts.text: Dilute aqueous magnesium sulfate

practice.stem: During electrolysis an electric current passes through both the external circuit and the electrolyte.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the particles that carry the current in the metal wires.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the particles that carry the current in the electrolyte.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the transfer of charge at the electrodes and in the external circuit when molten potassium chloride is electrolysed.
parts.answer: K⁺ ions move to the cathode and gain electrons forming potassium; Cl⁻ ions move to the anode and lose electrons forming chlorine; electrons flow through the external circuit from the anode to the cathode (pushed by the power supply).
parts.working: B1 cations to cathode, gain electrons; B1 anions to anode, lose electrons; B1 electrons leave at anode; B1 electrons travel through wire to cathode.

practice.stem: Concentrated aqueous copper(II) chloride is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Ar: Cu = 64. 1 mol of gas occupies 24 dm³ at room temperature and pressure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the products at the cathode and at the anode.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 0.32 g of copper is deposited. Calculate the volume of chlorine, in cm³ at room temperature and pressure, formed at the same time.

practice.stem: The mass of copper deposited at the cathode during electrolysis depends on the current.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an experiment to investigate how the current affects the mass of copper deposited on the cathode when aqueous copper(II) sulfate is electrolysed for a fixed time. You may use common laboratory apparatus, including a variable resistor and an ammeter.
parts.answer: Weigh cathode, electrolyse at set current and time, wash, dry, reweigh, repeat at different currents.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: clean and weigh the copper cathode (balance); set up cathode and anode in copper(II) sulfate solution connected to a power supply, ammeter and variable resistor in series; adjust the resistor to a set current (e.g. 0.2 A) and keep it constant; electrolyse for a fixed time (e.g. 20 min, stop-watch); remove, rinse with distilled water (and propanone), dry and reweigh cathode; repeat with different currents (e.g. 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 A) using the same volume/concentration of solution, same time; calculate mass gained and plot against current.

practice.stem: Aqueous silver nitrate is electrolysed using platinum electrodes. Ar: Ag = 108. 1 mol of gas occupies 24 dm³ at room temperature and pressure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the half-equation for the reaction at the cathode.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the half-equation for the reaction at the anode.
parts.working: B1 species; B1 balanced. Accept 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻.

parts.label: c
parts.text: 1.08 g of silver is deposited. Calculate the volume of oxygen formed at room temperature and pressure, in cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the only product of the reaction in a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell?
A carbon dioxide
B water
C hydrogen peroxide
D carbon dioxide and water
parts.working: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O; there is no carbon in the reactants, so no carbon dioxide can form.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A simple cell is made with zinc and copper electrodes in dilute acid. Which statement is correct?
A Zinc is the positive electrode.
B Electrons flow from copper to zinc in the wire.
C Zinc atoms are oxidised.
D Copper dissolves to form ions.
parts.working: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ is oxidation at the more reactive metal, which is the negative electrode. Electrons flow from zinc to copper. Copper does not dissolve.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the only product of the reaction in a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one advantage of a hydrogen fuel cell in a vehicle compared with a petrol engine.
parts.answer: No carbon dioxide or other polluting exhaust gases are produced (only water).
parts.working: Accept any one clear environmental benefit, such as no carbon dioxide, no carbon monoxide or no nitrogen oxides in use.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one reason why hydrogen is not yet widely used as a fuel.
parts.answer: Hydrogen is difficult and costly to store and transport safely.
parts.working: Accept: most hydrogen is made from fossil fuels; hydrogen needs a large amount of energy to produce; or it is hard to store.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a hydrogen fuel cell, state the type of energy conversion that takes place.
parts.answer: Chemical energy is converted into electrical energy (with some heat).
parts.working: accept chemical → electrical; the electrical output is the useful energy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the substance that is oxidised in the hydrogen fuel cell.
parts.working: hydrogen loses electrons at the negative electrode.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the function of the electrolyte in a cell.
parts.answer: It allows ions to move between the electrodes, completing the circuit inside the cell.
parts.working: accept: it carries charge (ions) between the electrodes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a simple cell stops producing electricity if the electrolyte is removed.
parts.answer: There is no path for ions to move between the electrodes, so the circuit is incomplete and the reactions stop.
parts.working: 1 mark: the circuit is not completed through the electrolyte; 1 mark: ions cannot carry charge, so no current flows.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one difference between a hydrogen fuel cell and a rechargeable battery.
parts.answer: A fuel cell keeps producing electricity as long as fuel and oxygen are supplied, whereas a battery runs down as its chemicals are used up.
parts.working: 1 mark: fuel cell needs a continuous supply of reactants (fuel and oxygen) rather than storing them; 1 mark: a battery runs down when its reactants are used up, while a fuel cell does not.

practice.stem: A city transport company is considering replacing diesel buses with hydrogen fuel cell buses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the overall equation for the reaction in a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two advantages of a hydrogen fuel cell bus compared with a diesel bus.
parts.answer: Only water is produced; no carbon dioxide (greenhouse gas), carbon monoxide, oxides of nitrogen or particulates released from the bus; quieter / more efficient.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two disadvantages.
parts.answer: Hydrogen is difficult/costly to store (needs high pressure, flammable/explosive); few refuelling stations; hydrogen is often made from fossil fuels or using electricity from fossil fuels; fuel cells are expensive.

practice.stem: Energy released when 1 mol of fuel reacts with oxygen: hydrogen, H₂, 286 kJ; methane, CH₄, 890 kJ. Mr: H₂ = 2, CH₄ = 16.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy released per gram of each fuel. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answers to suggest one advantage of hydrogen as a fuel for vehicles.
parts.answer: It releases more energy per gram (so a lighter fuel load is needed).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hydrogen has a very low density. Suggest why this is a problem for its use in vehicles.
parts.answer: A large volume is needed / it must be stored under high pressure in strong, heavy tanks.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell with an alkaline electrolyte, which equation describes the reaction at the negative electrode?
A H₂ + 2OH⁻ → 2H₂O + 2e⁻
B O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻
C 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻
D 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂
parts.working: Hydrogen is oxidised at the negative electrode (electrons are released). B is the reaction at the positive electrode; C is an oxidation of water to oxygen, not the fuel cell reaction; D is a reduction that produces hydrogen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hydrogen fuel cell produces 5.40 g of water. Calculate the moles of water formed. [Ar: H = 1, O = 16]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of hydrogen used to form this water.
parts.working: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, so moles H₂ = 0.300; mass = 0.300 × 2 = 0.600 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell has an acidic electrolyte. Write the half-equation for the reaction at the negative electrode.
parts.working: hydrogen loses electrons (oxidation); the 2 H⁺ ions are released into the electrolyte.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the half-equation for the reaction at the positive electrode.
parts.working: oxygen gains electrons (reduction) and combines with H⁺ ions to form water.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Combine the two half-equations to give the overall equation.
parts.working: multiply the first half-equation by 2 so the electrons cancel, then add the two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A simple cell is made with magnesium and iron electrodes in salt solution. Explain which metal is the negative electrode, which way the electrons flow, and which metal is oxidised.
parts.answer: Magnesium is the negative electrode because it is more reactive; electrons flow from magnesium through the wire to iron; magnesium is oxidised (Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻).
parts.working: 1 mark: magnesium is more reactive than iron so it is the negative electrode; 1 mark: electrons flow from Mg to Fe through the wire; 1 mark: Mg is oxidised, losing electrons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student makes three simple cells in salt solution: zinc and copper; magnesium and copper; magnesium and zinc. Predict which cell gives the greatest voltage, and explain why. (Reactivity: Mg > Zn > Cu.)
parts.answer: Magnesium and copper gives the greatest voltage.
parts.working: 1 mark: magnesium is the most reactive metal, so the cell with Mg and Cu has the largest difference in reactivity; 1 mark: greater difference in reactivity gives a greater voltage; 1 mark: the answer Mg and Cu.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A simple cell has zinc and copper electrodes in lemon juice. Describe the observation at the zinc electrode.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the observation at the copper electrode.
parts.answer: Bubbles of gas (hydrogen) form on the copper.
parts.working: H⁺ ions from the acid gain electrons at the copper.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the direction of electron flow in the external wire.
parts.working: electrons leave the negative electrode (zinc) and travel to the positive electrode (copper).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of oxygen needed to form 36 g of water in a hydrogen fuel cell. [Ar: H = 1, O = 16]
parts.working: moles H₂O = 36 ÷ 18 = 2.0 (1 mark); moles O₂ = 2.0 ÷ 2 = 1.0 (1 mark); mass O₂ = 1.0 × 32 = 32 g (1 mark).

practice.stem: A fuel cell bus uses 8.0 kg of hydrogen in one day. 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Mr: H₂ = 2, H₂O = 18. 1 mol of gas occupies 24 dm³ at room temperature and pressure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of hydrogen used.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of water produced, in kg.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen used, in dm³ at room temperature and pressure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Burning 1 mol of hydrogen releases 286 kJ of energy (H₂ + ½O₂ → H₂O(l); ΔH = −286 kJ/mol). Calculate the moles of hydrogen in 0.80 g of hydrogen. [Ar: H = 1]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy released when 0.80 g of hydrogen is burned in air.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The fuel cell converts 60% of this energy into electrical energy. Calculate the electrical energy produced.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A magnesium and copper cell operates in dilute acid. Write the half-equation for the reaction at the magnesium electrode.
parts.working: magnesium is oxidised at the negative electrode.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the half-equation for the reaction at the copper electrode.
parts.working: hydrogen ions gain electrons at the copper (bubbles of hydrogen are seen).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the overall ionic equation for the cell reaction.
parts.working: add the two half-equations; the electrons cancel.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the moles of hydrogen in 1.00 kg of hydrogen gas. [Ar: H = 1]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy released when 1.00 kg of hydrogen is burned, using ΔH = −286 kJ/mol. Give your answer in kJ.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hydrogen fuel cell uses 4.0 g of hydrogen. Each H₂ molecule releases 2 electrons at the negative electrode (H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻). Calculate the moles of electrons transferred. [Ar: H = 1]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen, in dm³ at r.t.p., consumed by this mass of hydrogen.
parts.working: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, so moles O₂ = 2.0 ÷ 2 = 1.0; volume = 1.0 × 24.0 = 24.0 dm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A steel spoon is to be electroplated with silver. Which row is correct?
A cathode: spoon; anode: silver; electrolyte: aqueous silver nitrate
B cathode: silver; anode: spoon; electrolyte: aqueous silver nitrate
C cathode: spoon; anode: silver; electrolyte: aqueous sodium chloride
D cathode: spoon; anode: carbon; electrolyte: aqueous iron(II) sulfate
parts.answer: A cathode: spoon; anode: silver; electrolyte: aqueous silver nitrate
parts.working: The object to be plated is the cathode, the plating metal is the anode, and the electrolyte contains ions of the plating metal (Ag⁺). B reverses the electrodes, which would dissolve the spoon.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An iron bolt is to be electroplated with zinc using zinc sulfate solution. Which row is correct?
A cathode: zinc; anode: bolt; electrolyte: zinc sulfate solution
B cathode: bolt; anode: zinc; electrolyte: zinc sulfate solution
C cathode: bolt; anode: iron; electrolyte: dilute sulfuric acid
D cathode: zinc; anode: iron; electrolyte: iron(II) sulfate solution
parts.answer: B cathode: bolt; anode: zinc; electrolyte: zinc sulfate solution
parts.working: The object to be plated is the cathode, where Zn²⁺ ions are reduced to zinc. The anode is the plating metal, which dissolves to replace the ions. A and D swap the cathode and anode; C uses the wrong electrolyte and anode.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A copper key is electroplated with copper using copper(II) sulfate solution, a copper anode and the key as the cathode. State what happens to: (i) the mass of the copper anode; (ii) the mass of the key; (iii) the colour of the solution.
parts.working: 1 mark each: copper dissolves from the anode to replace the Cu²⁺ ions used at the cathode; copper deposits on the key, increasing its mass; the concentration stays constant, so the colour stays blue.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In the anodising of aluminium, the aluminium is connected as which electrode? The electrolyte is dilute sulfuric acid.
parts.working: aluminium is oxidised to form an oxide layer on its surface, so it is the anode.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the gas formed at the cathode.
parts.working: H⁺ ions are reduced at the cathode to hydrogen gas.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the layer that forms on the aluminium.
parts.working: the oxide layer is thicker and protects the metal from corrosion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State why the carbon anodes in the extraction of aluminium must be replaced regularly.
parts.answer: The oxygen released at the carbon anodes reacts with the carbon to form carbon dioxide, so the anodes are used up.
parts.working: 1 mark: oxygen is produced at the anode; 1 mark: it reacts with the carbon to form CO₂ (carbon is used up).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Concentrated sodium chloride solution is electrolysed. Name the product formed at the anode.
parts.working: chloride ions are oxidised at the positive anode: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the test for this gas.
parts.answer: It bleaches damp litmus paper (turns it white).
parts.working: accept: turns damp blue litmus paper red and then white; chlorine is a bleach.

practice.stem: A bicycle workshop in Sialkot plates steel handlebars with nickel.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two reasons why metal objects are electroplated.
parts.answer: To improve appearance; to resist corrosion (rusting).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which electrode the handlebar should be, and name a suitable electrolyte.
parts.answer: Cathode; aqueous nickel(II) sulfate (or another soluble nickel salt).
parts.working: B1 cathode; B1 solution containing Ni²⁺ ions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the half-equation for the reaction at the handlebar.

practice.stem: Impure copper is purified by electrolysis. Pure copper is deposited on the cathode.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which electrode is made of the impure copper.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name a suitable electrolyte.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The impure anode loses 120 g. The anode contained 6.0% by mass of impurities, which collect below it. Calculate the mass gained by the cathode.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why copper used in electrical wiring is purified.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Molten aluminium oxide dissolved in molten cryolite is electrolysed with carbon electrodes. Which statement is correct?
A aluminium forms at the anode and oxygen at the cathode
B aluminium forms at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
C both aluminium and oxygen form at the cathode
D both aluminium and oxygen form at the anode
parts.answer: B aluminium forms at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
parts.working: Al³⁺ ions gain electrons at the negative cathode (Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al); O²⁻ ions lose electrons at the positive anode (2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Impure copper is purified by electrolysis. State which electrode is made of impure copper.
parts.working: the impure copper is the anode, so copper atoms are oxidised and dissolve.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction at the cathode.
parts.working: 1 mark for the Cu²⁺ and electrons on the left; 1 mark for Cu on the right and the balanced electrons.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what happens to the silver and gold impurities.
parts.answer: They do not dissolve and fall to the bottom of the cell as anode sludge.
parts.working: the less reactive impurities are not oxidised, so they collect below the anode.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A factory uses 1.02 tonnes of pure aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃, to extract aluminium by electrolysis. Calculate the maximum mass of aluminium, in tonnes. [Ar: Al = 27, O = 16]
parts.working: Mr Al₂O₃ = 102; Al in Al₂O₃ = 54; mass = 1.02 × 54 ÷ 102 = 0.540 tonnes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sodium is extracted by electrolysis of molten sodium chloride rather than by heating with carbon. Explain why.
parts.answer: Sodium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot displace it from sodium chloride; electrolysis uses the electrical energy to remove electrons from Cl⁻ and add electrons to Na⁺ ions, so the sodium is produced directly.
parts.working: 1 mark: sodium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot reduce its compound; 1 mark: electrolysis of molten NaCl (ions free to move) releases sodium at the cathode; 1 mark: electrical energy drives the reaction (or sodium would react again).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a copper anode is used, rather than a carbon anode, when electroplating an object with copper.
parts.answer: The copper anode dissolves to replace the Cu²⁺ ions removed from the solution at the cathode, so the concentration stays constant; a carbon anode would release oxygen instead.
parts.working: 1 mark: copper dissolves to replace the Cu²⁺ ions; 1 mark: carbon would produce oxygen, so the copper ion concentration would fall.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Aluminium is extracted by electrolysis, which uses a large amount of electricity. Explain why recycling aluminium saves energy compared with extracting it from aluminium oxide.
parts.answer: Extracting aluminium from its oxide needs a large amount of electrical energy to decompose the strong Al–O bonds and keep the ore molten; recycling only needs melting the metal, which uses much less energy.
parts.working: 1 mark: electrolysis of aluminium oxide needs large amounts of electrical energy; 1 mark: the oxide must be molten (kept in cryolite); 1 mark: recycling needs only melting, so much less energy is used.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to electroplate a metal key with nickel. Include: the electrodes and electrolyte, the source of current, and what happens to the masses of the electrodes.
parts.answer: The key is the cathode and a nickel rod is the anode, both connected to a d.c. power supply; the electrolyte is nickel(II) sulfate solution; nickel dissolves from the anode and deposits on the key, so the anode gets smaller and the key gets heavier.
parts.working: 1 mark: key as cathode and nickel as anode; 1 mark: d.c. power supply and nickel(II) sulfate electrolyte; 1 mark: nickel dissolves at the anode; 1 mark: nickel deposits on the key (key mass increases, anode mass decreases).

practice.stem: Aluminium is extracted by the electrolysis of aluminium oxide dissolved in molten cryolite, using carbon electrodes. Ar: Al = 27, O = 16.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the aluminium oxide is dissolved in molten cryolite.
parts.answer: It lowers the operating temperature (aluminium oxide has a very high melting point), so less energy is needed; the solution also conducts better.
parts.working: B1 lower temperature / melting point of electrolyte; B1 saves energy/cost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the half-equation for the reaction at the cathode.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the carbon anodes must be replaced regularly.
parts.answer: Oxygen is formed at the anode; it reacts with the hot carbon to form carbon dioxide, so the anodes burn away.
parts.working: B1 oxygen reacts with carbon; B1 CO₂ forms.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the maximum mass of aluminium, in tonnes, that can be obtained from 1.02 tonnes of aluminium oxide.
parts.working: M1 Mr Al₂O₃ = 102, contains 54 of Al; A1 1.02 × 54/102 = 0.54 t.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a chemical works, 585 kg of sodium chloride is electrolysed as concentrated brine: 2NaCl(aq) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H₂(g) + Cl₂(g). Calculate the number of kmol of NaCl used. [Ar: Na = 23, Cl = 35.5]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of sodium hydroxide formed. [Ar: Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1]
parts.working: 2NaCl gives 2NaOH, so 10.0 kmol NaOH; Mr NaOH = 40; mass = 10.0 × 40 = 400 kg.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of chlorine formed. [Cl₂ Mr = 71]
parts.working: 1 mol Cl₂ per 2 mol NaCl, so 5.0 kmol Cl₂; mass = 5.0 × 71 = 355 kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A copper anode loses 1.27 g of copper during electrolysis of copper(II) sulfate solution using copper electrodes. Calculate the moles of copper dissolved from the anode. [Ar: Cu = 63.5]

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the mass of copper deposited on the cathode, and explain why the copper sulfate solution keeps its blue colour.
parts.answer: 1.27 g; the same number of Cu²⁺ ions is removed at the cathode as is added at the anode, so the concentration stays the same.
parts.working: 1 mark: the mass deposited equals the mass lost from the anode; 1 mark: Cu²⁺ ions are replaced at the same rate as they are removed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A 2.70 g piece of aluminium is fully converted to aluminium oxide during anodising. Calculate the moles of aluminium. [Ar: Al = 27]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assuming all the aluminium forms Al₂O₃, calculate the mass of aluminium oxide formed. [Ar: O = 16]
parts.working: 2 mol Al form 1 mol Al₂O₃; moles Al₂O₃ = 0.0500; Mr = 102; mass = 0.0500 × 102 = 5.10 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student says: 'In electroplating, the object being plated is the anode.' Explain whether the student is correct.
parts.answer: The student is wrong: the object being plated is the cathode, where the metal ions are reduced and deposited.
parts.working: 1 mark: the statement is incorrect; 1 mark: the object is the cathode (negative electrode), where the metal ions gain electrons.

practice.subtopic: Kinetic particle theory & changes of state (incl. gas P/V/T)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement describes the particles in a liquid?
A close together, in a regular arrangement, vibrating about fixed positions
B close together, in an irregular arrangement, moving past one another
C far apart, in an irregular arrangement, moving quickly in all directions
D far apart, in a regular arrangement, moving slowly
parts.answer: B close together, in an irregular arrangement, moving past one another
parts.working: Liquid particles touch (close together), have no regular pattern and slide past each other. A describes a solid; C a gas.

practice.subtopic: Kinetic particle theory & changes of state (incl. gas P/V/T)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
