parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement is correct for the energy profile of an exothermic reaction?
A The products are at a higher energy level than the reactants.
B The products are at a lower energy level than the reactants.
C The reactants and products are at the same energy level.
D There is no activation energy.
parts.answer: B The products are at a lower energy level than the reactants.
parts.working: Exothermic: energy is given out, so the products end lower than the reactants. All reactions have an activation energy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define activation energy, Ea.
parts.answer: The minimum energy that colliding particles must have in order to react.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the energy profile for an endothermic reaction. Say where the reactants and products are, and show how Ea and ΔH are measured.
parts.answer: Products higher than reactants; curve rises to a peak above both; Ea = height from reactants to peak; ΔH = difference from reactants to products (upward, positive).
parts.working: B1 products above reactants; B1 Ea from reactants to peak; B1 ΔH reactants to products.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
On a reaction pathway (energy profile) diagram, what is shown by the energy difference between the reactants and the highest point of the curve?
A the activation energy
B the enthalpy change, ΔH
C the energy of the products
D the energy released by the reaction
parts.working: The activation energy is the minimum energy the colliding particles need to react: from the reactants up to the peak. B is the difference between reactants and products.

practice.stem: A reaction has ΔH = +30 kJ/mol and activation energy 80 kJ/mol. On its energy profile the reactants are drawn at 0 kJ/mol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the energy of the products.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the energy at the top of the curve.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether the products are above or below the reactants and what this tells you about the reaction.
parts.answer: Above; endothermic (energy is taken in from the surroundings).

practice.stem: Methane burns in a gas geyser: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. The reaction is exothermic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the shape of the energy profile for burning methane. State where the reactants and products are and how ΔH is shown.
parts.answer: The curve rises from the reactants to a peak and then falls to the products, which are lower than the reactants; ΔH is the downward drop from reactants to products (negative).
parts.working: B1 rises to a peak (activation energy); B1 products below reactants; B1 ΔH arrow from reactants to products, negative.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the sign of ΔH for this reaction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define activation energy.
parts.answer: The minimum energy that colliding particles need in order to react.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A match does not light by itself, but it lights when struck against the box. Explain this in terms of activation energy.
parts.answer: Striking (friction) supplies energy that is at least the activation energy; then the reaction releases enough energy to keep going.
parts.working: B1 striking provides the activation energy; B1 exothermic reaction then sustains itself.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
On an energy profile, the reactants are at 120 kJ/mol, the top of the curve is at 290 kJ/mol and the products are at 40 kJ/mol. What are the activation energy and the enthalpy change, ΔH?
A activation energy 170 kJ/mol, ΔH −80 kJ/mol
B activation energy 250 kJ/mol, ΔH −80 kJ/mol
C activation energy 170 kJ/mol, ΔH +80 kJ/mol
D activation energy 290 kJ/mol, ΔH −40 kJ/mol
parts.answer: A activation energy 170 kJ/mol, ΔH −80 kJ/mol
parts.working: Ea = 290 − 120 = 170 kJ/mol; ΔH = 40 − 120 = −80 kJ/mol. B measures Ea from the products.

practice.stem: A reaction has ΔH = +58 kJ/mol and activation energy Ea = 140 kJ/mol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Is the reaction exothermic or endothermic? Give a reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy of the top of the curve relative to the products.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the activation energy of the reverse reaction.

practice.stem: Many homes in Pakistan cook on piped natural gas (mainly methane).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The burning of natural gas is exothermic, yet a gas stove needs a spark or match to light it. Explain why.
parts.answer: The reaction has an activation energy; the spark supplies energy so particles collide with energy at least equal to Ea.
parts.working: B1 activation energy; B1 spark supplies it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the flame keeps burning once it has been lit.
parts.answer: The energy released by the reaction supplies the activation energy for more molecules to react.

practice.stem: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes slowly to water and oxygen. When a little manganese(IV) oxide is added, the reaction becomes much faster.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the energy profile for the catalysed reaction differs from that for the uncatalysed reaction.
parts.answer: The peak is lower (lower activation energy); the reactant and product levels are the same (same ΔH).
parts.working: B1 lower peak; B1 same start and end levels.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hydrogen peroxide decomposition is exothermic. State where the products are on the energy profile.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what happens to the mass of manganese(IV) oxide during the reaction.
parts.answer: It stays the same (the catalyst is not used up).

practice.stem:
A catalytic converter in a car exhaust speeds up: 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂  ΔH = −746 kJ/mol
Activation energy without catalyst = 250 kJ/mol; with catalyst = 120 kJ/mol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the effect of the catalyst on the activation energy and on ΔH.
parts.answer: Activation energy is lowered (250 → 120 kJ/mol); ΔH is unchanged (−746 kJ/mol).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the activation energy of the reverse reaction without the catalyst.
parts.working: M1 reverse Ea = forward Ea − ΔH; A1 250 + 746 = 996.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the activation energy of the reverse reaction with the catalyst.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, in terms of particles and activation energy, why a reaction is faster at a higher temperature.
parts.answer: Particles have more kinetic energy and move faster; more collisions per second; a larger fraction of collisions have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy, so more successful collisions.
parts.working: B1 more energy / faster; B1 more frequent collisions; B1 more collisions with energy ≥ Ea.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a catalyst increases the rate, using the idea of activation energy.
parts.answer: It provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, so more collisions have enough energy to react.
parts.working: B1 alternative route, lower Ea; B1 more particles have enough energy.

practice.stem: On an energy profile the products are at 75 kJ/mol. The reaction has ΔH = −125 kJ/mol and a forward activation energy of 60 kJ/mol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy of the reactants.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy at the top of the curve.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the activation energy of the reverse reaction.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the reverse reaction is much slower than the forward reaction at the same temperature.
parts.answer: It has a much higher activation energy, so far fewer collisions have enough energy.

practice.stem: State whether each statement is true or false. Correct any false statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 'The activation energy of an exothermic reaction is always negative.'
parts.answer: False – activation energy is always positive (energy must be put in to start the reaction).

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'A catalyst makes ΔH more negative.'
parts.answer: False – a catalyst does not change ΔH; it only lowers the activation energy.

parts.label: c
parts.text: 'In an endothermic reaction, the products have more energy than the reactants.'

parts.label: d
parts.text: 'A reaction with a large activation energy is usually slow at room temperature.'
parts.answer: True – few collisions have enough energy.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A catalyst is added to a reaction. What happens to the activation energy and to ΔH?
A activation energy decreases, ΔH decreases
B activation energy decreases, ΔH unchanged
C activation energy unchanged, ΔH decreases
D activation energy increases, ΔH unchanged
parts.answer: B activation energy decreases, ΔH unchanged
parts.working: A catalyst gives an alternative pathway with lower activation energy; the energies of reactants and products are unchanged, so ΔH is unchanged.

practice.stem:
An energy profile is described by these points (energy in kJ/mol):
reactants 50; top of curve 230; products 180.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for the forward reaction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the activation energy of the uncatalysed forward reaction.

parts.label: c
parts.text: With a catalyst the peak is at 150 kJ/mol. Calculate the new activation energy.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the activation energy of the uncatalysed reverse reaction.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Explain why the catalysed reaction is faster.
parts.answer: More of the colliding particles have energy equal to or greater than the lower activation energy, so there are more successful collisions per second.
parts.working: B1 lower Ea; B1 more successful collisions per unit time.

practice.stem:
Data for four reactions:
Reaction P: Ea 95 kJ/mol, ΔH −210 kJ/mol
Reaction Q: Ea 40 kJ/mol, ΔH −60 kJ/mol
Reaction R: Ea 180 kJ/mol, ΔH −390 kJ/mol
Reaction S: Ea 120 kJ/mol, ΔH +45 kJ/mol

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which reaction would be fastest at room temperature? Explain.
parts.answer: Reaction Q; it has the lowest activation energy, so the greatest proportion of collisions have enough energy to react.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which reaction is endothermic?

parts.label: c
parts.text: For reaction P, calculate the activation energy of the reverse reaction.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Which reaction gives out the most energy when 1 mole reacts?

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For a reaction, the activation energy of the forward reaction is 85 kJ/mol and the activation energy of the reverse reaction is 35 kJ/mol. What is ΔH for the forward reaction?
A −50 kJ/mol
B +50 kJ/mol
C +120 kJ/mol
D −120 kJ/mol
parts.working: The peak is 85 above the reactants and 35 above the products, so the products are 85 − 35 = 50 kJ/mol above the reactants: endothermic, ΔH = +50. A has the wrong sign; C and D add the two activation energies.

practice.stem: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂. In one set of measurements, the activation energy per mole of H₂O₂ was found to be 75 kJ/mol without a catalyst and 23 kJ/mol with an enzyme catalyst.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy at the peak of each curve, taking the reactants as 0 kJ/mol.

parts.label: b
parts.text: ΔH for the forward reaction is −98 kJ per mole of H₂O₂. Calculate the activation energy, per mole of H₂O₂, of the reverse reaction with the enzyme.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the catalyst has no effect on the total energy released by decomposing a bottle of hydrogen peroxide.
parts.answer: The catalyst does not change ΔH; the energies of reactants and products are unchanged.

practice.stem:
Calcium carbonate is heated in a lime kiln to make quicklime: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂  ΔH = +178 kJ/mol
The kiln is heated by burning coal: C + O₂ → CO₂  ΔH = −394 kJ/mol

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the lime kiln must be heated all the time, but coal keeps burning once it has been lit.
parts.answer: Decomposition of CaCO₃ is endothermic: energy must be supplied continuously to provide the energy taken in (ΔH positive) and the activation energy. Burning coal is exothermic: once the activation energy is supplied, the energy released is enough to give other particles the activation energy.
parts.working: B1 decomposition endothermic; B1 continuous energy input needed; B1 combustion exothermic; B1 energy released supplies Ea for further reaction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe one way in which the energy profile for decomposing calcium carbonate differs from the profile for burning carbon.
parts.answer: Products are above the reactants (not below).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which process is endothermic?
A burning methane
B neutralising an acid with an alkali
C thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate
D respiration
parts.answer: C thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate
parts.working: Thermal decomposition needs continuous heating – energy is taken in. Combustion, neutralisation and respiration all release energy.

practice.stem: A student mixed 25 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid with 25 cm³ of aqueous sodium hydroxide in a polystyrene cup. Initial temperature of both solutions = 22.5 °C; highest temperature reached = 29.0 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the temperature rise.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic. Give a reason.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a polystyrene cup is used instead of a glass beaker.
parts.answer: Polystyrene is a good insulator, so less heat is lost to the surroundings.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one further improvement to make the temperature rise more accurate.
parts.answer: Put a lid on the cup / use a thermometer reading to 0.1 °C / stir / repeat and average.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Classify each change as exothermic or endothermic.
(i) burning petrol in a car engine
(ii) electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide
(iii) adding magnesium to dilute hydrochloric acid
(iv) melting ice

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define an exothermic reaction in terms of energy transfer.
parts.answer: A reaction that transfers thermal energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings increases.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which change is exothermic?
A steam condensing to water
B ice melting
C water evaporating
D ammonium nitrate dissolving in water
parts.working: Condensation releases energy as forces form between particles. Melting and evaporating take in energy; dissolving ammonium nitrate makes the water colder, so it is endothermic.

practice.stem: A self-heating can of coffee has a separate compartment containing calcium oxide. When a button is pressed, water mixes with the calcium oxide and the coffee warms up.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the energy transfer that heats the coffee.
parts.answer: Chemical energy stored in the reactants is released as thermal energy, which is transferred to the coffee (surroundings).
parts.working: B1 energy released by reaction; B1 transferred to surroundings/coffee.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the sign of ΔH for the reaction.

practice.stem:
A student records temperatures before and after four reactions, using the same volume of solution each time.
Reaction P: start 20.0 °C, end 34.0 °C
Reaction Q: start 21.0 °C, end 15.5 °C
Reaction R: start 20.5 °C, end 23.5 °C
Reaction S: start 22.0 °C, end 20.5 °C

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the temperature change for each reaction. Use + for a rise and − for a fall.
parts.working: B2 all four; B1 two or three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which reactions are endothermic?

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which reaction released the most energy?

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define an endothermic reaction.
parts.answer: A reaction that takes in thermal energy from the surroundings (temperature of surroundings falls).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the thermal decomposition of limestone in a kiln is endothermic.
parts.answer: Energy must be continuously supplied (by heating) to break it down.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name one other endothermic process that happens in nature.

practice.stem: Sherbet sweets contain citric acid and sodium hydrogencarbonate. When they dissolve and react on the tongue, the mouth feels cold and fizzy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State whether this process is exothermic or endothermic.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the mouth feels cold.
parts.answer: The process takes in thermal energy from the surroundings (the mouth), so the mouth's temperature falls.
parts.working: B1 energy taken in; B1 from the mouth.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
When ammonium nitrate dissolves in water, the temperature of the solution falls from 21 °C to 13 °C. Which statement explains this?
A The process is exothermic; energy is transferred to the surroundings.
B The process is endothermic; energy is transferred from the surroundings.
C The process is endothermic; energy is transferred to the surroundings.
D The process is exothermic; energy is transferred from the surroundings.
parts.answer: B The process is endothermic; energy is transferred from the surroundings.
parts.working: A fall in temperature shows thermal energy is taken in from the surroundings (the water), so the process is endothermic.

practice.stem:
A student dissolved 5.0 g of each salt in 50 cm³ of water and recorded the temperatures.
Ammonium chloride: start 21.0 °C, end 16.5 °C
Calcium chloride (anhydrous): start 21.0 °C, end 32.0 °C
Potassium nitrate: start 21.5 °C, end 15.5 °C
Sodium chloride: start 21.0 °C, end 20.5 °C

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the temperature change for each salt. Use + for a rise and − for a fall.
parts.answer: Ammonium chloride −4.5 °C; calcium chloride +11.0 °C; potassium nitrate −6.0 °C; sodium chloride −0.5 °C
parts.working: 2 marks all four; 1 mark for two or three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which salt dissolves in the most endothermic process?

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which salt would be most suitable for a self-heating food can? Explain.
parts.answer: Calcium chloride; it dissolves exothermically, giving the largest rise.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give two variables that should be kept constant.
parts.answer: Mass of salt; volume of water; starting temperature of water; type of container.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A physiotherapist at a cricket match uses an instant cold pack. Squeezing it lets ammonium nitrate dissolve in water. Explain how this cools the injury.
parts.answer: Dissolving is endothermic; it takes in thermal energy from the surroundings (the injured skin), lowering its temperature.
parts.working: B1 endothermic; B1 energy taken from surroundings/skin.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A hand warmer contains iron powder that reacts with oxygen from the air. State whether this reaction is exothermic or endothermic, and describe the energy transfer.
parts.answer: Exothermic; thermal energy is transferred from the reacting chemicals to the surroundings (hands).
parts.working: B1 exothermic; B1 energy to surroundings.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the iron in the hand warmer is a fine powder rather than a lump.
parts.answer: Larger surface area so it reacts faster and releases heat quickly.

practice.stem:
25.0 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid is placed in a polystyrene cup. Aqueous sodium hydroxide is added 5 cm³ at a time and the highest temperature is recorded after each addition.
Volume added/cm³: 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30
Temperature/°C: 21.0, 23.4, 25.8, 28.2, 30.6, 29.8, 29.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the volume of alkali at which the temperature was highest.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the temperature rises up to this volume.
parts.answer: Neutralisation is exothermic; more acid reacts as more alkali is added, releasing more energy.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the temperature falls after this volume.
parts.answer: All the acid has been neutralised; the extra cooler alkali absorbs energy / dilutes the mixture without reacting.
parts.working: B1 acid used up / no more reaction; B1 cooler solution added.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the volume of alkali needed to neutralise 25.0 cm³ of the acid.

practice.stem:
Different masses of ammonium nitrate are dissolved in 50 cm³ of water each time.
Mass/g: 2.0, 4.0, 6.0, 8.0
Temperature fall/°C: 2.1, 4.2, 6.3, 8.4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship between the mass of ammonium nitrate and the temperature fall.
parts.answer: The temperature fall is directly proportional to the mass.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the temperature fall for 5.0 g.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the cup must contain the same volume of water each time.
parts.answer: The same energy change in a different volume of water would give a different temperature change.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why a polystyrene cup is used.
parts.answer: It is an insulator, reducing energy transfer from the surroundings.

practice.stem: Classify each change in a kitchen as exothermic or endothermic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: burning natural gas on a stove

parts.label: b
parts.text: ice cubes melting in a glass of lassi

parts.label: c
parts.text: water vapour from the cooking pot condensing on a cold window

parts.label: d
parts.text: In terms of bond breaking and bond making, explain why burning natural gas is exothermic.
parts.answer: Energy is taken in to break bonds in methane and oxygen, but more energy is released when the bonds in CO₂ and H₂O form.
parts.working: B1 breaking takes in energy, making releases energy; B1 more released than taken in.

practice.stem:
Excess zinc powder was added to 50 cm³ of aqueous copper(II) sulfate in an insulated cup at time 0. The temperature was recorded every 30 seconds.
Time/min: 0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 3.5
Temperature/°C: 21.0, 27.5, 32.0, 34.0, 34.5, 34.0, 33.5, 33.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum temperature rise.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the temperature falls after 2.0 minutes.
parts.answer: The reaction has finished and heat is lost to the surroundings.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the ionic equation for the reaction.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The experiment is repeated with magnesium powder instead of zinc, using the same number of moles of metal. Predict how the maximum temperature rise would compare. Explain.
parts.answer: Larger rise; magnesium is further above copper in the reactivity series, so more energy is released.
parts.working: B1 larger; B1 magnesium more reactive.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Suggest why zinc was used in excess.
parts.answer: So that all the copper(II) ions react / the temperature rise depends only on the amount of copper(II) sulfate.

practice.stem: Respiration: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O   ΔH = −2800 kJ/mol

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the value of ΔH for photosynthesis, 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂, and say whether it is exothermic or endothermic.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy released per gram of glucose in respiration. [Mr glucose = 180] Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the energy level diagram for respiration.
parts.answer: Reactants (glucose + oxygen) at a higher level than products (carbon dioxide + water); downward arrow labelled ΔH = −2800 kJ/mol.
parts.working: B1 products lower; B1 ΔH labelled negative.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State where the energy for photosynthesis comes from.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
When two solutions are mixed in an insulated cup, the temperature falls from 22 °C to 15 °C. Which statement is correct?
A ΔH is negative and the products have less energy than the reactants.
B ΔH is positive and the products have more energy than the reactants.
C ΔH is positive and energy is transferred to the surroundings.
D ΔH is negative and energy is taken in from the surroundings.
parts.answer: B ΔH is positive and the products have more energy than the reactants.
parts.working: A fall in temperature means energy is taken in from the surroundings: the reaction is endothermic, ΔH positive, and the products store more energy. C has the right sign but the wrong direction of energy transfer.

practice.stem: Experiment 1: 25 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid was mixed with 25 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide in an insulated cup. The temperature rose by 6.8 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Experiment 2 used twice the concentration of each solution. Predict the temperature rise and explain.
parts.answer: 13.6 °C; twice as many moles react in the same volume (mass) of solution, so twice the energy heats the same mass.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Experiment 3 used the original concentrations but 50 cm³ of each solution. Predict the temperature rise and explain.
parts.answer: 6.8 °C; twice the energy is released but it heats twice the volume of solution, so the temperature change is the same.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student says that dissolving ammonium nitrate is not a chemical reaction, but it still has a ΔH. Explain, in terms of bonds or forces, why the process is endothermic.
parts.answer: More energy is needed to separate the ions in the lattice (overcome the attractions) than is released when they become surrounded by water molecules.
parts.working: B1 energy taken in to separate ions; B1 greater than energy released when ions interact with water.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why evaporation of sweat cools the body, linking your answer to whether evaporation is exothermic or endothermic.
parts.answer: Evaporation is endothermic; energy needed to overcome the forces between water molecules is taken from the skin.
parts.working: B1 endothermic; B1 energy from the skin.

practice.stem:
Energy released on complete combustion:
methane, CH₄: 890 kJ/mol
butane, C₄H₁₀: 2877 kJ/mol
hydrogen, H₂: 286 kJ/mol

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy released per gram for each fuel. Give your answers to 3 significant figures. [Mr: CH₄ = 16, C₄H₁₀ = 58, H₂ = 2]
parts.answer: methane 55.6 kJ/g; butane 49.6 kJ/g; hydrogen 143 kJ/g

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason why hydrogen is not yet widely used for cooking in Pakistan, despite your answer to (a).
parts.answer: It is difficult/expensive to store and transport (low density gas, flammable/explosive); most is made from fossil fuels.

practice.stem:
At the high temperatures inside a car engine, nitrogen reacts with oxygen: N≡N + O=O → 2 N=O
Bond energies in kJ/mol: N≡N 945, O=O 498, N=O 630

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy needed to break the bonds in the reactants.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy released when the bonds in the products form.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the energy change, ΔH, for the reaction and state whether it is exothermic or endothermic.
parts.working: M1 1443 − 1260; A1 +183 kJ/mol with endothermic (more energy taken in to break bonds than released making bonds).

practice.stem:
In the Haber process: N≡N + 3 H–H ⇌ 2NH₃ (each NH₃ has three N–H bonds)
Bond energies in kJ/mol: N≡N 945, H–H 436, N–H 391

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy change, ΔH, for the reaction in kJ/mol.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the sign of ΔH for the reverse reaction, the decomposition of ammonia.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement about bond energies is correct?
A Breaking bonds releases energy and making bonds takes in energy.
B Breaking bonds takes in energy and making bonds releases energy.
C Both breaking and making bonds release energy.
D Both breaking and making bonds take in energy.
parts.answer: B Breaking bonds takes in energy and making bonds releases energy.
parts.working: Energy must be supplied to pull atoms apart (endothermic); energy is released when bonds form (exothermic). A is the common reversal.

practice.stem: For a reaction, the total energy taken in to break bonds is 1850 kJ/mol and the total energy released in making bonds is 2100 kJ/mol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for the reaction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic and explain your answer.
parts.answer: Exothermic; more energy is released in making bonds than is taken in to break bonds (ΔH negative).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what happens to the temperature of the surroundings during the reaction.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For an exothermic reaction, which statement about bond energies is correct?
A The energy released in making new bonds is greater than the energy taken in to break bonds.
B The energy taken in to break bonds is greater than the energy released in making new bonds.
C No bonds are broken; energy is only released as new bonds form.
D The energy taken in to break bonds equals the energy released in making new bonds.
parts.answer: A The energy released in making new bonds is greater than the energy taken in to break bonds.
parts.working: ΔH = energy in (bond breaking) − energy out (bond making); this is negative (exothermic) when more energy is released in making bonds. B describes an endothermic reaction.

practice.stem:
Hydrazine can be made from nitrogen and hydrogen: N≡N + 2 H–H → H₂N–NH₂
Hydrazine contains one N–N bond and four N–H bonds.
Bond energies in kJ/mol: N≡N 945, H–H 436, N–N 158, N–H 391

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy needed to break the bonds in the reactants.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy released when the bonds in the product form.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for the reaction and state whether it is exothermic or endothermic.

practice.stem:
Chlorine reacts with fluorine to form chlorine monofluoride: Cl–Cl + F–F → 2 Cl–F
Bond energies in kJ/mol: Cl–Cl 242, F–F 158, Cl–F 253

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy taken in to break the bonds in the reactants.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy released in forming the bonds in the product.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for the reaction.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State what happens to the temperature of the surroundings as the reaction takes place, and why.
parts.answer: It rises: the reaction is exothermic and releases energy to the surroundings.

practice.stem:
Natural gas (methane) burns in a gas stove:
CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
Bond energies in kJ/mol: C–H 413, O=O 498, C=O 805, O–H 464

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total energy needed to break all the bonds in the reactants.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total energy released when the bonds in the products form.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the energy change for the reaction, in kJ/mol.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain, in terms of bond breaking and bond making, why this reaction is exothermic.
parts.answer: More energy is released when the new bonds in CO₂ and H₂O form than is taken in to break the bonds in CH₄ and O₂.
parts.working: B1 bond breaking takes in energy, bond making releases energy; B1 more released than taken in.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Hydrogen iodide decomposes: 2HI → H₂ + I₂
Bond energies in kJ/mol: H–I 299, H–H 436, I–I 151
What is the energy change for this reaction?
A −11 kJ/mol
B +11 kJ/mol
C +148 kJ/mol
D −288 kJ/mol
parts.working: Broken: 2 × 299 = 598; formed: 436 + 151 = 587; ΔH = 598 − 587 = +11 kJ/mol (endothermic). A has the sign reversed (formed − broken).

practice.stem:
A city plans hydrogen-powered buses. Hydrogen burns in oxygen to form water.
Bond energies in kJ/mol: H–H 436, O=O 498, O–H 464

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for the reaction 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O in kJ/mol.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy released per mole of hydrogen, H₂, burned.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one advantage of hydrogen as a fuel for buses.
parts.answer: The only product is water (no carbon dioxide).

practice.stem:
Methane reacts with chlorine: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl
Bond energies in kJ/mol: C–H 413, Cl–Cl 242, C–Cl 327, H–Cl 431

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for this reaction in kJ/mol.
parts.working: M1 broken (one C–H and Cl–Cl): 413 + 242 = 655; M1 formed C–Cl 327 + H–Cl 431 = 758; A1 −103

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the condition needed for this reaction to happen.

practice.stem: Bond energies in kJ/mol: H–H 436, F–F 158, H–F 568, Cl–Cl 242, H–Cl 431

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for H₂ + F₂ → 2HF in kJ/mol.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl in kJ/mol.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which reaction releases more energy? Use the bond energies to explain why.
parts.answer: Hydrogen with fluorine; the F–F bond is weak (easy to break) and the H–F bond is very strong (much energy released on forming).
parts.working: B1 fluorine reaction; B1 reference to weak F–F and/or strong H–F.

practice.stem:
Methanol is being tested as a cheaper fuel for vehicles: 2CH₃OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 4H₂O
One CH₃OH molecule contains 3 C–H, 1 C–O and 1 O–H bond.
Bond energies in kJ/mol: C–H 413, C–O 358, O–H 464, O=O 498, C=O 805

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy needed to break all the bonds in 2CH₃OH + 3O₂.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy released when the bonds in 2CO₂ + 4H₂O form.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for the combustion of one mole of methanol.

practice.stem:
Some shipping companies are testing ammonia as a fuel: 4NH₃ + 3O₂ → 2N₂ + 6H₂O
Bond energies in kJ/mol: N–H 391, O=O 498, N≡N 945, O–H 464

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for the reaction as written.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy released per mole of ammonia burned.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one environmental advantage of ammonia over diesel as a ship fuel.
parts.answer: No carbon dioxide is produced (no carbon in the fuel).

practice.stem:
Ethene reacts with hydrogen using a nickel catalyst: CH₂=CH₂ + H–H → CH₃–CH₃
Bond energies in kJ/mol: C=C 612, C–C 347, C–H 413, H–H 436

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for the reaction, in kJ/mol.
parts.working: M1 broken C=C 612 + H–H 436 = 1048 (C–H unchanged); M1 formed C–C 347 + 2 × C–H 826 = 1173; A1 −125. (Counting all bonds gives the same answer.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why bond-energy calculations give only an approximate value of ΔH.
parts.answer: Bond energies are average values taken from many different compounds.

practice.stem:
H₂ + Br₂ → 2HBr   ΔH = −103 kJ/mol
Bond energies in kJ/mol: H–H 436, Br–Br 193

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the bond energy of the H–Br bond.
parts.working: M1 ΔH = broken − formed so −103 = (436 + 193) − 2x; M1 2x = 732; A1 x = 366

parts.label: b
parts.text: Is the H–Br bond stronger or weaker than the H–Cl bond (431 kJ/mol)? Explain.
parts.answer: Weaker; less energy is needed to break it.

practice.stem:
Ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH, is used as a fuel in some countries:
C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O
Ethanol contains 5 C–H, 1 C–C, 1 C–O and 1 O–H bond.
Bond energies in kJ/mol: C–H 413, C–C 347, C–O 358, O–H 464, O=O 498, C=O 805

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy needed to break all the bonds in one mole of ethanol and three moles of oxygen.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for the combustion of ethanol in kJ/mol.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the energy released per gram of ethanol. [Mr ethanol = 46] Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

practice.stem:
Hydrogen peroxide decomposes: 2H–O–O–H → 2H–O–H + O=O
Bond energies in kJ/mol: O–H 464, O–O 146, O=O 498

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for this reaction in kJ/mol.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The value measured by experiment is −196 kJ/mol. Suggest why the calculated value is different.
parts.answer: Bond energies are average values / the substances are not all gases in the experiment.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Manganese(IV) oxide speeds up this reaction. State its effect on the value of ΔH.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Ethene reacts with bromine: CH₂=CH₂ + Br–Br → CH₂Br–CH₂Br
Bond energies in kJ/mol: C=C 612, C–C 347, Br–Br 193, C–Br 276
The C–H bonds are unchanged. What is the energy change for the reaction?
A −94 kJ/mol
B +94 kJ/mol
C +182 kJ/mol
D −899 kJ/mol
parts.working: Broken: C=C + Br–Br = 612 + 193 = 805. Made: C–C + 2 C–Br = 347 + 552 = 899. ΔH = 805 − 899 = −94 kJ/mol. B reverses the sign; C uses only one C–Br bond (805 − 623); D gives only the energy released.

practice.stem:
Ethyne is burned in oxy-acetylene welding torches: C₂H₂ + 2½O₂ → 2CO₂ + H₂O  ΔH = −1256 kJ/mol
Ethyne contains two C–H bonds and one C≡C bond.
Bond energies in kJ/mol: C–H 413, O=O 498, C=O 805, O–H 464

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total energy released in making the bonds in the products.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use ΔH to calculate the bond energy of the C≡C bond in ethyne.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The C≡C value in data books is a little different. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Bond energies are average values from many compounds.
